Sūrat al-Furqān

The majority of scholars held that it is Meccan without qualification. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) and Qatādah said that it is Meccan except for three verses revealed in Medina, namely ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Furqān: 68–70]. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is Madinan except for its beginning up to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿nor resurrection﴾ [al-Furqān: 3], which is Meccan. The number of its verses is seventy-seven, without disagreement, as mentioned by al-Ṭabarsī and al-Dānī in the book al-ʿAdad (The Counting).

When, at the end of the preceding sūrah, Allah, majestic is His majesty, mentioned the obligation of the believers to follow the Messenger (ﷺ), praised those who followed, and warned those who opposed, He opened this sūrah with what indicates His exaltation, majestic is His majesty, above all else in His essence, attributes and actions, or indicates the abundance and permanence of His goodness, and that He sent down the Criterion (al-Furqān) upon His servant so that he might be a warner to the worlds, in hope of His goodness and as a warning against His punishment, majestic is His majesty. Also in this sūrah is, by way of reinforcing what was in the preceding one, praise of the Messenger (ﷺ), so He, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾. That is, He is exalted, majestic is His majesty, in His essence, attributes and actions, in the most perfect and most eloquent manner, as is indicated by the attribution of the form of tafāʿul (تَفاعَلَ) to Him. This verb is, for the most part, not attributed to anyone other than Him, exalted is He, and it is not inflected: no present tense and no imperative are formed from it, at least for the most part. Otherwise, Ubayy recited, as will come, if Allah wills, ﴿tabārakat al-arḍu wa man ḥawlahā﴾ (the earth and whoever is around it blessed itself). It has come, as in al-Kashf, as tabārakati al-nakhlah, meaning it rose high. al-Aṣmaʿī related that a Bedouin climbed a hill and said to his companions: "Tabārakat ʿalaykum" (it has risen above you). And the poet said:

"To the trunk, the trunk of the palm-tree, the blessed one (al-mutabārik)."

al-Khalīl said: the meaning of tabāraka is tamajjada (He is glorified). al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: taʿaẓẓama (He is magnified), and this is close to close. From al-Ḥasan and al-Nakhaʿī, the meaning is that His goodness and His bounty increase and multiply; this is one of two narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both). The second is that the meaning is "He has not ceased, and does not cease."

The verification of this: tabāraka derives from barakah, which is originally taken from baraka al-baʿīr (the camel crouched), and it is the chest of the camel. From it, baraka al-baʿīr when he lays his chest upon the ground. The sense of constancy (al-luzūm) is considered in it, so one says barākāʾ al-ḥarb (the stand of battle) and barakāʾuhā, for the place where the champions remain. The water-holding pond is called barakah, like sidrah, then it was applied to the firm establishment of divine goodness in a thing, like the firm establishment of water in the pool. It was also said: that in which that goodness is is mubārak (blessed). Since divine goodness proceeds from where one does not perceive it and in a manner that cannot be counted or confined, everything in which one observes an unperceived increase is called mubārak and has barakah. Whoever considers the sense of constancy, like Ibn ʿAbbās on the basis of his second narration, said: the meaning is "He has not ceased and does not cease," or something similar. Whoever considers the sense of increase divides into two groups. One group took it with respect to the perfection of the essence in itself and the deficiency of what is other than it, and so they explained it by taʿālī (exaltation) and the like. Another group took it with respect to the perfection of action, and so they explained it as the increase and multiplication of goodness. No consideration is given to the change that is based on the sense of constancy, because of the scant benefit of speech in it and the unsuitability of that meaning to what follows. From here the majority left the meaning between what we mentioned first and what was narrated from al-Ḥasan and those with him. The ordering of His description, by the word ﴿tabāraka﴾ in the first meaning, to His sending down the Criterion, is because it speaks of the loftiness of His rank, glorified is He, the sublimity of His attributes, and the foundation of His actions upon the basis of wisdom and benefits, free entirely from any flaw. The arrangement of that with the second meaning upon it is because of the abundant goodness in it, for it is guidance and mercy to the worlds, and in it is that by which the affairs of livelihood and the Hereafter are ordered. Both meanings are fitting to the context, but the first was preferred as more suitable on account of the words ﴿that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾. al-Ṭībī said: in singling out "warner" rather than "bearer of good tidings," there is the manner of excellence in opening the discourse, and an announcement that this sūrah contains mention of the opponents who take for Allah, exalted is He, a son and a partner, who defame His books, His messengers and the Last Day [al-Nisāʾ: 136]. This meaning supports the interpretation of tabāraka as "increasing beyond everything and exalted above it in His attributes and actions, majestic is He," for it conveys the attribute of majesty and awe and announces from the outset His exaltation, glorified is He, above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation. It is of great beauty.

al-Furqān is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of farraqa al-shayʾ (he separated the thing) and ʿanhu, when he detached it. It is also said, as al-Rāghib mentioned, farraqat bayna al-shayʾayn (she distinguished between the two things) when she separated between them, whether that separation is by a division perceived by sight or by a division perceived by insight. Al-tafrīq has the same meaning, except that it indicates multiplicity while the other does not. It was said that al-farq is in meanings and al-tafrīq is in bodies. The intended meaning is the Qur'an, and it is so called because it separates truth from falsehood by the clarity it contains, or separates the one who is right from the one who is wrong because of its miraculousness, or because part of it is separated from part in itself or in its revelation, in that it was not sent down all at once like the other books. What the Ṣūfiyyah say about this will come, if Allah wills. So it is a maṣdar with the sense of the active participle, or with the sense of the passive participle. It is permissible that this is from the pattern of "hiya iqbālun wa idbār" (it is coming and going), so do not be heedless.

By "His servant" is meant our Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ). The use of this title for him, upon him be prayer and peace, is to honour him and to announce that he, Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, is at the highest rank of servanthood, and to alert that the Messenger is only a servant of the One who sent him, in refutation of the Christians. It was also said: the intended meaning of al-Furqān is all the heavenly books, since they all separate truth from falsehood; and by "His servant" is meant the collective, including all upon whom they were revealed. It was supported by the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr, "ʿalā ʿibādihī" (upon His servants). The distance in this is not hidden. The intended meaning of "servants" in the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr is the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, and his community. Revelation (al-inzāl), just as it is attributed to the Messenger (ﷺ), is attributed to his community, as in His saying, ﴿We have indeed sent down to you﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 10; al-Nūr: 34], because it reaches them and its descent is for their sake, so it is as though it was sent down upon them, even though its actual sending down was upon him, upon him be prayer and peace. It was also said that the intended meaning of the plural is himself (ﷺ), and it was expressed with it as glorification. The pronoun in "yakūna" refers to "His servant." It was said it refers to "al-Furqān," and the attribution of warning to it is metaphorical. It was said it refers to the relative pronoun, which is an expression of Him, exalted is He. This was preferred because it is the principal subject to which the verb is attributed, and warning is among His attributes, mighty and majestic is He, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed We were warners﴾ [al-Dukhān: 3]. It was said it refers to the sending down (al-tanzīl) understood from "nazzala," but the first is what comes to mind most readily, and it is what what follows requires. "Nadhīr" (warner) is an adjective in the form of the attributive adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah) in the sense of "mundhir" (one who warns).

It is permitted that it be a maṣdar in the sense of "indhār" (warning), like "nakīr" in the sense of "inkār" (denial). The rule of informing by a maṣdar is well known. Warning (al-indhār) is an informing containing intimidation, and its opposite is good tidings (al-tabshīr). He did not address it, because of what passed just now. By "the worlds," according to a group, is meant, of the worlds, humans and jinn, of those contemporary with him (ﷺ) up to the Day of Resurrection. This is supported by the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr, "lil-ʿālamīn" (for the worlds) referring to jinn and humans. His being sent to them is known by necessity from the religion, so whoever denies it disbelieves. Likewise the angels, peace be upon them, as has been preferred by a group of verifying scholars like al-Subkī and those who followed him, who refuted those who disagreed. Some asserted that the verse indicates this, because the "world" (ʿālam) is everything other than Allah and His attributes, the Most High, so it includes the angels, peace be upon them. The form of "all rational beings" is used by way of predominance (taghlīb), or as a plural after restricting it to the rational.

As for one who says, like al-Bārizī, that he, upon him be prayer and peace, was sent even to inanimate things, after making them perceiving on the apparent sense of the report, "and I was sent to all creation" (Muslim), which was not restricted, and he was content with predominance; the benefit of his being sent to the infallible and to the non-accountable is seeking their submission, for his nobility upon him be prayer and peace, and their entry under his call and their following him, honouring him above the rest of the messengers, peace be upon them.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before what it governs is for suspense (tashwīq) and for the sake of the rhyme (fawāṣil), and also for restriction according to the first view regarding "the worlds." The highlighting of the sending down of the Criterion in the form of the relative clause, whose proper function is that its content be known to the hearer as established for the relative pronoun, despite the disbelievers denying it, is to treat it as a known, accepted matter, to alert to the strength of its proofs and that it is such that hardly anyone could be ignorant of it, like His saying: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2, and elsewhere]. The same is said of its like among the relative clauses that the disbelievers deny. Some said: there is no need for what has been mentioned, for it suffices in the relative clause that it be known to the addressed hearer, and it is not required that it be known to every hearer. The addressee here is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he, upon him be prayer and peace, knows its establishment for the relative pronoun. In the commentary on al-Tashīl it is said that it is not required in it that it be known, and that the definiteness of the relative pronoun is like the definiteness of "al," which may be for specification (ʿahd) or for the generic (jins), and that its relative clause may be vague for the sake of glorification, as in the verse:

"If I am able to overcome, and desire overcomes, then like what I have met, desire overcomes its companion."

What was mentioned first, regarding treating it as the known, is more eloquent, because it is a metonymy for what was mentioned, fitting for refuting those who denied prophethood and the oneness of Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 2:

﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, to Him alone, exclusively and not to anyone else, neither independently nor in partnership, belongs the sovereignty (al-sultan al-qahir) and the overwhelming dominion over them, which necessitates complete power and absolute disposal over them, in bringing into existence, annihilating, giving life, causing death, commanding and forbidding, as His will dictates, a will founded upon wisdom and benefits. The place of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is in the nominative case, as it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is resumptive (mustanRafa), confirming what precedes it; or it is in the nominative as an adjective (na't) of the first relative pronoun, or as an explanation (bayan) of it, or as a substitute (badal) from it. What lies between them is not foreign, because it is part of the complement (al-silah) and connected to it, so separating the follower from the followed by it does no harm, as in al-Bahr. Or its place is in the nominative or accusative, in praise, with the implied meaning "he is" or "I praise more".

Al-Tibi preferred that its place is in the nominative as a substitute, and he justified this by saying: because it is necessary that the complement be known to the addressee, and the complement was not known to the obstinate opponents, so "Alladhi lahu" etc. is substituted as an explanation and elaboration. This is far-fetched from such a one, and Glorified is He, of whom nothing can be faulted. ﴿And has not taken a son.﴾ That is, no one has taken the position of a son. It has also been said: that is, He has no son, as those who say about the Messiah, Uzair and the angels, peace be upon them, what they say claim. ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe.﴾ The sentence is conjoined to what precedes it from the adverbial clause, and likewise His words, exalted is He: ﴿And has no partner in the dominion﴾, that is, the dominion of the heavens and the earth. It was singled out for mention, although what was mentioned about the exclusive ownership of both by Him, exalted is He, necessarily implies it with certainty, for the explicit refutation of the claim of the dualists who hold that there are multiple gods, and the rejection of it in their throats, and the emphasis on denying the taking of a son between them, serve to draw attention to its independence and originality and to guard against the assumption that it is a completion of the first. ﴿And He created everything﴾, that is, brought it into being in a manner proceeding according to the courses of measure and proportion, as His will, founded on profound wisdoms, required, such as the creation of man from specific materials and in determined forms and shapes. ﴿And determined it﴾, that is, prepared it for what He willed for it of properties and fitting actions, and the devising of diverse crafts, and the practice of various works, and so on. Thus there is no repetition in the verse, since it is clear that the measuring indicated by the creating, in the sense of proportioning, and the measuring expressed by its own word, in the sense of preparation, are two different things, and the creating in this case is in its literal sense. It is also possible that the creating is figurative, or rather a customary conventional transfer, in the sense of bringing into existence and originating, without the measure being considered in it, though it is not free of it; and for this reason the figurative usage is valid. The explicit mention of the measure then indicates that each one is intended in itself, so it is as if it were said: He originated everything and determined it in its origination, not bringing it into being unevenly, but bringing it into being balanced and proportionate. It has also been said that the second measure is the measure for remaining until the appointed term, so it is as if it were said: He originated everything according to the courses of measure, and sustained it until the appointed term. The first view is the one preferred by al-Zajjaj, and it is, as in al-Kashf, more evident. The fa' according to it is for sequence with order.

Some claimed that there is an inversion (qalb) in the speech, but even so this does not prevent the necessity of repetition without one of the aforementioned aspects, as is not hidden. The clause "and He created" etc. is conjoined to what came before, and in it is a refutation of the dualists who hold that the creator of evil is other than the creator of good. Its being known from what preceded does no harm, because it conveys a new benefit through its added meaning. It has also been said: it is a refutation of those who hold the Mu'tazilite belief regarding the voluntary acts of animals. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it is stated that it functions as a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it of the sentences arranged in the string of the complement, for His creation of all things in a wondrous pattern requires, just as His exclusive independence through the attributes of divinity requires, that everything else, whatever it may be, be included under His overpowering dominion, in such a way that nothing escapes it; and one who is such, how could it be supposed that he has a son or a partner in his dominion, glorified is He and exalted is He. Al-Tibi mentioned that His words, exalted is He: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ are a preparation and a introduction to His words, glorified is He: ﴿has not taken a son and has no partner in the dominion﴾, and He followed it with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He created everything﴾, because His being the originator of the heavens and the earth, their Creator and their Owner, is incompatible with taking a son or a partner. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth; how could He have a son?﴾ [al-An'am: 101], the verse. It may be said that this sentence is an explicit statement of what was already known, so that the censure of the polytheists may come with His words, glorified is He:

[Verse 3:] ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, gods who create nothing, while they themselves are created.﴾ This reading is the more apparent one. The pronoun in (*ittakhadhu*, "they have taken") refers to the polytheists, which is understood from His words, ﴿and He has no partner in the dominion﴾, or from the context, and from His words, ﴿a warner﴾. Al-Kirmani said: it refers to the disbelievers, who are included in His words, ﴿to the worlds﴾. The purpose is to relate their falsehoods concerning monotheism (*tawhid*) and prophethood and to demonstrate their invalidity, after He, glory be to Him, had explained the reality of the Truth at the beginning of the noble surah. That is: they have taken for themselves, going beyond Allah, who has been described with some of His great attributes, gods who are unable to create anything at all, while they themselves are created by Allah, the Exalted. Or, "they themselves are fashioned" by their worshippers through carving and sculpting.

The first meaning was preferred on the grounds that the discourse is more comprehensive under it and is not restricted to idols, unlike the second. Under the first meaning, the use of the present tense in ﴿they are created﴾ in the passive voice matches ﴿they create﴾ in the active voice, while also evoking the past state. The second meaning was preferred on the grounds that it is more suitable to the context, since those whom our Prophet ﷺ warned face to face were idol-worshippers, and the following rulings (*ahkam*) are more fitting for them. Indeed, under it, "creation" is interpreted as *iftial* (fabrication), as in His words, ﴿and you fabricate a lie﴾, since this is what can be correctly attributed to others besides Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Likewise, "creation" in the sense of measuring (*taqdir*) is found in the verse of Zuhayr:

*"Indeed you measure what you measure, and some of the people measure but do not carry it through."*

What is understood from it is bringing a thing into being, determined by a measure, as is the intended meaning of the preceding (sense). Interpreting it in that way also, as al-Zamakhshari did, is far-fetched, so it is said. It was objected that it is possible that this apparent sense is intended, and that the idols, in their essences, forms and shapes, are created by Allah, the Exalted, according to the People of Truth (*ahl al-haqq*), because the actions of servants, and what follows from them and arises from them of effects, are created by Him, the Mighty and Majestic, according to them, as has been verified. Indeed, if it were said that this meaning is specifically intended in that sense, it would not be far-fetched.

His words, the Exalted, ﴿and they do not possess for themselves any harm or benefit﴾, are to explain their state after their creation and existence. The meaning is: they are unable to exercise any power over any harm, so as to repel it from themselves, nor over any benefit, so as to bring it to themselves. Since repelling harm is more important and more beneficial, He mentioned their inability to do so first. It was also said: "for themselves" (*li-anfusihim*) is to indicate the extreme of their incapacity, because whoever is unable to do that concerning himself is, by a fortiori reasoning, even more unable to do it concerning others.

Whoever restricted the rulings to idols said: this is to explain what was not indicated by what came before of the levels of their incapacity and weakness, for some created beings who are unable to create may well possess the ability to repel harm and bring benefit in general, such as animals. It may be said: exercising power over harm and benefit, by repelling and bringing, in an absolute sense, is truly only for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as His words to His Prophet ﷺ indicate, the Glorified: ﴿Say: I possess for myself no benefit or harm except what Allah wills﴾ [al-A'raf: 188]. And His words, the Exalted: ﴿and they do not possess death or life or resurrection﴾, meaning they are unable to exercise power over any of these, by causing the living to die and bringing the dead to life in this world, or resurrecting them in the Hereafter. This is to state explicitly their incapacity regarding each of what has been mentioned in detail, and to alert that the god must be capable of all of that. The mention of death first is in keeping with the mention of harm before it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 4:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "This is nothing but a fabrication."﴾ The speakers, as Jami' (a group of scholars) transmitted from Qatada, are the polytheists of the Arabs, not all disbelievers, by the indication of their claim that some People of the Book were helping the Prophet ﷺ. Some narrations name among them al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abd Allah ibn Umayya, and Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid. It is also possible that what is meant is their extremists, such as these, and those who joined them. A report from Ibn Abbas supports this. It is also reported from al-Kalbi and Muqatil that the one who said it was al-Nadr, and the plural form is used because the rest supported him in that. Whoever restricts the pronoun in (ittakhadhu) [the verb "they took"] to the polytheists of the Arabs and makes the relative pronoun here refer to all of them, has placed the relative pronoun in the position of their pronoun in order to censure them through what is in the relative clause (sila, the clause following the relative pronoun), and to indicate that what they uttered is great disbelief. In the word ﴿this﴾ there is a lowering of the rank of what is pointed to; that is, they said: "This is nothing but a lie, turned away from its true course." ﴿It is a fabrication he has invented﴾: they mean that he invented it as a messenger of God ﷺ, and that it was not sent down to him, peace be upon him. ﴿And others helped him with it﴾: that is, helped him in his fabrication and his invention of it, or in the falsehood. ﴿A different people﴾: they mean the Jews, who would convey to him ﷺ the reports of the earlier nations, and he ﷺ would express them in his own words. It is also said they were Addas, and it is said they were Ayish, mawla (client) of Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza, Yasar, mawla of al-Ala' ibn al-Hadrami, and Jabr, mawla of Amir. They were People of the Book who read the Torah; they embraced Islam, and the Messenger ﷺ used to look after them, and so what was said was said. Al-Mubarrad said: by "a different people" they meant the believers, because "another" (akhar) can only be of the same kind as the first. But in this there is the point that sharing a quality is not necessary. Do you not see the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿a company fighting in the way of God, and another disbelieving﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13]. ﴿Then they have come﴾: that is, those who disbelieve, as is the apparent meaning. ﴿Injustice﴾ is in the accusative governed by "they have come." Jaa and ata are used in the sense of a verb of motion, so they take its transitivity, as al-Kisa'i said. al-Tabarsi preferred this view and cited the verse of Tarafa:

*"Without a fault I came to him, except that I begged, and I did not neglect the camels of Ma'bad."*

Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, so it is of the type of deletion and transitivity. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning "as wrongdoers." The first is preferable. The tanwin (nunation) on it is for magnification, meaning: they came with what they said as a dreadful, great injustice, whose measure cannot be reckoned, since they made the pure truth, which falsehood cannot reach from before it or behind it, into a fabricated lie from the side of a human. This is from the standpoint of its exquisite composition and its superb excellence, such that if humans and jinn were gathered to match it, they would be unable to produce anything like one of its verses; and from the standpoint of its including hidden wisdoms and rulings that bring about both religious and worldly well-being, and matters of the unseen, such that human intellects cannot grasp it, and the powers and measures cannot encompass its understanding. Likewise is the tanwin in ﴿and falsehood﴾: that is, a great lie that does not reach its extent, since they said what has no possibility of truth at all. The lie is called zur (falsehood) because it swerves (izwirar) from the direction of truth. The fa' (then) is for the ordering of what follows upon what precedes, but not on the basis that they are two really distinct matters, one occurring after the other or caused by it. Rather, the second is in reality the same as the first, and the ordering is only according to a conventional difference. Qad (indeed) is for confirming this meaning, for what came to him of injustice and falsehood is the very same as what was reported of them. But because it differs from it in concept and is more manifestly false, he ordered it with fa' as the ordering of a consequence upon its cause, to magnify its matter, as Shaykh al-Islam said. And it is said: the pronoun in ﴿they have come﴾ refers to "a different people," and the clause is part of the speech of the disbelievers, and they meant that those specific people came with injustice through their help, and with falsehood through what they helped with. And this, as you see, is weak.

[Page 236]

﴿And they said: "Tales of the ancients."﴾ After they had described the truth, which cannot be denied, as a fabricated lie produced with the help of humans, they explained, according to their corrupt assumption, the manner of that help. The discussion of *asatir* (tales, sing. *ustura*) has already occurred. It is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the nominal sentence), meaning: "This is," or "He is," or "It is, tales of the ancients." His exalted words, ﴿ktatabaha﴾ ("he had it written down"), are a second predicate. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) with an implied *qad* (قد). This was objected to on the grounds that when the governing element of a circumstantial clause is implicit (*ma'nawi*, i.e. understood in meaning rather than stated), it may not be omitted, as stated in *al-Mughni* (Ibn Hisham). But this is not accepted, as stated in its commentary.

It is also permitted for *asatir* to be the topic (*mubtada'*), with the clause ﴿ktatabaha﴾ as the predicate. Their meaning would then be: he wrote them down for himself. The attribution is figurative (*majaz*), as in "the governor built the city." The meaning could also be that he ordered them to be written down. Or it may be read literally as *uktutiba* (passive): "an order was given for writing," since the *ifta'ala* form has become established with this meaning, as in *uhtujima* ("he had himself cupped") and *uftusida* ("he had himself bled") when one orders cupping or bloodletting. It has also been said that they said this either because they supposed that he wrote in reality, or purely as slander against him, peace be upon him, based on their knowledge that he did not write (ﷺ). It has further been said that their meaning was to gather them, from *katabat al-shay'* (he gathered the thing). The majority of scholars hold the first view.

Talha read ﴿ktutiba﴾ in the passive voice, and the original form was: "a writer wrote it for him" (*iktatabaha lahu katibun*). He deleted the preposition *lam* and the verb reached the pronoun, so it became *iktatabaha iyyahu katibun* ("a writer wrote it for him"). Then he deleted the agent because the scholarly purpose did not depend on its specific identity. He then made the verb passive and attached it to the pronoun, which changed from an accusative, detached pronoun to an implicit nominative. This is based on the permissibility of making a non-explicit object take the place of the subject while an explicit object exists, here the pronoun referring to *asatir*. This is what al-Radi and others preferred, while the majority of the Basran grammarians hold that it is not permitted. For them, the explicit object must take the place of the subject, so one says: *uktutibat-hu* ("it was written for him"). This is the basis of al-Farazdaq's verse:

"And among us is he whom men chose for generosity and liberality, when the violent winds blow."

Here *al-rijal* is in the accusative case (*nasb*). According to the first view, the construction should have been *ukhtiyara-hu al-rijalu* with *al-rijal* in the nominative. The original form was *ikhtarahu min al-rijal mukhtar* ("he is chosen from among men"). It is clear that when the preceding verb governs it in this way, it reverts to what has been mentioned.

﴿So they are dictated to him﴾, i.e. those tales are cast upon him after they have been written down, so that he may memorize them from the mouths of the one who dictates them to him from that writer, since he was illiterate and could not receive them from him by reading. Thus *al-imla'* (dictation) means casting for memorization after writing. It is a metaphor, not the casting for writing, which is the familiar meaning. Thus it cannot be argued that the obvious form would be the reverse, namely "I dictated to him, so he writes them." Or the meaning is: he intended their writing, or requested their writing, so "I dictated to him" means dictated to him himself, or to his scribe. In that case, *al-imla'* remains in its apparent sense.

Talha and Isa read ﴿tutla﴾ with a *ta'* in place of the *mim*. ﴿Morning and evening﴾, i.e. continually, or before people disperse and when they return to their homes. By this they meant that the tales were dictated to him in secret, so that people would not learn the true situation. This is a tremendous act of audacity on their part. May God fight them: how are they deluded!

It is related from al-Hasan that the words ﴿ktatabaha﴾ and what follows are the speech of God, Mighty and Majestic, refuting them. This would only be valid if the hamza in ﴿ktatabaha﴾ were an interrogative (*istifham*) carrying the sense of denial. Its form would be like the statement of Hadrami ibn 'Amir, when he went out speaking in the assembly of a people while wearing two garments. Juz' ibn Sinan ibn Mu'lah said: "By God, Hadrami is glad at the death of his brother, that his heir..."

"Am I glad to plunder the noble, and to leave behind as inheritance a few slender, sharp-tipped arrows..."

These are among several verses. Al-Hasan rightly, according to what is in *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari), should stop at ﴿al-awwalin﴾ ("the ancients").

Say (to them) as a refutation of them and a confirmation of the truth: ﴿He who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth sent it down.﴾ His description (Exalted is He) as having encompassing knowledge of all things known, the hidden and the manifest, is mentioned a fortiori, to signal that what He sent down contains secrets concealed from human minds. It also carries an implicit allusion to requiting them for their crimes, which are recounted and which are among the things He knows. That is, it is not as you claim; rather, it is a matter from heaven, sent down by God, the One whose knowledge nothing escapes, and in which He deposited varieties of wisdom and secrets in a wondrous manner that minds cannot approach. He has defeated you all in its eloquence and rhetoric, and He informed you of its unseen future matters and hidden affairs, which no one can discover or grasp except by the success granted by God, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware of them. And when they intended "in the morning and the evening" (cf. 25:5) in secret from people, the place of the secret was increased in beauty. As for the concluding statement, ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, it serves to alert that they deserved punishment for the crimes recounted that they committed, but He delayed it for them, because He, glory be to Him, is eternally constant in forgiveness and mercy, which both result from the delay. It is as if it were said: He, majestic and exalted, is characterized by forgiveness and mercy continuously; therefore He does not hasten your punishment for what you are upon, even though you fully deserve it and He is entirely capable of it. Were it not for that, He would have poured punishment upon you in torrents. Al-Tayyibi mentioned that in this sense there is also the meaning of wonder, as in His saying: ﴿They have grown arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

It is also permissible that the statement be a metaphor (kinaya) for great capability to punish them, because forgiveness and mercy are attributed only to one who is able to punish. In choosing these attributes there is a rebuke to them and a reproach for their deed; that is, you, in your state, are such that the one who would take up your punishment has among his attributes forgiveness and mercy, and he is not (characterized) by that. The author of al-Fara'id said: It may be said that He mentioned forgiveness and mercy afterward so that they would know that these great sins, which exceed all bounds, are forgiven if they repent, that His mercy reaches them after them, and that they should not despair of His mercy, Exalted is He, because of what they have neglected, despite their persistence in their enmity and fierce hostility. And that, as you see, is (far-fetched).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 25, verses 7–8:**

﴿They said, "What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ etc. It was revealed concerning a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that: "'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu al-Bukhturi, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, Umayya ibn Khalaf, al-'As ibn Wa'il, Nabih ibn al-Hajjaj and Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj gathered together. Some of them said to others, 'Send to Muhammad (ﷺ), speak to him and argue with him until you have an excuse before him.' So they sent to him, 'The nobles of your people have gathered for you so that they may speak with you.' He, peace and blessings be upon him, came to them. They said, 'O Muhammad, we sent for you so that we might have an excuse concerning you. If you came with this message seeking wealth, we will gather for you some of our wealth. If you seek nobility, we will make you our chief. If you want kingship, we will make you king.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'There is nothing in me of what you say. I did not come to you with what I have brought seeking your wealth, nor nobility among you, nor rule over you. But Allah has sent me to you as a messenger, has revealed to me a Book, and has commanded me to be for you a bringer of good news and a warner. I have conveyed to you the message of my Lord and given you sincere counsel. If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it from me, I will be patient over the command of Allah, until Allah judges between me and you.' They said, 'O Muhammad, if you will not accept anything from us of what we have offered you, then, for your own sake, ask your Lord to send an angel with you who will confirm what you say and answer us on your behalf. Ask Him to give you gardens and palaces of gold and silver that will make you independent of what you seek. For you walk in the markets and seek livelihood as we do, so that we may know your merit and your rank with your Lord, if you are a messenger as you claim.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them, 'I will not do that. I am not one who asks his Lord for this, and I was not sent to you with this, but Allah has sent me as a bringer of good news and a warner.' Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed concerning their saying that: ﴿They said, 'What is this messenger?'﴾."

Etc.

This was brought here to narrate their offence concerning the specific matter of the one upon whom the Criterion (al-Furqan) was sent down, after narrating their offence concerning what was sent down. The interrogative particle *ma* (what) here carries the sense of denying and negating the occurrence, and it is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'); the preposition and its object following it (*li-hadha*) are related to an omitted predicate (khabar) of it. The *lam* has been written separated from this genitive in the script of the Imam, and this is a followed tradition (sunna mutaba'a). By the indication and by the expression "the Messenger," they intended mockery and derision.

The clause *ya'kulu al-ta'am* (eats food) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from *al-rasul* (the messenger), and its governing element is what governs the preposition, namely the sense of being established (al-istiqrar). It is also permitted that the preposition and its object be a sense of "what, and by what cause has this claimant come to be a messenger, while he eats food as you eat?" *Wa-yamshi fi al-aswaq* (and walks in the markets) is for seeking provision, as we do, according to directing the denial and negation toward the cause alone, while the causative (the effect) which is the content of the circumstantial clause is established.

Some people permitted making the clause a resumptive (isti'nafiyya) sentence, but what we have mentioned is preferable. Their intention is to deem the message improbable, since it is incompatible, in their view, with eating food and seeking livelihood. So it is as though they said: "If what he claims is true, why is his condition not similar to ours?" This is nothing but a sign of their blindness, the feebleness of their minds, and the shortcomings of their perception concerning sensible things. For the distinction of the messengers, peace be upon them, from others is not by bodily matters, but by soul-related matters, namely what Allah, the Exalted, has created in them of perfection, as His saying, the Exalted, indicates: ﴿Say, "I am only a human like you; it is revealed to me that your God is one God."﴾ [al-Kahf: 110]. The verse has been used as evidence for the permissibility of entering the markets for scholars and people of religion and righteousness, contrary to those who disliked it for them.

﴿"Why has an angel not been sent down to him, so that he might be a warner with him? Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden from which he eats?"﴾

This descends from what preceded. It is as though they said: "If there is no difference between us and him in eating and livelihood, then why is there not someone with him who differs from him in these, to be a support for him in warning? If that is not found, why does he not differ from us in one of them, namely seeking livelihood, by having a treasure thrown down to him from heaven, through which he is supported and his need of livelihood is entirely removed? If that is not found, then at least the need is removed in general by his having a garden from whose yield he lives, as the landowners and the well-off among people have." Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that by their saying "What is this messenger, who eats food and walks in the markets?" they meant that he should have been a king. Then they descended from his being a king to his being accompanied by a king who helps him, then they descended from that to his being supported by a treasure, then they descended and were content that he should have a garden from which he eats and earns his provision.

It has been said that only the last clause is a descent from them, and what precedes it is a resumptive sentence, an answer to what might be said: "How does his condition differ from yours, and by what means is this achieved and he is distinguished from you?" There is no concealing what is in this (i.e., its weakness).

*Fa-yakuna* (so that he might be) is in the accusative (naşb) as an answer to the exhortation (tahdid) (a construction after which a verb in the subjunctive follows as a response). It was read *fa-yakunu* in the nominative, transmitted by Abu Mu'adh, and it is explained as being coordinated with *unzila* (was sent down), because if the present tense occurred in its place, it would be nominative, since you say at the beginning *law yanzilu* with the nominative. Then it is coordinated upon it with *yulqa* and *takunu*, both of which are nominative. Or it is the answer to the exhortation with an implied *huwa* (he), i.e., *fa-huwa yakunu* (so he is one who would be). It is not permissible in such a construction to put *yulqa* and *takunu* in the accusative by coordinating them with *yakuna*, which is accusative, because these two are in the sense of what is demanded by the exhortation, not in the sense of the answer.

Perhaps the expression with the past tense first, although the original in the *awwalan* (first) that is used for exhortation or offering is that it follows the present tense, is because the sending down of an angel, regardless of whether he is with him, peace and blessings be upon him, as a warner, is a certain matter, one that he has always been claiming for himself (ﷺ). So they expressed the statement in the way he claims, though it was not accepted by them. In this there is a kind of mockery from them, may Allah fight them. In contrast, for casting down and the obtaining of a garden, the present tense is used in both, though it is the original. Perhaps the use of the present tense in both indicates continuous renewal, as though they asked for something that would never run out.

Ibn Hisham mentioned in *al-Mughni*, citing al-Harawi, that he said that *law la* comes for interrogation, and he gave two examples for it. One of them is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾. He was criticized for this, on the ground that it is a meaning which most grammarians do not mention. The apparent sense is that in the example mentioned it is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses?﴾ [al-Nur: 13]. He mentioned that it is in that case for reproach and censure, and then it is restricted to the past tense. It is not concealed that if by His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ he meant what occurred here, then the matter of its being for reproach and censure is in the utmost obscurity, so reflect.

Qatada and al-A'mash read *aw yakunu* with the *ya'* (third person), and Zayd ibn 'Ali, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab, Talha and al-A'mash read *na'kula* with the *nun* (first person plural), attributing the verb to the pronoun of the disbelievers who said what was mentioned.

﴿And the wrongdoers said﴾: they are the first ones who spoke. The apparent noun was placed in the position of their pronoun in order to brand them with wrongdoing in what they said, since it is a misguidance that goes beyond the limit of error, along with attributing to him (ﷺ) what reason and transmission both testify to his innocence of, or to what is not fit to be a basis for their claim of denying the message. It has been said: it is possible that what is meant is: "And the most extreme of wrongdoers among them said."

Whichever it is, the meaning is that they said to the believers: ﴿You follow only a man bewitched﴾, i.e., you do not follow except a man who has been bewitched, whose reason has been overcome. So the meaning of *sihr* (bewitchment) here is what causes disorder of the mind. It has been said that his *sihr* (windpipe/lung, a homonym) was struck, i.e., his lung, so his condition was disturbed, as one says *mar'us* (one whose head is struck) meaning his head was struck. It has also been said: he is bewitched by food and drink, i.e., he is nourished. Or *dhu sihr* (one who has a windpipe), with the *sihr* being an attribution, the object being in the relative sense, and they meant that he, peace and blessings be upon him, is a human like them. It has been said: *ayyu dhu sihr*, with the *sin* vowelled with a kasra, and they meant, may Allah fight them, "a sorcerer." The more apparent interpretation, according to what is in *al-Bahr*, is the first, and he mentioned that it is the more suitable for their state.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 9:

﴿Look how they have struck out for you the parables!﴾ This is an expression of amazement at the falsehoods they dared to utter, and a marvelling at them. That is, look how they have made for you strange statements, departing from sound reason, which, because of their strangeness, have become like proverbs, and how they have invented for you those odd attributes and states, far removed from occurring. ﴿So they have gone astray, and they cannot find a way﴾: they remain bewildered in error, finding no statement in discrediting your prophethood on which they can settle, even though it is false in itself. Thus the first "fa" (fa') is causal, and what "dallu" (they went astray) depends on is unstated. The second "fa" is explanatory, or the meaning is: they strayed from the path of truth, so they find no path that leads to it, for whoever is accustomed to employing these falsehoods can hardly be guided to employing sound premises. Thus the "fa" in both places is causal, and what "dallu" depends on is stated (implied), though the first is more likely. The intended meaning is the negation that what they brought is discrediting to his prophethood (ﷺ), and the negation that they have anything fit to discredit it, definitively, in the most emphatic manner. For discrediting it can only be done by discrediting the miracles that indicate it, and what they brought does not indicate that at all. And how could they possess what would indicate it?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 10:

﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He will give you palaces.﴾ That is, "Exalted is the One (Allah) who, if He wills, grants you in this world something better for you than what they proposed, namely that He would make for you the like of what He has promised you in the Hereafter of gardens and palaces." Thus is it in al-Kashshaf. And from Mujahid: "If He wills, He will make for you the gardens of the Hereafter and palaces in this world," and what is in it is not hidden. It was also said: the meaning is, "If He wills, He will make that in the Hereafter." The particle ﴿in﴾ (إنْ, "if") was placed before the verb of willing (al-mashi'ah) as an alert that this is not attained except by His mercy, may He be exalted, and that it is contingent upon the pure exercise of His will, glorified is He; and no one among the servants has any right upon Allah, mighty and majestic, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. The first (view) is more eloquent in rebuking the disbelievers and refuting them. And it does not refute, as Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed, His saying, exalted is He:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 11:**

﴿Nay, they denied the Hour.﴾ [Al-Furqan: 11] As you will know, God willing. The apparent meaning is that the reference is to what they proposed: the treasure and the garden, and the superiority of the garden that was mentioned, because it contains a multiplicity of gardens, flowing rivers, and lofty dwellings in those gardens, either with a dwelling in each of them or dwellings in all of them. [It is also superior because of] the treasure, since it is sought for its own sake in relation to him, whereas it is only sought to obtain the like of that. It is also more evident in splendour and more filling to the eyes of people than the treasure. The non-addressing of the answer to the first proposal is because its contradiction to the legislative wisdom (al-hikmah al-tashri'iyyah) is evident. Perhaps this is known from many of the verses, so it has been said.

In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud), [it is stated] that the reference is to what they proposed, namely that he (ﷺ) should have a garden from which he eats, and ﴿gardens﴾ is a substitution (badal) for ﴿better﴾, confirming its superiority over what they said, because that [previous proposal] was unrestricted by the condition of multiplicity and of flowing rivers. The linking of this to His will, may He be exalted, is to indicate that the non-making [of it] is due to the absence of a will that is founded upon wisdom and benefits. The non-addressing of the answer to the first two proposals is to draw attention to their going beyond the sphere of reason, and their being independent of an answer because their falsehood and their contradiction to the legislative wisdom are evident. What has a certain validity is only the last proposal, for it is not wholly contrary to wisdom, since some of the prophets, peace be upon them, were given, in this world together with prophethood, a great kingdom. End of quotation.

The Imam al-Razi attributed this explanation regarding the reference to the statement of Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. What was mentioned first was deemed the more probable by Abu Hayyan, who related it from Mujahid. It is related from Ibn Abbas that the reference is to what they reproached him for: eating food and walking in the markets. He said: "This is far-fetched." The Imam related it from Ikrimah. It seems to me that you prefer what the author of Irshad chose.

The apparent reading is that ﴿yaj'al﴾ (will make) is jussive (majzum), and so it is in a position of conjunction (ma'tuf) with the place of the conditional response, which is the making, which is itself also a response. It has been brought as a nominal-future sentence in accordance with the original form of the response. The rhetoricians (ahl al-ma'ani) mention that the original form of the two clauses of the conditional sentence is that both should be verbal and future in wording, just as they are future in meaning. Deviation from this in wording occurs only for a particular purpose.

[Page 240]

It seems that the expression according to this is in the two past-tense clauses in wording, in ﴿if He wills, He makes…﴾ etc., to increase the rebuke of the disbelievers regarding what they proposed of its kind. Since they did not propose what is of the kind of making palaces, this path was not taken with it, so consider this carefully. It has also been said: The apparent thing was that, when we mentioned the expression in the response with the past tense first, it should be expressed here too in the same way, but he turned to the present tense because the making of palaces in the gardens is future in relation to the making of the gardens. Then this conjunction requires that the palaces are not included in the good thing that is substituted for by His words, may He be glorified: ﴿gardens﴾. What was previously mentioned from al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) was an explanation of the resultant meaning with the aid of the context.

It is also permitted that it be in the nominative (marfu'), its lam assimilated into the lam of ﴿for you﴾. However, the assimilation of two identical letters when the first of them is vocalized is only the doctrine of Abu Amr. Those among the seven readers who read with the sukun (vowelless) were he, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Nafi'. In the narration of Mahbub from him (Abu Amr), he read with the raf' (nominative) without assimilation. This is the reading of Ibn Amir, Ibn Kathir, Mujahid, Humayd, and Abu Bakr. The conjunction according to this reading, and the possibility of assimilation, according to Ibn Atiyyah, is in view of the meaning of ﴿made﴾, because the place of the conditional response is a place of resumption (istinaf). Do you not see that a nominal sentence may occupy the place of a conditional response? Al-Zamakhshari said: It is conjoined to ﴿made﴾, because when the condition is in the past tense, it is permissible for its response to be either jussive or nominative, as in the saying of Zuhayr in praise of Harim ibn Sinan:

"And if a friend comes to him on a day of hunger,
he says: 'My wealth is neither absent nor withheld.'"

The doctrine of Sibawayh is that in such a case the response is omitted, and the present tense in the nominative is with the intention of fronting (taqdim). The Kufans and al-Mubarrad held that it is itself the response, and that it is by omission of the fa' (the particle of response). The construction according to the majority is eloquent and permissible in prose as in poetry. Abu Hayyan related from one of his companions that it is not permitted except in cases of poetic necessity, since it has come only in poetry. The complete discussion in establishing the doctrines belongs in its own place.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa said: The nominative is by resumption. It has been said that it is a grammatical resumption, and the statement is a promise to him (ﷺ) of making those palaces in the Hereafter, and for this reason he turned from the past tense to the present, which indicates the future. It has also been said that it is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), as if a speaker were saying: "What is the situation in the Hereafter?" So it was said: "He will make for you therein palaces." Some [commentators] made this making, by way of resumption, also in this world, meaning: "If He wills, He makes for you gardens in this world, and He will make for you palaces in those gardens," if the conditional is established. This is, as you see, unacceptable. It has also been said that the nominative is by conjunction to ﴿flow﴾ as a qualifier, with an implied ﴿and He will make in them﴾, i.e. in the gardens. But this is nothing.

Ubaydullah ibn Musa and Talhah ibn Sulayman read ﴿wa-yaj'ala﴾ with the accusative (nasb) by the implied ﴿an﴾. Its basis, according to what is related from al-Sirafi, is that since the condition was not jussive, it resembled interrogation. It has also been said that since it was not an actual state of the stipulation, it resembled negation. Sibawayh also mentioned the accusative after it and said that it is weak. It has also been said that the verb is in the nominative and its lam is vocalized with a fatha by imitation of the lam of ﴿for you﴾, similar to what has been said regarding the saying of the poet:

"Nothing prevented them from drinking from it except that a dove spoke
in the branches of the tree with its thorns."

It is said that he vocalized the ra' with a fatha, not by imitation of the hamzah of "anna," and this is one of two possibilities in the verse. The parallel of the verse in these readings is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"If Abu Qabus perishes, the springtime of people will perish,
and the sacred month."

"And we take after him the tail of a life,
its back shorn, without a hump."

For it is narrated in ﴿we take﴾ as jussive, nominative, and accusative.

﴿Nay, they denied the Hour﴾: a transition to relating another kind of their falsehoods, which is connected with the matter of the return (al-ma'ad), whereas what preceded was connected with the matter of monotheism (al-tawhid) and the matter of prophethood. Returning to what is connected with the preceding speech does no harm in this, and the variation in the styles of relating is due to the variation in what is related. How elegant is the opening of the relating of what is connected with the Hereafter with the transitional ﴿nay﴾ (bal).

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blazing fire﴾ and so on, are to explain what awaits them in the Hereafter because of it. That is: We have prepared for them a great fire, very intensely blazing, whose state is such-and-such because of their denial of it, as indicated by the placing of the relative pronoun in the place of the pronoun ﴿them﴾, or [it refers] to everyone who denies it, whoever he may be, and they are included in this by primary inclusion. The placing of ﴿the Hour﴾ in place of its pronoun is for the sake of emphasis in censure. Although this preparation is not caused by their denial of it alone, but rather their committing of falsehoods in the matter of monotheism and the matter of prophethood also shares in its causation, nevertheless, since the Hour itself is the immediate cause for their entering the blaze, it is pointed to by what was mentioned, indicating the causation of denying it for entering it, and it did not address any other causation. It has been said that whoever denies the Hour becomes like a designation for those polytheists who deny the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and who deny the Hour, meaning those who combine the three attributes, because denial of it is the most significant of their ugly attributes and the most frequently on their tongues.

For among the disbelievers there are those who associate partners with God and deny the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, but do not deny the Hour. So what is meant by ﴿those who deny the Hour﴾ is that category of the disbelievers. This is, as you see, unacceptable.

It has been said that His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay, they denied the Hour﴾, are conjoined to His words: ﴿And they said, "What is this Messenger…"﴾ and so on, and it is a turning away from that to what is more astonishing than it, meaning that the former is a denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), and this is a denial of God, glorified and exalted be He.

For in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: God said: "The son of Adam denied Me, and it was not for him to do so… up to His words, may He be exalted: 'As for his denial of Me, he claims that I cannot re-create him as I created him at first.'"

Its apparent meaning is that the astonishing thing about denying the Hour is that it is a denial of God, mighty and majestic. Some have said: The astonishing thing is that they denied God's power to re-create, despite what they witnessed in themselves and in the horizons, and what was fixed in their imaginations, namely that re-creation is easier than initial creation. This is not because it is a denial of God, mighty and majestic, for they did not hear the matter of the Hour except from the Prophet (ﷺ), so it is a denial of him, upon him be prayers and peace. You know that in the hadith there is an indication of what he approved.

It has been said: It is a turning away from that, meaning that they came with something more astonishing than it, in that they denied the Hour and rejected it, while the situation is that We have prepared for whoever denies it a blaze. For their boldness in denying it and their lack of fear of what has been prepared for whoever denies it, of kinds of punishment, is more astonishing than the previous statement. It was objected to that we do not grant that boldness in denying the Hour is more astonishing than boldness in the previous statement after the manifestation of the miracle, and we do not grant that the combining of lack of fear of what follows from it, if that consequence is in the Hour, benefits anything. There is consideration in this.

It has been said: It is a turning away from that, meaning that they came with something more astonishing than it, in that they denied the Hour which all the prophets, peace be upon them, have reported. So boldness in denying it is boldness in denying them, and boldness in denying them is more astonishing than boldness in the previous statement. It was objected to that their intended meaning in the previous statement is the negation of his prophethood, upon him be prayers and peace, and their denial of him. God forbid, and then God forbid that he lied in his claim of it, because his state does not contradict theirs, and he is characterized by what they claimed was incompatible with the Message. This exists and is established in all the prophets, peace be upon them. So his (ﷺ) denial of that is a denial of them too. Therefore denial of the Hour, according to what has been mentioned, is not more astonishing than the denial of the Prophet (ﷺ), since both denials share in being in the category of denial of all.

It has been said: It is connected to His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills…﴾ and so on, which came as a response to them, and the announcement of the promise of gardens and palaces in the Hereafter introduces an explanation that this is of no benefit, in the manner of the saying of one who said:

[Page 242]

"Turn aside to Nu'm and greet the abode's remnant traces,
what will you greet of the stone-heap and the rocks?"

The meaning is that they do not believe in the Hour, so how would they be convinced by this answer, and how would they accept the hastening of the like of what He promised you in the Hereafter? It has also been said: It is a turning away from the answer to an explanation of the motive that induced them to deny, and the meaning is: "Nay, they denied the Hour, so their horizons were confined to worldly pleasures, and they thought that honour lies only in wealth, and they took your empty hand of it as a means to denying you."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 12:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿When it sees them﴾ to its end, is a description of the blaze (al-sa'ir), and the feminine form is in consideration of the fire (al-nar). It has been said that it is because it is a proper name for Jahannam (Hell), as is related from al-Hasan. But in this there is an objection: if it were so, the definite article (al) could not be attached to it, and it would be barred from taking nunation (tanwin, i.e., it would be indeclinable) due to the feminine form and proper-noun status.

It is answered that the definite article is attached to indicate the descriptive sense, and that a name may take it for this reason, like al-Hasan and al-'Abbas. And also that it is declined (with tanwin) for the sake of harmony and observing the rhyme (fasila). Or because it is interpreted as a place (makan), and its feminine form here is for variety of expression (al-tafannun). The attribution of seeing to it is literal, according to what is apparent, and likewise the attribution of rage (taghayyuz) and roaring (zafir) that follows, since there is no impossibility in God, may He be exalted, creating the fire alive, enraged, and roaring against the disbelievers. So there is no need to interpret the apparent texts that indicate it has perception, such as this verse. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day We say to Jahannam, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30].

And His saying, peace and blessings be upon him, as in Sahih al-Bukhari: "The Fire complained to its Lord, saying: 'My Lord, some of me has consumed other parts of me.' So He permitted it two breaths: a breath in winter and a breath in summer."

And other than that. And since what al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated is authentic, through the chain of Makhul from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat from between the two eyes of Jahannam." They said: "O Messenger of God, does Jahannam have eyes?" He said: "Yes. Have you not heard God, may He be exalted, say: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place﴾ — and do they see them except with eyes?"

What we have stated is the correct view. Its attribution to it, not to them, is to signal that the rage and roaring come from it, due to the surging of its anger against them at the sight of them. ﴿From a distant place﴾ is the farthest distance from which it can be seen. It has been related that here it is a distance of five hundred years. Adam ibn Abi Iyas, in his Tafsir, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is a distance of one hundred years, and this is related from al-Suddi and al-Kalbi. It is also related from Ka'b. And it has been said:

a distance of one year. al-Tabarsi related it from Imam Abu 'Abd Allah, may God be pleased with him, and in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim he attributed it to al-Suddi and al-Kalbi. ﴿They will hear from it a raging﴾, i.e., a sound of raging, so that hearing can be connected to it. In al-Raghib's Mufradat: al-ghayz is the intensest anger, and al-taghayyuz is the manifestation of anger, and this may be accompanied by an audible sound, as in this verse. It has been said: hearing here means perception in general, as if it were said: they perceived from it a raging. ﴿And a roaring﴾: it is the exhaling of breath after a period, according to the Qamus. al-Raghib said: it is repeated breathing until the ribs swell from it, and its usage became common for the very sound of that breath. There is no doubt that it is among things to which hearing relates, and for this reason they raised the difficulty of connecting hearing to raging but not to roaring, and they interpreted it accordingly as you have heard. Some said: what is mentioned is of the kind of the poet's saying:

"And you saw your wife had become one wearing a sword and a spear,"

and it is by the estimate "they heard for it and perceived raging and roaring," and each is returned to what suits it. Some people said: the speech comes in the manner of hyperbole, by making raging—though raging is not among the things heard—heard. The tanwin in it and in "roaring" is for magnification.

Reports have come concerning its intense roaring, may God protect us from it. In a report that Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated with an authentic chain (page 243) from Ibn 'Abbas, that it roars a roar that no one remains who does not fear. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir and others narrated from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that he said concerning God's saying ﴿They heard for it﴾ etc.: Jahannam roars a roar, and no angel brought near nor prophet sent remains except that his limbs tremble, until Abraham, peace be upon him, kneels on his knees and says: "My Lord, I ask You today for nothing but myself."

Abu Nu'aym narrated from Ka'b who said: When the Day of Resurrection comes, God, may He be exalted, gathers the first and the last in one plain, and the angels descend in rows. God, may He be exalted, says to Gabriel, peace be upon him: "Bring Jahannam," and he brings it, and it is led by seventy thousand bridles, until when it is at a distance of a hundred years from the creatures, it roars a roar by which the hearts of the creatures fly. Then it roars a second time, and no angel brought near nor prophet sent remains except that he falls to his knees. Then it roars a third time, and hearts reach the throats and intellects are dumbfounded, and each person flees to his deeds. Until Abraham, peace be upon him, says: "By my friendship, I ask You for nothing but myself"; and Moses, peace be upon him, says: "By my intimate speech with You, I ask You for nothing but myself"; and Jesus, peace be upon him, says: "By what You honored me with, I ask You for nothing but myself, I do not ask You for Mary who bore me"; and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, says: "My nation, my nation, I ask You today for nothing but my own soul." Then the Majestic, great is His majesty, answers him: "Indeed My friends from your nation, there is no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve. By My might, I shall delight your eye." Then the angels, peace be upon them, stand before God, may He be exalted, awaiting what they are commanded. These reports clearly indicate that it is the Fire that roars, and that the roaring is in its literal sense.

Some claimed that its roaring is the sound of its flame and blazing. It has been said that each of the seeing, the raging and the roaring belongs to its guardians (zabaniya), and it is attributed to it by eliding a noun; this is transmitted from al-Jubba'i. It has been said that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿saw them﴾ is from His peace and blessings be upon him saying: "The fires of the believer and the disbeliever do not see each other," and the saying of the Arabs: "their dwellings see each other and face each other"; so one of them sees the other by way of metaphor by implication and figurative usage (al-isti'ara bi-l-kinaya wa-l-majaz al-mursal). It is permitted that it be from the category of imagery (tamthil). In any case, the meaning is "when it is in their sight." His saying, glorified is He: ﴿They heard for it raging﴾ is by likening the sound of its boiling to the sound of one who is enraged and his roaring; in it is an explicit or implicit metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya aw makniyya), and it is permitted that it be an allegorical image (tamthiliyya). Al-Zamakhshari mentioned this interpretation first. Some of the imams mentioned that this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, because they made structure (bunya) a condition of life.

In al-Kashf, it is more likely that this is not because structure is a condition. From where is the knowledge that the structure of the Hereafter's fire is such that it cannot prepare for life? Rather, it is because it is necessary to commit something contrary to the apparent meaning, by making a thing known for its inanimacy living and speaking, so it would be a report contrary to what is customary, or to carry it on the widespread allegorical imagery in their speech, especially in the speech of God, may He be exalted, and His messengers, peace be upon them. Since the aspect has become clear, then you be the judge in leaving the apparent meaning toward this or that. Opening this door does not lead to the doctrine of the philosophers, as the author of al-Intisaf imagined, and it does not contradict our being bound to the apparent meanings, for what they claim is also not apparent. End of quote. And you know, setting aside discussion of what has been mentioned, that taking it literally here is more forceful in conveying awe, and perhaps this eases the matter of a report contrary to what is customary. This holds if the preceding report is not authentic; but if it is authentic, then one should not depart from what it requires, and no one has a view against his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, for he is the most knowledgeable of the outward and inward of the Book.

And when they are thrown into a narrow place of it, bound together ﴿in chains﴾, they will call out there for destruction.

Let me be precise here, since the instructions require a faithful full translation rather than a condensed rendering. Here is the complete translation:

﴿And when they are cast into a place of it, narrow⁠—﴾ meaning: into a place, so it is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarfiyyah). "Of it" (minhā) is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relating to it, because originally it is an attribute (ṣifah). He also permitted that it be connected to "cast" (alqaw).

And His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿narrow﴾ is an attribute of "a place," restricting it, to add to the intensity of the distress together with the narrowness, just as the spirit (rūḥ) is with spaciousness; and this is the secret in describing Paradise as having a breadth equal to the heavens and the earth.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Yaḥyā ibn Usayd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿And when they are cast...﴾ etc., and he said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, they will be pressed in the Fire just as a peg is pressed into a wall." And from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it narrows upon them just as a spearhead (zajj) narrows in a spear.

al-Kalbī recited: "The lowest will be raised up by the flame, and the highest will be lowered down by those entering, so they will crowd together." Ibn Kathīr recited "ḍayqan" with the yā' sukūn.

﴿Bound together⁠﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "were cast," meaning: when they are cast into a narrow place from it while they are bound together, their hands having been tied to their necks with shackles. It was said: bound together with the devils in chains, each disbeliever with his devil; and their feet are in fetters. This is related from al-Jubbāʾī. Abū Shaybah, the companion of Muʿādh ibn Jabal, recited "muqarranūn" in the nominative, and Ibn Khālawayh attributed it to Muʿādh. Its explanation, according to al-Baḥr, is that it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "were cast," a substitute of an indefinite noun from a definite one.

﴿They will call out there⁠﴾ meaning: in that terrifying place, ﴿for destruction⁠﴾ meaning: ruin, as Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatādah said, and it is the object of "called out," meaning: they cry out and say, "Woe to us!" in the sense of "Come, this is your time." Many have said that the calling out carries the meaning of wishing, so they wish for destruction in order to be spared what is worse, as it is said: "Worse than death is that in which one wishes for death."

Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that "thubūran" be in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "called out," meaning: they called out a calling. It was also said: in the accusative as a verbal noun for a deleted verb, with the object of "called out" implied, meaning: they called upon one who would not answer them, saying, "We have perished a perishing." Both of these statements are as you see, and the calling for destruction is not restricted to the disbelieving humans, for it is also for Satan.

Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bazzār, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Baʿth transmitted with a sound chain from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The first to be clothed in a garment of Fire will be Iblīs. He will place it upon his two brows, and drag it behind him, and his offspring after him, while he calls out, "Woe to me!" and they say, "Woe to them!" until he stands at the Fire, and he says, "Woe to me!" and they say, "Woe to them!"'" — the hadith.

In some narrations, the first to say this is Iblīs, and then his followers follow him. Its apparent meaning includes the followers, both disbelievers of mankind and of the jinn, and it should not be imagined that this is restricted to some disbelievers of mankind, based on what was said: that the verse was revealed about Abū Jahl and his companions, as is not hidden. And His statement, Exalted is He:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 14:**

﴿Do not call out today for one destruction; call out for many destructions.﴾ This is in the sense of a hidden speech, and it is either in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿they called out﴾, meaning: they called out while being told this in reality, as is the apparent meaning, since the angels address them to alert them to the eternity of their punishment and that they will not be granted what they ask for, or that they will not attain the saving destruction that they wish for. Or it is a figurative depiction of their state, likened to the state of one who is told this without any actual speech or address taking place there, as has been said. That is, they called out in a state where they were deserving of being told this. Or it has no place in the grammatical structure (i'rāb), being coordinated with what precedes it: that is, when they are thrown into a narrow place there, they call out ﴿destruction﴾, and then it is said to them: ﴿Do not call out...﴾ etc. Or it is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnaf) that comes as an answer to a presumed question that the discourse implies, as if it were said: "What will be their response when they make the aforementioned call?" So it is said: "It will be said to them this." The purpose of this is to despair them of what they had hung their hopes upon of destruction, and to alert them that their punishment, which compelled them to that call, is everlasting, with no escape from it, in the most eloquent manner, since it indicates that what delivers one from the punishment they are in is ordinarily not delivering, and what would deliver is not possible. It is as if it were said: "Do not call out today for one destruction, for it will not rescue you," ﴿but call out for destruction﴾ and perdition ﴿many﴾, with no limit to its multiplicity, so that you may be freed by it. And how could a multitude of destructions be of any use?

*"Whoever does not die by the sword dies by other means; the causes multiply, but death is one."*

This is a subtle meaning that I do not know anyone has mentioned. It has also been said: the describing of destruction (thubūr) as many refers to the multiplicity of the expressions that signal it, as if it were said: "Do not say only 'Oh destruction!' but say 'Oh destruction! Oh perdition! Oh woe! Oh alas!' and so on," and this, as you see, is weak.

Page 245

Shaykh al-Islam said: He described it thus according to the multiplicity of the calls connected to it, not according to its multiplicity in itself, for what they call out for is one destruction in its own essence. But whenever a call from those many calls is connected to it, it becomes as if it were a different destruction from that to which another call is connected. Its realization is: do not call out to it as one call, but call out to it with many calls, for what you are in of punishment, given its extreme severity and long duration, requires repeating the call at every moment.
