Then he said: This indicates more strongly the horror of the punishment, and it is more suitable for it than making the multiplicity and renewal of the calling due to the multiplicity of the punishment through the multiplicity of its kinds and forms, or due to its multiplicity through the renewal of the skins, as is not hidden. As for what has been said, that the meaning is "you have fallen into a situation in which your destruction is not one, but rather many destructions, either because the punishment has kinds and forms, each kind being a destruction in its severity and horror, or because whenever their skins are cooked they are replaced with other skins, so there is no limit to their destruction," this does not suit the context. How so, when they are only calling for a destruction that would end their punishment and deliver them from it? So the answer must be a despairing of them regarding that, by explaining its impossibility and the permanence of what necessitates their calling for it, namely the severe punishment, to the end. He followed the view that the describing of destruction as many is according to the many calls with the statement that this does not fit the arrangement of the verse. Likewise, that it is according to the multiplicity of expressions signalling destruction, because the apparent wording would have been "a great many calls." As for his statement, "As for what has been said..." etc., it is not free of scrutiny, so consider it carefully.

Ali ibn Isa related that *mā thabaraka ʿan hādhā al-amr* means: what diverted you from this matter. He also permitted that thubūr in the verse may be of this kind, as if they regretted what they had done and said: "Divert him from obedience to Allah, the Exalted," just as one says "Woe to my regret!" So they were answered with what they were answered. The restriction of the prohibition and command to "today" is for greater intensification of the terror and horror, and as an alert that it is not like the other familiar days in which one is delivered from its punishment by a single destruction. It is also permissible that this is to remind them of the hour which befell them because of their denial of it, and thereby there is additional pain for them. And ʿUmar ibn Muḥammad read *thubūran* with the letter thāʾ vowelled with fatḥah in all three places, and the vowelling of the fāʾ with fatḥah in verbal nouns (maṣādir) of the pattern fuʿūl is rare, as in *qufūl*.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 15:**

﴿Say﴾, as a rebuke to them, a mockery of them, and a lament over what they have lost. ﴿Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised?﴾ The demonstrative ﴿that﴾ refers to the Blaze mentioned earlier, in view of its being described by the terrifying conditions that were detailed, since it is the Blaze that is often contrasted with the Garden. The sense of distance in the demonstrative indicates that the Blaze is at the furthest extreme of horror and dreadfulness. It has also been said that the demonstrative refers to the Garden and the treasure mentioned in their words: ﴿or a treasure be thrown down to him﴾, and so on.

It has also been said that it refers to the Garden and the palaces that would be made for them in this world, on condition of God's will. Neither of these two opinions should be relied upon, especially the last one. That is, ﴿that﴾ refers to the Blaze which has been prepared for those who denied the Hour, whose state is such-and-such, and whose people's condition is such-and-such.

﴿Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised?﴾ That is, which the God-fearing have been promised, because the verb ﹀waʿada (to promise)﹀ is transitive to two objects, and this omitted object is the returning pronoun to the relative pronoun. The idafa (construction) of ﴿Garden﴾ to ﴿Eternity﴾: if the attribution is known, it is for praise, since praise is given by what is known. If it is not known, it serves to convey the eternity of the Garden. The verse ﴿abiding therein﴾ that follows does not undermine this, because it is to indicate the eternity of its people, not the eternity of the Garden itself, although the two are inseparable. Or that is to distinguish it from the gardens of this world. It has been said that ﴿Garden of Eternity﴾ is a proper name, like ﴿Garden of Eden﴾, and that by the God-fearing is meant those characterised by God-fearing (taqwa) in general, not only by its second or third degree alone. This is indicated by their being contrasted with the disbelievers in the noble composition. It has been said:

It is permissible that what is meant is those who are complete in God-fearing, and that He promised them the promise of entering it immediately, without prior punishment, and this is exclusive to them. But this is not the case.

The questioning and the comparative form in ﴿better﴾ (even though there is no doubt that there is no goodness in the Blaze) is for mockery and rebuke, as we have indicated.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Since the speech is an interrogative, the comparative form may occur in it concerning good between the Garden and the Blaze, because the situation permits that the questioner may test his interlocutor on whatever he wishes, to see whether he answers correctly or wrongly. Sibawayh and others forbade the comparative form when the speech is declarative, because it contradicts reality, but when it is interrogative, that is permissible. Abu Ḥayyan said: ﴿better﴾ here is not for indicating preference, but rather it is in accordance with the Arab custom in expressing the excellence of a thing and its particularity in excellence over its opposite, like the saying of Ḥassān:

"So your evil is for your good: the ransom."

And their saying: "Is misery more beloved to you or happiness?" and "Honey is sweeter than vinegar." And the saying of God, Exalted, related about Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿The prison is more beloved to me﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. This is not restricted to interrogative or declarative speech.

What he mentioned of the examples of the declarative undermines Ibn ʿAṭiyya, unless the good for which he claimed Sibawayh's prohibition is restricted to a case where the ruling is not clear. But if the ruling is clear to the hearer, such that it does not stir in his mind and he does not hesitate about what is better, then the comparative is permissible in it. The verification of this discussion has already been presented in this place, and what we have pointed to here is more deserving of consideration than what Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abu Ḥayyan pointed to.

﴿It shall be for them﴾, that Garden, ﴿for them﴾, that is, in God's knowledge, or in the Preserved Tablet, or the meaning is that it will be, as a promise from the Most Generous of the generous. He expressed it with the past tense by way of metaphor (isti'ara), to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, for He, glorified is He, does not break the appointment. It is also permitted that this is in view of the prior promise of God, Exalted, in His books and on the tongues of His messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, to give them it. ﴿A reward﴾ for their deeds according to the requirement of the promise, not by obligation. ﴿And a destination﴾ to which they return. He did not suffice with His saying, Exalted: ﴿It was for them a reward﴾, because that does not necessitate the second element, for a king in this world may reward a person with an orchard, for example, without the person seeing it, let alone living in it.

The clause ﴿It was for them﴾ and so on, according to what al-Ṭabarsī mentioned, occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the omitted pronoun returning to the relative pronoun in ﴿have been promised﴾, with or without the particle qad. It is also permitted that it be a substitute for ﴿have been promised﴾ and an explanation of it, and that it be a resumptive clause in the position of a causal justification.

Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned what indicates that this clause is a concluding clause (tadhyil) to remind of the blessing with what God, Exalted, bestowed upon them and the pleasantness of their life in that elevated place, in a manner that implies the opposite of that for their opposites. So it is as if it were said: It was for them a reward abundant, beyond description, and a destination, that is, a destination whose measure cannot be estimated, and not like the destination of the disbelievers, referred to in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when they are cast into a narrow place therein﴾. From this one learns the benefit of mentioning the destination along with mentioning the reward, so reflect. And His saying, glorified is He:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 16:**

﴿For them therein is whatever they wish.﴾ It has been said that this is a resumed statement (*istie'naf*), coming as an answer to a question that arises from what precedes it, since it conveys that Paradise is their dwelling. A person who dwells in a home needs many things so that his soul may be content in living there. So it is as if a questioner says: "What do they have when they arrive there and dwell in it?" Then it is said: ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish.﴾

Al-Tabarsi said: the sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾. *Ma* is a relative pronoun serving as the subject (*mubtada'*), or the returning pronoun is omitted. (*Wa lahum*) is its predicate, and (*fiha*) is related to what is related to it, meaning: existing for them therein is what they wish of the varieties of delights, the desirable things, and the kinds of bliss, both spiritual and physical. Perhaps each group among them is content with what has been permitted to it of the degrees of bliss, and sees what it is in as the most delightful of things, and their aspirations do not stretch beyond that to the lofty ranks, nor does the thought of seeking them occur to them, nor is it attainable for them. Thus no single believer wishes for the rank of the prophets, peace be upon them, nor do they seek intercession for one who is decreed to abide forever in the Fire, for example. So deprivation is not necessitated, and the ranks of the people of the Gardens are not made equal. In contrast to these, concerning the people of the Fire, God, exalted is He, has said about them: ﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire.﴾ [Saba: 54].

**(Page 247)**

﴿Abiding eternally (khalidina)﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of one of their pronouns, according to what has been said. Its apparent meaning is that there is no preference. Some of the eminent scholars said: making it a *hal* of the first (the pronoun of the righteous) requires that it be a *hal muqaddarah* (a qualifier with anticipated time), and making it a *hal* of the third (the pronoun of "what they wish") gives the impression of restricting the will by it. So the best of matters is the middle course. Some preferred the third because it is closer, and the restriction is not harmful; rather, it is significant. It was also permitted that it be a *hal* of "the righteous," but its status is not hidden. There is a discussion by one of the great scholars here which contains an examination, mentioned by al-Himsi in the margins of *al-Tasrih*, so let it be consulted.

﴿Was (kana)﴾, meaning: the promise with what was mentioned, or the promised thing understood from the speech, so it includes the promise of Paradise, the attainment of what they wish therein, and eternal abiding according to the first view; and Paradise and the attainment of desires and the eternal abiding promised therein according to the second. Some said: the pronoun refers to eternal abiding, and another to the attainment of what they wish therein, first, and to Paradise being a reward and a destination. The singular form is in accordance with what has been mentioned, and what you have heard suffices for it. Most scholars hold that it refers to what they wish, and it is the subject of *kana*. The words of God, exalted is He, ﴿upon your Lord (ala rabbika)﴾ are related to it or to an omitted element, and it occurs as a circumstantial qualifier of His words, glory be to Him: ﴿a promise (wa'dan)﴾, and it is its predicate. He did not permit the prepositional phrase to be related to it, whether it remains in its verbal-noun status or is interpreted as a passive participle, meaning "promised," because of what you know of the disagreement about the referent of the pronoun, based on prohibiting the fronting of a complement of the verbal noun before it. Even if it is interpreted otherwise, or if the fronted element is an adverbial, and there is disagreement about this. It was permitted that ﴿upon your Lord﴾ be related to an omitted element which is the predicate, and (*wa'dan*) is an emphatic verbal noun. The more apparent view is to make this the predicate, meaning: that was a promise, or a promised thing. ﴿Asked for (mas'ula)﴾, meaning: truly deserving to be asked and sought, because it is among the things competed for by those who compete, or a cause of attaining it. So its being "asked for" is a metaphor for it being a great matter. It is also permitted that what is meant is that the promised thing is literally asked for, in the sense that people ask for it in their supplications by saying: ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ [Al Imran: 194]. Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal said: I heard Abu Hazim, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the believers will say: 'Our Lord, we have acted for You according to what You commanded us, so fulfill for us what You promised us.' That is the meaning of His words: ﴿a promise to be asked for.﴾"

Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of Sa'id (mentioned above), from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, that he said concerning the verse: the angels, peace be upon them, will ask for that in their saying: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to Gardens of Eternity which You have promised them﴾ [Ghafir: 8]. The mention of the title of Lordship (*rububiyyah*) with its addition to his pronoun, upon him be prayer and peace, is for honoring him (ﷺ), and to indicate that he, upon him be prayer and peace, is the one who attains the spoils of the noble promise.

The verse presents a difficulty according to the doctrine of the *ishara* (esoteric allusory interpretation), because it indicates an obligation upon God, exalted is He, by virtue of the word "upon" (*ala*). According to them, nothing is obligatory upon Him, glory be to Him, since that would entail the negation of free choice and the non-entitlement to praise. It has been answered that the obligation indicated by the verse is an obligation by the requirement of the promise, and what is impossible is the imposition of compulsion and coercion from outside, because that is what negates free choice and necessitates corruption. It is not His imposing upon Himself something by the requirement of His promise and His generosity, for that is preceded by the will, and an obligation arising from the will does not contradict free choice. This is clear if the promise is originated. As for if it is eternal, then priority and posteriority are in terms of essence, and that does not entail origination. Or it may be said: what is originated by will is its connection to the thing promised. So understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 17:

﴿And on the day He gathers them﴾ is in the accusative case, as an object of a hidden, preceding verb that is coordinated with His words, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Is that better﴾ etc. That is, it was said to them: that, and mention to them, after the rebuke and the expression of regret, the day when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gathers them. The purpose is to remind them of the terrifying events that occur on it, as you have heard concerning its parallels. Or it is an adverb of time for a hidden, delayed verb that has been omitted, to alert the listener to the completeness of its terror and the monstrousness of what occurs in it, and to announce that expression cannot encompass its explanation. That is: on the day He gathers them, there will be among the states and terrors what speech cannot fully explain.

Page 248

Al-Hasan, Talha, Ibn 'Amir and many of the Seven read ﴿نَحْشُرُهُمْ﴾ (nahshuruhum) with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah), by way of iltifat (the shift) from the third person to the first person.

Al-A'raj read ﴿يَحْشُرُهُمْ﴾ (yahshuruhum) with a kasrah on the shin. The author of al-Lawami' (Sahib al-Lawami') said: this occurs throughout the Qur'an, and it is the analogical form for transitive triliteral verbs, because the pattern yaf'ulu with a damma on the 'ayn may be from an intransitive verb whose past tense has a damma. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is rare in usage but strong in analogy, because the pattern yaf'ilu with a kasrah on the 'ayn in transitive verbs is more analogous than yaf'ulu with a damma on the 'ayn. There is a discussion of this which Abu Hayyan mentioned in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit).

﴿And what they worship besides Allah﴾ is coordinated with the object of ﴿He gathers them﴾, and the waw is not for accompaniment (ma'iyyah). Abu al-Baqa' permitted this. According to al-Dahhak, 'Ikrimah and al-Kalbi, the relative (al-mawsul) refers to the idols, on the basis that the context concerns them, and Allah, who is not incapable of anything, will cause them to speak. It has also been said that they will speak by the tongue of their state (lisan al-hal), but this is not the right view.

A group related from Mujahid that what is meant is the angels, 'Isa, 'Uzayr and their like among the rational beings who were worshipped besides Allah, glorified and exalted is He. This is the view of the majority, according to al-Bahr, because the question and answer require it, since these are specific to rational beings customarily, even though inanimate things may speak on that day. What resembles the question that follows is explicitly stated concerning them, such as His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then He will say to the angels: Did these people worship you?﴾ [Saba': 40] and His words, glorified is He: ﴿Did you say to the people: Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. The apparent meaning, on this view, is that by ﴿ma﴾ is meant the worshipped rational beings from whom there is no misguidance, such as the angels and the prophets, peace be upon them, not what would include them and the devils, for example, since the answer, by its apparent meaning, rejects that, as is evident. The word ﴿ma﴾ was applied to rational beings either because it is applied to them literally or figuratively, or in terms of attribute, as if it were said: or their objects of worship. Some eminent scholars said: what is meant is what includes rational beings and others, either because the word ﴿ma﴾ is designated for everything, as indicated by your saying when you see a figure from afar: "What is it?", or because it is intended to denote an attribute, so it is not then restricted to non-rational beings, just as when it is intended to denote the essence; or in order to give precedence to the idols over others, as an alert to their distance from deserving worship, and treating them in that respect as one who has neither knowledge nor power; or in consideration of the predominance and multitude of their worshippers.

﴿Then He will say﴾, that is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to those worshipped besides Him, after gathering all of them, as a rebuke to the worshippers and a reproach to them.

Al-Hasan, Talha and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿فَنَقُولُ﴾ (fanaqulu) also with the nun of majesty. As for those among the others who read there with the nun and here with the ya', on their reading here it is an iltifat from the first person to the third person. In the nun of majesty there, there is an indication that the gathering is a great matter.

﴿Did you mislead these, My servants?﴾ by your calling them to your worship. It has been said that the idafah (possessive construction) of ﴿عِبَادِي﴾ (My servants) is for mercy, or to magnify the gravity of their crime in worshipping other than their Creator, or to magnify the matter of their misleading by calling them to worship you, given that they are servants of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿هَؤُلاءِ﴾ (these) is an apposition (badal) of it, and it is permitted that it be an adjective (na't) of it. ﴿Or did they themselves stray from the way?﴾ That is, from the way by their own selves, through their neglect of correct reflection and their turning away from a guide, whether a book or a messenger. So the preposition was omitted and the verb reached its object directly, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and He guides to the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4]. The original is ﴿إِلَى السَّبِيلِ﴾ or ﴿لِلسَّبِيلِ﴾.

Some eminent scholars mentioned that He did not say ﴿عَنِ السَّبِيلِ﴾ (from the way) for the sake of emphasis, since ﴿ضَلَّهُ﴾ (to lose it) means to lose track of it, and ﴿ضَلَّ عَنْهُ﴾ (to go astray from it) means to exit from it. The first is more eloquent, because it implies that it has no existence at all. The placing of the two pronouns before the two verbs is because the intended meaning of the rebuking question is the one who undertakes the act, not the act itself.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 18 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They will say﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) answering a question that arises from the narration of the question, as if it were said: "What did they answer in reply?" So it was said: "They said":

﴿Glory be to You﴾. The apparent expectation was that it would be expressed in the present tense, so it would say "yaqulu" (he says) first. And it seems that the shift to the past tense serves to indicate the certainty of the glorification and absolution, and that this was their state in the world. It was also said: it draws attention to the fact that their answer with this statement is the focus of concern, for in it lies the rebuke and the obligation (of accountability). Thus the form indicates the certainty of its occurrence. "Subhana" is either an expression of wonder at what was said to them, or because they are inanimate objects with no power over anything, or because they are angels, or prophets protected from such things, or saints protected from the like of that. Or it is a metaphor (kinaya) for their being marked by the glorification and monotheism of Him, exalted is He, so how could they lead His servants astray? Or it is upon its apparent meaning of declaring Him free from imperfection, and the intended meaning is His exaltation above rivals. In all the other aspects it is a general answer, except that in its being so on the last view there is a kind of obscurity compared with the first two. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It was not fitting for us﴾ etc., is like an emphasis for that and a detailing of it.

Al-Tibi made their saying "Glory be to You" a preparation and introduction to the answer, their saying "It was not" etc., meaning: it was not right nor proper for us ﴿to take any protectors besides You﴾, i.e., protectors, with "min" being extra for emphasizing the negation. Its extra use is good after a negation and what is negated, though "kana" is here; but this is the object of its object, so the negation extends to it. The meaning is the negation that they themselves should be its misleaders, in the most emphatic way, as if they said: it was not right nor proper for us to take, going beyond You, protectors whom we worship, due to our condition which is incompatible with it. How then can it be imagined that we would cause others to take a protector other than You, let alone that they would take us as a protector? He also allowed that the meaning could be: it was not fitting for us to take, besides You, followers, for the protector (wali) is applied both to the one followed and to the follower, and from this comes "the protectors of Satan," i.e., his followers. Abu 'Isa al-Aswad al-Qari read "yunbagha" in the passive voice. Ibn Khalawayh said: Sibawayh claimed that this is a dialect.

Abu al-Darda', Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Raja', Nasr ibn 'Alqama, Zayd ibn 'Ali and his brother al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with them both, Makhul, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Hafs ibn 'Ubayd, al-Nakha'i, al-Sulami, Shayba, Abu Bishr and al-Za'farani read "(yuttakhadha)" in the passive voice.

al-Zamakhshari explained this as: the verb "ittakhadha," which is transitive to two objects, with the first object being the pronoun of the speaker standing in place of the subject, and the second being "min awliya'," and "min" is partitive, not extra; i.e., that they take us as some of the protectors. He did not allow its being extra, based on the view of al-Zajjaj that it is not extra with the second object. In al-Kashf he justified this: it is treated as the first, it is generalized by its generality and restricted by its restriction. His meaning is that when it is a predicate not intended to apply to other than its subject, it is generalized and restricted in intent, so the predicate "Zayd is an animal" is not refuted, since the predicate remains general despite the specificity of the subject. It was also said: his meaning is that difference does not fit when unity is possible, and the example is not like that. When al-Zamakhshari built his statement on that doctrine and adopted the partitive sense, the problem arose regarding the indefiniteness of "awliya'." He answered that it is for indicating particularity and distinguishing them by what distinguishes them, and it is in fact for classification.

al-Sajawandi said: the meaning is: it is not fitting for us to count among what falls under the name of protection even a part of it, let alone the whole, for the protector may be an object of worship, a master, a helper, or one served. Al-Zajjaj, on his view, was unaware of the matter of this reading and said: this reading is an error, for you say: "I did not take any protector from anyone," and it is not permitted to say: "I did not take anyone from among protectors," because "min" entered only because it negates one in the sense of all; one says: "There is no one standing" and "There is no man loving what harms him," but one does not say: "No one standing is from anyone" and "No man is from a lover of what harms him." We see no basis for this whatsoever, and if this were permitted, it would be permitted in ﴿So there is none of you who could withhold from Him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47]
صفحة 250
"there is none of you from whom anyone could withhold." al-Farra' permitted this reading with weakness, and claimed that "min awliya'" is the subject and what is in "nattakhidha" is the predicate, as if he made it inverted. End of quote.

The author of al-Matla' related from the author of al-Nazm that he said: What makes this reading untenable is that "man" only enters upon an object with no object before it, such as His saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35]. So when there is an object before the object, other than it, its entry is not good, as in the verse on this reading. It is not hidden from you that to proceed to say it is an error or invalid, while it is transmitted from those whom you have heard from among the great, is a grave matter, and its source is ignorance, whose harms are countless. Ibn Jinni went to the permissibility of the extra "min" in the second object, so one says: "I did not take Zayd as any agent (min wakil)," meaning: I did not take him as an agent, of whatever kind of agents. The meaning of the verse on this basis is: it is not fitting for them to take us, besides You, as protectors, i.e., of protectors, i.e., of whatever falls under the name of protection.

He also allowed that "nattakhidha" on this reading may be from what has one object, with "min dunika" being the complement, "min awliya'" being a circumstantial (hal) element, and "min" being extra; this was attributed in al-Bahr to Ibn Jinni. Some allowed that "nattakhidha" in the well-known reading is from the verb transitive to two objects, and Abu al-Baqa' made on this view "min awliya'" the first object with an extra "min," and "min dunika" the second object; and on the view that it is from the verb transitive to one object, this would be a circumstantial element.

al-Hajjaj read "an nattakhidha min dunika awliya'," and it reached 'Asim, who said: "The defective one (al-mukhaddaj) detested it, or did he not know that there is a 'min' in it?" His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment﴾ etc. is a transitional statement (istidrak) that prepares for clarifying that they themselves were the ones who went astray, after clarifying their freedom from misleading them in the most emphatic way, as you have heard. Their evil conduct has been censured, in that they made the means of guidance into means of misguidance. That is: we did not mislead them, but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment with kinds of blessings so that they would recognize their due and be thankful for them, but they became immersed in desires and indulged in them, ﴿until they forgot the Remembrance﴾, i.e., they became heedless of Your remembrance and of believing in You, or of Your monotheism, or of reflecting on Your blessings and the signs of Your divinity and unity.

In al-Bahr: "the Remembrance" is what was conveyed to people through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, or the revealed books, or the Qur'an. The last is not without issue if it is said that it includes the disbelievers and those spoken of in the verse, and encompasses the disbelievers of this community and others. ﴿And they were﴾, i.e., in Your eternal knowledge, which relates to things as they are in themselves, or in what will proceed from them, in what does not cease by their choice and their poor preparedness, of evil deeds, ﴿a people ruined﴾, perishing. This is on the basis that "bur" is a verbal noun described as the agent for emphasis, and for this reason it is used the same for singular and plural. They recited:

So do not disbelieve what we have done for you, and cover it; disbelief is ruin for its doer.

And Ibn al-Zib'ara's saying:

O Messenger of the King, indeed my tongue is a mender of what I have torn, when I was ruined.

Or it is plural after the pattern of "'awdh" in "'a'idh." Its interpretation as "perishing" was transmitted by Ibn Jarir and others from Mujahid. It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him about it, and he said: "Ruined," in the dialect of 'Uman, and they are from Yemen. It was also said: "bura" means corrupt in the dialect of the Azd, and they say: "a corrupt matter" (amr ba'ir), and "the merchandise became corrupt" (barat al-bidaa'a) when it spoiled. al-Hasan said: "bura," with no good in them, from their saying: "a bur land," i.e., left idle, with no vegetation in it. It was also said: "bura," blind to the truth. The clause is a concluding parenthetical (i'tiradi tadhyili) confirming the content of what precedes it, according to what Abu al-Su'ud said.
صفحة 251
Al-Khafaji said: it is a circumstantial clause with "qad" understood, or coordinated with an understood element, i.e., "they disbelieved and were," or coordinated with what precedes it. al-Zamakhshari severely criticized, on the Sunni scholars, the question and answer mentioned, saying: "In it is a breach for those who claim that Allah, exalted is He, misleads His servants in reality, since He says to those worshipped besides Him: 'Did you mislead My servants, or did they go astray by themselves?' so they disown their misleading and seek refuge with Him from being misleaders, and they say: 'Rather You bestowed favor without precedent on these and their fathers, the favor of a generous, noble benefactor.' So they made the blessing, which should have been a cause of gratitude, a cause of disbelief and forgetfulness of the Remembrance, and that was the cause of their destruction. When the angels and messengers, peace be upon them, cleared themselves of attributing misguidance, which is the work of the devils, to themselves, and sought refuge from it, then they are, toward their Lord, the Rich, the Just, even more clear of it and more exalted above it. Indeed they exalted Him, exalted is He, when they attributed to Him, glory be to Him, the bestowing of favor with the blessing and the granting of enjoyment with it, and attributed the forgetting of the Remembrance and its causing of ruin to the disbelievers. Thus they explained the metaphorical misguidance which Allah, exalted is He, attributed to His own Essence in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He misleads whom He wills﴾. Had He, glory be to Him, been the misleader in reality, the ready answer would have been: 'Rather You misled them.'" End of quote.

Al-Khafaji's author of al-Fara'id answered his saying "they disown their misleading etc." by saying: they disowned it only because they deserve punishment for their misleading, and they had not done it, so it was necessary for them to say that, so that the punishment they deserve would be averted from them, since they are questioned about what they do, while Allah, mighty and majestic, is not questioned about what He does, so no deficiency falls upon Him if it is established against them, and it is impossible for it to reach Him, exalted is He, because He does what He wills and decrees what He intends. And to his saying "they exalted Him when they attributed etc." he answered that their saying "But You gave them enjoyment etc." does not contradict attributing misguidance to Him, glory be to Him, in reality. Also, what leads to misguidance, if it comes from Him, exalted is He, and it is known to Him, mighty and majestic, that they will be misguided by it, has in it what misguidance in reality has, which by his view necessitates that it is not permissible of Him, glory be to Him, although they attributed it to Him, glory be to Him. To his saying "Had He, exalted is He, been the misleader in reality, the ready answer would have been 'You misled them'": this is not sound, because He, exalted is He, asked them only about one of the two matters, and what was mentioned is not suitable as an answer to it, but rather it is an answer to one who said: "Who misled them?" End of quote. In al-Kashf he gave an answer to the last point: the question is not about specifying who misled, since He is knowing of that, but it is a question of rebuke, like His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. So if they had said: "You misled them," it would not match; rather the answer is what they gave, as 'Isa, peace be upon him, answered with his saying: ﴿Glory be to You; it is not for me to say﴾ etc. He followed the Imam in this. He also mentioned before this answer that if it were said that in ﴿You gave them and their fathers enjoyment﴾ there is what indicates that He, exalted is He, is the true agent of misguidance, and that it is not attributed to Him, glory be to Him, out of courtesy, it would be a valid view; but it should not be after accepting the intended point of the answer through their enjoyment etc., that the meaning is the answer "You misled them," but he turned from it to what is in the glorious wording out of courtesy, because answering with that is not what the context requires, as is not hidden.

Ibn al-Munir said: The answer of those who were questioned, in the terms mentioned, indicates their belief, which agrees with what the People of Truth (*ahl al-haqq*) hold. The People of Truth believe that although God Most High created misguidance, the servants have a choice (*ikhtiyar*) in it. They hold that every voluntary act has two relations: if it is considered as something created, it is attributed to God Most High, and if it is considered as something chosen by the servant, it is attributed to the servant. These respondents attributed forgetfulness, that is, being absorbed in desires, which results in forgetfulness, to the disbelievers, because they chose it for themselves, so the attribution to them is accurate. They attributed the cause that brought about their forgetfulness and their absorption in desires to God Most High, namely His gradual leading of them on (*istidraj*) by extending blessings upon them and pouring them out abundantly. There is therefore no contradiction between the belief of the People of Truth and the content of what they said in the answer; rather, the two agree on one matter. End of quotation.

It is not hidden what is problematic in the demonstration of this agreement. It may be said: since the purpose of the question was to rebuke and reproach the polytheists, and since the questioners knew this, which should not be denied, especially if they were the angels and the prophets, peace be upon them, the answer came containing this in the most complete form, including the establishment of the matter in the source of their misguidance. All of this is for the sake of attending to God's intended purpose in rebuking and censuring them. For this reason they did not limit themselves in the answer to "they themselves went astray." Rather, they opened with glorification (*tasbih*), then denied misguidance from themselves in a manner of emphasis beyond which there is nothing. Then they explained that they had gone astray after the realization of what ought to have been a means for them to be guided, namely their being granted enjoyment of various blessings. That is among the worst forms of misguidance. They drew attention to its increased ugliness beyond what was mentioned by describing it as forgetting the remembrance. Then they mentioned the source of their misguidance and its original root through their saying: ﴿and they were a people lost﴾. As for the meaning "they were in reality a corrupt people," or, if you wish, "destroyed people," and similar meanings already mentioned, then they manifested themselves according to what they were, because what is in reality does not change. Or the meaning is "they were in knowledge, which follows the known as it is in itself, thus," and so they manifested themselves according to that, lest the impossible reversal be implied. The summary is that the source of their misguidance is the corruption of their predisposition in itself, without any other thing having an effect upon it. This is the case with all the quiddities of things in themselves, for the influence of another is only in their external existence and nothing more. This view was held by a group of philosophers and Sufis, and Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kawrani, may God have mercy on him, established its pillars in most of his books. So if it is acceptable, there is no harm in applying the noble verse to it. Then reflect.

[p. 252]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 19:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they have indeed denied you﴾ is a report of His, the Exalted's, argument against the worshippers, by way of shifting the address (talwin al-khitab) and turning it away from the worshipped ones upon the completion of their reply and directing it toward the worshippers, for the sake of intensifying their rebuke and reproach. It is according to an implied statement that follows the reply, meaning: God the Exalted then said at that point, "The ones you worshipped, O disbelievers, have denied you." Some of the eminent scholars said that the fa' (then) is eloquent (fasiha), like it is in the words of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

"They said, 'Khurasan is the farthest that is sought of us,' then the return; indeed we have come to Khurasan."

The implied meaning here is: We said, or the Exalted said, "If you say they are gods, then they have indeed denied you ﴿in what you say﴾," meaning in your saying. This is on the basis that the ba' (in) means "in," and ma is a verbal-noun (masdariyyah), and the prepositional phrase is connected to the verb, and "the saying" is in the sense of "the thing said." It is also permissible for ma to be a relative pronoun (mawsulah) with an omitted returning pronoun, meaning "in that which you say." It was also permitted that the ba' be an extra particle (silah), and the prepositional phrase be a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the pronoun in the accusative in "they have denied you." What is meant by their statement is that they are gods, or "these have led us astray." It was objected that their denial in this statement has no connection to what follows of their inability to turn away or to give help at all; rather what it entails is their denial in their claim that they are their gods and helpers. There is room for consideration in this, as we will indicate shortly, God willing, the Exalted. It was also said that the address is to the worshipped ones, meaning: "So the worshippers have denied you, O worshipped ones, in your saying, 'Glory be to You; it was not fitting for us to take any protectors apart from You,' since they claimed that you were gods." What is meant is a judgment against those deniers by way of disbelief, in a manner that increases the anger of the worshipped ones against them, and he made what follows it, God willing, the Exalted, a consequence of it.

Also the fa' is eloquent, and the clause is a conditional response with respect to the reports. It was also said: it is an address to the believers in the world: "So the disbelievers have denied you, O believers, in the world, in what you say of monotheism." The speech was brought so that what follows may be made a consequence of it. Both sayings, as you see, are [weak], and the second is the more remote of the two. Abu Haywa read "yaqulun" with the letter ya' at the beginning, and this is a transmission from Ibn Kathir and Qanbal. The address in "kadhdhabukum" is to the worshippers, and the plural pronoun in it and in "yaqulun" refers to the worshipped ones, meaning: "So the worshipped ones have denied you, O worshippers, by your claim, by their saying 'Glory be to You,' etc." The ba' is for accompaniment or instrumentality. In this reading also are the two earlier sayings, meaning: "So the worshipped ones have denied you, O worshippers, by their saying that you are gods," or "So the believers, the disbelievers, have denied you in monotheism by their saying: 'Indeed these of whom they speak are gods.'"

﴿So you are not able﴾, meaning: you do not possess, O worshippers, ﴿any turning away﴾, meaning a repelling of punishment from yourselves by any means, as the indefiniteness indicates; that is, neither directly nor through an intermediary. It was said: it is a stratagem (hilah), from their saying: "he turns (yasrifu) in his affairs," meaning he schemes in them. It was said: repentance. It was said: ransom (fidyah). The first is more apparent, for the origin of sarf is turning a thing from one state to another, and its application to stratagem, repentance or ransom is metaphorical. What is meant is: you do not possess the repelling of punishment before its descent, ﴿nor any help﴾, meaning an individual instance of help, that is, aid, not from your own selves nor from others after its descent. It was said: nasran is the plural of nasir, like sahb is the plural of sahib, but this is nothing. The fa' expresses the consequence of the inability on what came before it of denial, but not in the sense that were it not for that, ability would truly exist; rather in their assumption, since they used to claim that they would repel punishment from them and help them. In this there is a striking mockery of them. What is meant by the denial that is consequent upon it, which was mentioned, is their denial by their saying that they are gods. It is also permissible that what is meant by it is their denial by their saying, "These have led us astray," and this implies the negation of their being gods, and by this the order of consequence is completed.

Ali, may God honor his face, and most of the Seven read "yastati'un" with the letter ya' below (third person).

Meaning: so the gods you have cannot repel punishment from you. It was said: a stratagem to repel it. It was said: a ransom on your behalf. ﴿Nor help you.﴾ It was said regarding the meaning of the verse, on the supposition that the earlier address is to the believers, that He, glorified is He, intended that these disbelievers are stubborn and obstinate in the denial that necessitates punishment, so you yourselves cannot turn them away from it, nor give you help regarding what befalls them of the punishment that they deserve. This is according to the reading of Hafs, "tastati'un" with the upper ta'. As for the reading of the majority, "yastati'un" with ya', the meaning is: they cannot turn away from themselves what they are upon, nor give help to themselves regarding the punishment they have merited by their denial; or: they cannot turn you away from the truth you are upon, nor [give] help to themselves against the punishment. End. And it is as you see.

﴿And whoever does wrong﴾, meaning disbelieves, ﴿among you﴾, O responsible ones, and worships besides God the Exalted another god like these disbelievers, ﴿We shall make him taste﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿a great punishment﴾ whose measure cannot be grasped, and it is the punishment of the Fire. It was read "yadhuqhu" with the pronoun referring to God, may He be mighty and majestic. It was said: the verb is with a verbal noun from "yazlim", meaning the wrongdoing makes him taste it, and the attribution is metaphorical. The interpretation of wrongdoing as disbelief is that transmitted from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj, and it is supported by the fact that the context requires it, for the discussion concerns disbelief and its threat from the beginning of the surah. It is also permissible that it be meant to include polytheism and all other sins, and the threat of punishment does not contradict pardon with respect to other than the polytheist, as has been established in its proper place. Al-Tibi preferred the first interpretation and made the address to the disbelievers too, because the discussion concerns them from the start, and "So they have indeed denied you," and this verse is for what befalls them of terrors and punishment from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When it sees them from a far place﴾ [al-Furqan: 12]. The meaning of ﴿whoever does wrong﴾ then is: whoever persists in wrongdoing. In al-Kashshaf: the point is that the address is general and the wrongdoing is disbelief; ﴿whoever does wrong﴾ is an explicit noun placed in the position of a pronoun, to draw attention to their immersion in disbelief and their exceeding the limit of fairness and justice into pure injustice and disputation regarding what they accused the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of. The original would have been "so they are not able to turn away or to help, and We make them taste a great punishment," or "We make you taste" according to the difference of the two readings. Taking it as referring to whoever among you persists in wrongdoing, so that the address is specific to the disbelievers, is also sound, but it misses the point we have mentioned. End. It is not hidden that its being a placing of an explicit noun in the position of a pronoun is contrary to the apparent sense, so reflect.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 25, verse 20:**

﴿Never did We send before you any messengers but that they ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ It has been said that this is a consolation to him (ﷺ) concerning their saying, "What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?", by informing him that in the other messengers, peace be upon them, you have an excellent example, for they were likewise.

[Page 254]

Al-Zajjaj (the grammarian and Qur'an scholar) said: It is an argument against them concerning their saying that. As if it were said: thus were those messengers who came before him, eating food and walking in the markets. So how could Muhammad (ﷺ) be an innovation among the messengers, peace be upon them?

Al-Tibi (Sharaf al-Din al-Tibi, the commentator) rejected this, saying that the sublime structure of the verse does not support it, because their taunting has already been answered by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Look how they strike similitudes for you﴾ (Al-Isra 48; Al-Furqan 9). Al-Kashf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*) criticised him with the words: "A speaker may say that this is another answer, just as it was answered there in several respects, as has been reported from the Imam (al-Razi)." He regarded His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Nay, they denied﴾ as a third answer, and followed it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have prepared a blaze for those who deny the Hour﴾, because of the suitability of the context, and the threat was complete. Then He, glorified is He, answered them with another answer that also includes consolation, and this is what the sublime structure supports.

The clause after *illa* (except) is said to be a second attribute of an implied noun-antecedent placed before ﴿from among the messengers﴾. The meaning is: We did not send before you any one of the messengers except that they were eating and walking. It has been criticised that this involves separating the described noun from its attribute by *illa*, and most grammarians have rejected this, as stated in *al-Mughni* (Ibn Hisham's grammar). For this reason, some made it an attribute of an implied noun placed after *illa*, and that is a substitute (*badal*) for what was omitted before it, and its attribute was put in its place. The meaning is: We did not send before you anyone of the messengers except men or messengers, that they, etc. In this there is separation between the substitute and what it substitutes, which is permissible according to them.

Al-Farra' (the Kufan grammarian) assumed *min* (from) after *illa*, and this may be a relative pronoun or an indefinite described noun. Some made the clause in the accusative position by an omitted verb of saying, and the clause of saying is an attribute, meaning: except men or messengers, it was said that they, etc. This, as you see, is [unsatisfactory]. Ibn al-Anbari said: the clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the exception is from the most general of circumstances, and the estimate is: except while they. Abu Hayyan (the Andalusian grammarian and exegete) said: this is the preferred view. He estimated the *waw* (and), on the basis that dispensing with the pronoun alone in such a circumstantial clause is not eloquent. Perhaps one may prefer not to estimate it, and reject the claim that it is not eloquent, or carry this on what is not combined with *illa*, because in reality it is a substitute.

The reason for the breaking of *inna* (that) is that it occurs at the beginning [of a clause], and the *lam* occurs after it as well.

It was read as *annahum* (with a *fatha*), on the basis that a *lam* is added after it, and a preposition is estimated before it, meaning: because they eat, etc. The meaning is: We did not make them messengers to mankind except because they were like them.

Ali (may God honour his face), Ibn Mas'ud, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah read *yamassuna* (with a doubled *shin* that is *fatha*-vowelled and a *damma* on the *ya*), in the passive, meaning: it causes them to walk to their needs, or [the subject is] people. The doubling is for intensification, as in the saying of the Hudhali poet:

*Yamshi baynana hanutun kharram*

Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read, as in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit* of Abu Hayyan), *yamshuna* with a *damma* on the *ya* and the *shin*, with doubling, in the active voice, and this is an intensive form of *yamshi* (unstressed). It agrees with the well-known reading and does not need the estimate "it causes them to walk to their needs" or similar. They cited his saying:

*Wa-mashā bi-aghsān al-mabā'ati wa-btagha*
*Qalā'iṣa minhā ṣa'batun wa-dhalūlu*

And his saying:

*Fa-qad tarakat khazīnatu kulla waghdin*
*Yamshī bayna khātāmin wa-ṭāqi*

In some copies of the *Kashshaf* there is something indicating that he did not obtain this reading.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient?﴾ It has been said that this is also a consolation to him (ﷺ), but concerning their saying: ﴿Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or why does he not have a garden?﴾ (Al-Furqan 8). That is: We have made your rich, O people, a test for your poor, to see whether they will be patient. ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾, that is, knowing what is right concerning what they are tested with and other things. So let not your breast be constricted, nor let their sayings make you light-headed.

It has also been said: it is an encouragement to be patient for him, upon him be prayer and peace, regarding what they said and considered strange, his eating food and walking in the markets, after arguing against them with the other messengers. The speech is a turning of address, by generalising it to all the other messengers, peace be upon them, by way of predominance (*taghlib*), as some have chosen. By "the first part" is meant the disbelievers of the nations, and their specific relation to the messengers makes it correct, because [the first part] is among them. By "the second part" is meant their messengers, on the sense that We made each specific part of the nations a trial for a specific part of the messengers. As if it were said: and We made every particular disbelieving nation a trial for its specific messenger. He did not state this explicitly, relying on the testimony of the situation. Its summary is: Our custom has run, according to the requirement of Our wisdom, to test the messengers through their peoples, and through their hostility towards them, and the unbridled tongues against them with words beyond the limits of fairness, and their conduct in harming them in every way, so that We may know their patience. Or it is an address to mankind as a whole, as has been said, and this is the apparent meaning.

The first part is more general, including disbelievers, the wealthy, the healthy and others who are suitable to be a trial. The second part is more general, including the messengers, the reciters, the sick and others who are suitable to test. The discourse concerning it is beneficial for his patience (ﷺ) regarding what they said, and an increase.

It has also been said: by the first part is meant the one among the messengers who has no wealth, and by the second part their peoples. And our Prophet (ﷺ) and his community enter into this by primary inclusion. So it is as if it were said: We have made you a trial for your community, because if you were the possessor of treasures and gardens, their inclination towards you and their obedience to you would be for the sake of this world, or mixed with this world. But We sent you with no wealth, so that the obedience of whoever obeys you among them may be sincerely for the sake of God, exalted is He, without any worldly desire. Likewise is the case of every messenger without wealth with his people.

The more apparent view is the generality of the address and of the two parts, and this is what the reports require. Ibn Atiyya (the Andalusian exegete) went this way and said: this is general to the believer and the disbeliever. So the healthy is a trial to the sick, the rich is a trial to the poor, and the messenger specially honoured with the dignity of prophethood is a trial to the nobles among the disbelievers of his age. Likewise the scholars and the just rulers. Ibn al-Qasim recited this verse when he saw Ashhab (a jurist of the Maliki school) ... (end of quote). Abu Hayyan chose this as well. The specific occasion of revelation does not harm it, for it has been reported from al-Kalbi that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, and those of their rank. They said: If we become Muslim, and Ammar, Suhayb, Bilal, and so-and-so and so-and-so, who embraced Islam before us, have risen above us, relying on their precedence.

The interrogative (*istifham*) is either within the scope of the causal clause for the making, with its counterpart omitted, as it is omitted in countless examples, and the estimate is: so that We may know whether you will be patient or not, that is, so that what is in Our knowledge may become manifest. The estimate of knowledge is supported by the fact that the trial implies it. Or it is not within the scope of causation, and there is no omitted counterpart, by being for encouragement and incitement, and the meaning is: be patient, for I have tested some of you with others.

It is also permissible not to estimate a counterpart even on the assumption of the causal sense, by the address being to the messengers, peace be upon them, as you have heard. Ibn Atiyya made the address in what preceded general, and in ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ specific to the believers, for he made the respite of the disbelievers a trial for them within the preceding generality. He estimated a counterpart and said: as if He made the respite of the disbelievers a trial for the believers, then He put them to the question: will you be patient or not? He made His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾ a promise to the patient and a threat to the disobedient. Some of them made it a promise to the Messenger (ﷺ) of a great reward for his beautiful patience, with an added honour for him, upon him be prayer and peace, by turning to the name of the Lord, joined to his pronoun (ﷺ). He allowed that it could be a threat to those opponents of his, upon him be prayer and peace, brought as a completion of the consolation or of the encouragement to patience, but this is not the case.

He cited the verse as evidence for predestination and decree, for it indicates that the acts of servants, such as the enmity and harm of the disbelievers, are by God's making and will, and the trial, in the sense of testing, even if it is not among the acts of servants, is yet a consequence and implies what is from them. There is much obscurity in this.

His saying, exalted is He,

*(Here the text ends.)*

Completed, and praise belongs to God. The eighteenth part of the *Tafsir Ruh al-Ma'ani* is complete, and it is followed, God willing, by the nineteenth part, which begins with ﴿"And those who do not hope [for meeting Us] say﴾.

[p. 2]

In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

﴿And those who do not hope for Our meeting say...﴾ etc. This begins the recounting of another part of their false statements and the demonstration of their falsehood, following the recounting of the refutation of their earlier fallacies, and the mention of what relates to that. The clause is coordinated with His, exalted be He, words: ﴿And they say, "What is this Messenger...?"﴾ to the end. Placing the relative pronoun (al-ladhina) in the position of a pronoun serves to draw attention, through what occurs in its relative clause, to the fact that what is reported of them is so shameful that it could not come from one who hopes for the meeting of God, mighty and majestic.

*Al-raja'* (hope) in its common meaning is *al-amal* (aspiration), and most lexicographers have explained one of the two by the other. In Ibn Hilal's *Furuq* (Distinctions): *al-amal* is a hope that continues, which is why gazing at a thing when it continues and lengthens is called *ta'ammul* (contemplation). It is also said: *al-amal* occurs with both the possible and the impossible, whereas *al-raja'* is specific to the possible.

In *al-Misbah* (al-Fayyumi's *al-Misbah al-Munir*): *al-amal* is the opposite of despair, and it is most often used of what is far from being attained; *al-tama'* (covetousness) is used of what is near to being attained; and *al-raja'* lies between *al-amal* and *al-tama'*, for the one who hopes fears that what he hopes for may not be attained, which is why it has been used in the sense of *al-tama'*. End of quotation.

Abu 'Ubayda and a group explained it as *al-khawf* (fear). Al-Farra' said: "This word is Tihami (from the Tihama region), and it is also from the dialect of Hudhayl. When it is accompanied by negation, they take it to mean fear. So they say: 'So-and-so does not hope for his Lord, exalted be He,' meaning, 'does not fear his Lord, exalted be He.' Among this is the verse: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾, i.e., you do not fear the greatness of God, exalted be He. But when they say, 'So-and-so hopes for his Lord,' this is in the sense of hope, not fear." The poet said:

When the bees sting him, he does not hope for their sting, and he swears (an alliance) with them within a hive of combs.

And another said:

He does not hope when he meets the defender, whether seven (of them) have met him or one.

End of quotation.

It has been mentioned that the use of *al-raja'* in the sense of fear is figurative (*majaz*), because one who hopes for a matter fears its loss. The root meaning of *al-liqa'* (meeting) is the encountering and confronting of a thing; this is what is meant by one who said: "It is arriving at a thing, not touching it." It is also applied to seeing, because seeing is arriving at what is seen. The meeting with Him here is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the meeting with His recompense on the Day of Resurrection, or it is intended with an elided noun (*mudaf*) understood. The meaning according to the well-known explanation of *al-raja'*: "And those who do not aspire to the meeting of Our recompense of good and reward for obedience, because they deny the Resurrection." According to the other explanation: "And those who do not fear the meeting of Our recompense of evil and punishment for disobedience, because they deny the Resurrection." Thus it is said.

It is also said: what is intended is seeing Him, exalted be He, in the Hereafter, and *al-raja'* on this reading means aspiration, not fear, since there is no sense in seeing being something feared. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, although what follows does not object to it, for the meaning on this reading would be: "Those who do not hope to see Us in the Hereafter, which is the expected place of seeing for many people, have proposed that We be seen in this world, which is not the expected place for that." It may also be said: negating the hope of meeting Him, exalted be He, is a metonymy for denying resurrection and gathering, and this is perhaps better than what preceded it. That is: "And those who deny resurrection and gathering say: ﴿Why have the angels not been sent down to us?﴾, i.e., would that they were sent down to us so that they might inform us of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿or [why] do we not see our Lord?﴾ so that He may inform us of that, as narrated from Ibn Jurayj and others." In requesting the sending down of angels for confirmation, rather than the sending down of a single angel, there is an indication that they had reached such a level of denial that the confirmation of one angel would not benefit them. And if the definite article in *al-mala'ika* (the angels) is taken as encompassing all (*li'l-istighraq al-haqiqi*), the indication of the strength of their denial is greater. That strength increases if the meaning of each one of us is taken in *'alayna* (upon us), without considering distribution.

[p. 3]

It also points to the strength of this the way they expressed themselves with the present tense, which denotes a continuous and renewed state, in ﴿or do we see our Lord?﴾ As if they were not satisfied with seeing Him, exalted be He, and His informing them, exalted be He, of the truthfulness of His Messenger (ﷺ), until they see Him, exalted be He, and He informs them of that repeatedly. And the intention of continuity from the present tense does not conflict with the fact that the original use of *law-la* (why not / if only), which is for urging or proposing, is to be followed by the present tense, and whatever is not in the present tense is interpreted as such. Perhaps their shift to the past tense in the case of the sending down of angels, the clause that is coordinated with it, although it is in the sense of the present, is in the manner we mentioned in explaining His, exalted be He, words: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ So reflect, for what is in the covenant of an old matter.

It has also been said: the meaning is: "Why have the angels not been sent down to us, so that they may convey the command and prohibition of God, instead of Muhammad (ﷺ)? Or do we not see our Lord, so that He may inform us of that without any intermediary?" The first has been preferred, on the ground that the context concerns denying him (ﷺ) — and far be it from him, and further far be it from him from lying — and the insistence in seeking one who would confirm him, peace be upon him, not seeking one who would convey command and prohibition apart from him (ﷺ). We do not concede that ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ is repeated with the earlier ﴿Why have the angels not been sent down to us?﴾, since the difference between the two requested things is evident. And even if repetition between them is assumed, it does no harm, as is not hidden.

The second has been defended on the ground that the setting concerns nothing but mentioning the deniers and recounting their fallacies arising from their denial. Some of these were already listed earlier, including their insistence in seeking one who would confirm him (ﷺ). So it is better that what is here be the recounting of another type of them, so that it is further from repetition and more indicative of obstinacy and arrogance.

Perhaps His, exalted be He, words are more suitable to what has been mentioned: ﴿Indeed they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression.﴾

The meaning of ﴿they have become arrogant within themselves﴾ is that they committed arrogance regarding themselves and regarded themselves as of great standing. In this there is the treatment of the transitive verb as if it were intransitive, as in the line of poetry: "...his blade wounds their hamstrings." *Al-'utuww* (transgression) is going beyond the limit in wrongdoing, and it is the common verbal noun of *'ata*. The *lam* is in the response to an oath, meaning: "By God, they have indeed become arrogant regarding their own standing and have exceeded the limit in wrongdoing and insolence, exceeding it greatly, reaching its utmost extent, in that they denied the Messenger, peace be upon him, and did not submit to a human like themselves to whom revelation is sent concerning their command and prohibition, and they did not heed his overwhelming miracles and his dazzling signs. So they sought what the eyes of nations scarcely turn toward, and aspired to what only some of the Messengers of firm resolve attained, may God's blessings and peace be upon them all."

[The word] ﴿they have become arrogant within themselves﴾ has been explained as: "they concealed arrogance," which is denial and obstinacy in their hearts. This is clearer than what preceded, though what preceded is more eloquent and better suited to what has been defended. Likewise *al-'utuww* has been explained as turning away from obedience, though what preceded is more eloquent and better suited to that as well.

In following the report of the falsehood of those disbelievers with the oath clause, there is an announcement of the extreme ugliness of their state, and an indication of wonder at their arrogance and transgression. This is in reality an implication from context (*fahwa*). Such usage is common in speech: one says to someone who committed an offence, "You did such and such," expressing amazement and wonder at it. It is used in all languages. Al-Zamakhshari counted among this the verse of Muhalhil:

"And the neighbour of Jassas has informed us of their fang, Kulayb; the fang of Kulayb has become ghalt (ravaged) by its wrath."

And al-Tibi (counted among it) His, exalted be He, words: ﴿How great a word it is!﴾ It was objected that this is not of this kind, because the triliteral verb transformed into a verb (verbally or implicitly) is used for wonder, as the grammarians have stated. The Imam (al-Razi), mentioning the preferred opinion of the first view regarding the explanation of ﴿Why has [an angel] not been sent down?﴾ etc., said that this sentence is a response to their saying "Why has [an angel] not been sent down?" etc., on several grounds:

First: that when the Qur'an became evident as miraculous, his prophethood was established (ﷺ). After that, proposing these signs is nothing but pure arrogance.

[p. 4]

Second: that if the sending down of angels upon them (peace be upon them) had occurred, it would also be among the miracles, and it would not indicate truthfulness by the specific fact that it is the sending down of an angel, but by the general fact that it is a miracle. So accepting that and rejecting the other would be preferring one of two equals without a preference.

Third: that even if they were to see the Lord, exalted be He, and He confirmed His Messenger (ﷺ), they would gain no knowledge beyond the confirmation of the miracle, for there is no difference between the Prophet saying, "O God, if I am truthful, then revive this dead man," and He, mighty and majestic, reviving him, and between his saying, "If I am truthful, then confirm me," and He confirming him. So specifying one of the two ways is pure obstinacy.

Fourth: that the servant has no right to object to his master, either by the rule of ownership according to the Ash'aris, or by the rule of benefit according to the Mu'tazilis.

Fifth: that the persistent, obstinate questioner who is not content with what is bestowed upon him is blameworthy, and displaying a miracle is among the great bounties. So rejecting one of them and proposing another is not in any way proper conduct.

Sixth: perhaps the meaning is: "If I knew that they were not arrogant and transgressive, I would have given them what they asked for. But I know that they only asked out of stubbornness and obstinacy, so I certainly will not give them anything."

Seventh: perhaps they knew from the People of the Book that God, exalted be He, is not seen in this world, and that He does not send down angels upon ordinary people; then they made their faith conditional upon that, so they are arrogant and mocking. End of quotation, and in it is what is not free from discussion.

The Ash'aris have used His, exalted be He, words "who do not hope for Our meeting" as evidence that seeing God, exalted be He, is possible. The Mu'tazilis have used His, exalted be He, words "they have become arrogant" and "transgressed" as evidence that it is impossible. The weakness of both arguments is not hidden.

﴿يَوْمَ يَرَوْنَ المَلائِكَةَ﴾ *(On the day they see the angels)* is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a clause that begins a new sentence), brought to explain what they will suffer when they witness the angels, after the magnitude of their request that angels be sent down to them has been declared and after it has been shown to be extremely monstrous.

The phrase is stated as "on the day they see" rather than "on the day the angels descend," as an early signal that their seeing the angels will not be a response to what they asked for, but in a different manner that never occurred to them.

"Yawma" (*on the day*) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*), governed by what is indicated by His statement: ﴿لا بُشْرى يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾ *(No good tidings that day for the guilty)*. This is because it means: "The guilty will not be given good tidings on that day." The shift to negating the genus (*nafy al-jins*, negating the category as a whole) is for emphasis in negating good tidings, as if it had been said: "They will not be given good tidings on the day they see the angels." Some scholars estimated: "They will be denied good tidings, or they will lose them," but the first is further from the possibility of the misconception that the matter is being made light of. Some scholars estimated: "There is no good tidings before a day," and made it an adverb of time for that. Abu al-Baqa permitted its connection to a supposed verb *yu'adhdhabun* (they are punished), the supposed verb being indicated by ﴿لا بُشْرى﴾ etc. Its being an object of a verb implied and omitted, he said, Abu Hayyan said: "This is closer."

The author of *al-Fara'id* said: "It is possible that it is in the accusative governed by an implied *yanzilu* (descends) which is indicated by their saying: ﴿لَوْلا أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْنَا المَلائِكَةُ﴾ *(Why were the angels not sent down upon us?)*, as if it had been said: 'The angels descend on the day they see them.' Do not say: 'How can the time of seeing be a time for descent?' For we say: The adverb admits of that because of its breadth." Al-Tibi approved this, saying: "This is a view beyond which there is nothing further, because when it is in the accusative governed by *yanzilu*, the two statements fit together: His statement ﴿يَوْمَ يَرَوْنَ﴾ etc. is an elaboration (*nashr*, an unfolding in the same order) of His statement ﴿لَوْلا أُنْزِلَ﴾ etc., and His statement ﴿وَقَدِمْنَا﴾ is an elaboration of His statement ﴿أَوْ نَرَى رَبَّنَا﴾ *(or let us see our Lord)*." Most scholars did not permit its connection to the mentioned *bushra* (good tidings) because it is a verbal noun, and a verbal noun does not govern what comes after it, and because it is negated by *la* (the negation particle), and *la* does not govern what precedes it.

"Yawma'idhin" is an emphasis of the first (*ta'kid*), or an apposition to it (*badal*), or a predicate (*khabar*). "Lil-mujrimin" is an explanatory complement (*tabyin*) connected to an omitted element, as in "*saqyan lahu*" (*watering for him*), or a second predicate, or it is an adverb for what the preposition *lam* is connected to, or for *bushra* if it is read as nunated (*munawwanah*) and not built (*ghayr mabniyyah*) with *la*, because it does not govern: if the subject of *la* governed, the phrase would be lengthened and would resemble an *idafa* construction (a noun in construct), and so would be in the accusative.

In *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*): *bushra* may be built with *la* (*mabniyy*, fixed in form), and it may be in the accusative in its intended nunation, with the form of an accusative but prevented from declension (*mamnu' min al-sarf*) because of its necessary feminine marking. If it is built with *la*, it may be that the predicate is "yawma'idhin" and "lil-mujrimin" is a second predicate, or a qualifier of *bushra*, or connected to what the predicate is connected to. And "yawma'idhin" may be a qualifier of *bushra*, with the predicate "lil-mujrimin." There is also the disagreement of Sibawayh and al-Akhfash over whether the predicate belongs to *la* itself or to the subject which is the whole of *la* together with what is built with it. If it is in the intended nunation and is declinable, then "yawma'idhin" may be the object of *bushra* and may be a qualifier, with the predicate "lil-mujrimin." It may be that "yawma'idhin" is the predicate and "lil-mujrimin" is a qualifier. It may be that "yawma'idhin" is the predicate and "lil-mujrimin" is a second predicate. When the noun is not built with *la* itself, there is agreement that the predicate belongs to the subject.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Yawma'idhin* is a repetition (*takrir*). This is not permitted, whether by repetition is meant verbal emphasis or apposition, because *yawma* is in the accusative governed by what was mentioned before, namely *udhkur* (remember) or *yafqidun* (they lose). What comes after *la*, which governs the noun, cannot be governed by what comes before it. And if it is estimated thus, then what comes before it is the governing element." End of quotation. You are not unaware of the flaws in the possibilities he mentioned.

As for what was raised as an objection against al-Zamakhshari, it was responded to by the claim that the negated clause is governed by an implied verb of saying which occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the angels, who are the object of *yarawna* (they see), and *yarawna* is the object of *yawma* (day). So *la* and what is within its scope are part of the first adverbial phrase, insofar as it is governed by something within its scope. Such a thing is not considered objectionable. Moreover, that *la* always has the first position (*sadr*), or that its subject, when built with it, has the first position, is not accepted by all grammarians, for because of its frequent occurrence, it has departed from the first position. So consider this. This is what we have found of the earlier scholars' views on the grammatical analysis of the verse, and what is in it of criticism and approval.

Some contemporary scholars said: "It is permitted to connect *yawma* to *kabir* (great), or to restrict its greatness to that day, not to negate its greatness in itself, but to make its cause manifest on that day. Its parallel is: 'Zayd has great knowledge on the day he debates the opponents.' The clause ﴿لا بُشْرى يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾ is then a resumptive clause explaining that." And that, as you see, is [weak]. Whatever the case, the intended meaning of that day, according to what is related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), is the day of death. Abu Hayyan said: "The apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Resurrection, because of His later statement: ﴿وَقَدِمْنَا إِلَى مَا عَمِلُوا﴾ *(and We will turn to what they did)*, etc." And in this there is room for consideration.

The negation of good tidings is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for affirming their opposite, just as the negation of love in a statement such as His ﴿فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُحِبُّ الكافِرِينَ﴾ *(indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers)* is a metonymy for hatred and detestation. Thus it indicates that a warning is established for them in the most eloquent way. The intended meaning of "the guilty" is those who do not hope for meeting Him, Exalted is He. Placing the noun in place of their pronoun is a recording of guilt against them, along with their disbelief and obstinacy, and an indication of the cause of the ruling. Whoever takes the implicit meaning (*mafhum*) of such a construction as valid claims that the verse indicates the non-realization of the ruling for others besides them. His statement, Exalted is He, concerning the believers: ﴿تَتَنَزَّلُ عَلَيْهِمُ المَلائِكَةُ أَلا تَخافُوا وَلا تَحْزَنُوا وَأَبْشِرُوا﴾ *(The angels descend upon them, saying: Do not fear and do not grieve, and rejoice in the good news)*, etc., indicates that good tidings are attained by them.

It has been said: "The intended meaning of them is what includes the disobedient and the disbelievers who do not hope for meeting Him, Exalted is He." The statement conveys the removal of good tidings from the disbelievers in the most complete way, because it indicates that what prevents the attainment of good tidings is guilt, and there is no greater guilt than the guilt of those who do not hope for meeting Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, and who say what they say. So they are more deserving of it.

The Mu'tazila's argument from this verse, to deny intercession and pardon for the disobedient, is completed by it, because it does not indicate negation at all times, so it is permissible that the disobedient may be given good tidings of what was mentioned at another time.

It was responded to: the clause before the negation, because it is a nominal sentence, indicates continuity.
