So after the negation enters, to intend the negation of the continuity of good tidings for the guilty, in the sense that good tidings will be theirs but will not continue, is something no one is thought to hold. Therefore it is necessary to intend the continuity of the negation, as in His statement concerning their opposites: ﴿لا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ *(No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve)*. Then His statement "it does not indicate negation at all times" cannot hold. Therefore it is better that the guilty be understood as those you have heard of.

"*Wa-yaqulun*" (*and they say*) is coordinated with *la yubashsharun* (they are not given good tidings) or with *yumna'un al-bushra* (they are prevented from good tidings) or similar, as an implied element before *yawma*.

It is also permitted that it be coordinated with what precedes it according to what is understood from it, as if it had been said: "They witness the horrors of the Resurrection, and they say," and that it be coordinated with *yarawna* (they see). The clause *la bushra* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) with an implied verb of saying, so the separation by it does no harm. The plural pronoun, according to what Abu Hayyan preferred, refers to them, because they are the ones being spoken of. Al-Tabarsi related from Mujahid and Ibn Juraij that it refers to those who do not hope, meaning: "And those disbelievers say: ﴿حِجْرًا مَحْجُورًا﴾ *(a forbidding, forbidden)*." This is a phrase the Arabs say upon encountering an enemy who has wronged them, or upon the assault of a terrifying calamity. They use it in the place of seeking refuge, asking Allah, Exalted is He, to prevent the hated thing so that it does not reach them. So the meaning is: "We ask Allah, Exalted is He, to prevent that absolutely and to bar it barring."

Al-Khalil said: "A man in the Pre-Islamic period would see a man he feared would kill him during the sacred months, and he would say: 'Ḥijran maḥjuran,' meaning: 'It is forbidden for you to confront me in this month,' so the other would not begin with evil." Abu Ubayda said: "It is a charm (*'awdha*) of the Arabs, which one says when he fears another in the Sanctuary or in a sacred month, when he meets him and there is a blood-feud between them." Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "It is among what the Arabs used, and then their saying '*ḥijran maḥjuran*' was abandoned. This had two meanings for them:

The first is that it is said at refusal: when a person is asked and says that, the questioner knows that he intends to deny him. From this is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

*She yearned for the farthest palm, so I said to her: A forbidding, forbidden, is that not the (desert) sands?*

The other meaning is seeking refuge: when a person travelled and saw what he feared, he said: 'Ḥijran maḥjuran,' meaning: 'Forbidden for you is confronting me.'" End of quotation.

Sibawayh mentioned *ḥijran* (*a forbidding*) among the unchanging accusative verbal nouns (*al-masadir al-manṣuba ghayr al-mutasarrifa*), and that it is obligatory to omit its governing verb. He said: "A man says to a man: 'Will you do such and such?' and he says: '*Ḥijran*.'" It is from *ḥajara* (to bar) when he prevents, because the one seeking refuge asks Allah, Exalted is He, to prevent the hated thing from reaching him. Its original form has an open *ḥa*', and it was read with it, as Abu al-Baqa said. But when they restricted its use to seeking refuge or to refusal, it became like a transmitted term, and when its meaning changed, its form changed from its original, which is the fatḥa (the vowel *a*), to the kasra (the vowel *i*). It has also come with a ḍamma (the vowel *u*), which is the reading of Abu Raja, al-Hasan, and al-Dahhak. It is also said: *ḥijrā* with the feminine *alif* (*alif al-ta'nith*). Similar in its change from its original is "*qa'dak Allah*" with the 'ayn sukun and open *qaf*. Its kasra is reported from al-Mazini, and al-Azhari denied it. Also *qu'aydak*, which is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: Allah the Exalted is your guardian and protector. Then it was transferred to an oath: "*qa'dak* or *qu'aydak Allah, la taf'al*" (By Allah who watches over you, do not do it). Its original is "*bi-iq'ad Allah*" (by Allah's keeping you), that is, His continuing you. Similarly: "*'amarak Allah*" with fatḥa on *ra'* and fatḥa or ḍamma on *'ayn*, which is in the accusative as a verbal noun, then specialized for an oath. Its original is "*bi-ta'mirika Allah*," that is, by your acknowledging to Him continuance. What was mentioned, that it necessarily takes the accusative as a verbal noun with an obligatorily omitted verb, was objected to in *al-Durr al-Masun* by what al-Zamakhshari recited:

*She said, and in it is confusion and terror: "I seek refuge in my Lord from you, and a forbidding."*

For it occurred in it in the nominative. Describing it as "*maḥjuran*" (*forbidden*) is for emphasis, like "*sha'ir sha'ir*" (a poem, a poet), "*mawt mayit*" (death, dying), and "*layl alyal*" (night, very dark). It has been mentioned that *maf'ul* here is for attribution, meaning "possessor of a barring," and it is like *fa'il* which comes for that. It has also been said that it is on metaphorical attribution (*al-isnad al-majazi*), but that is not right.

The meaning is that they ask for the descent of the angels, peace be upon them, and when they see them they dislike meeting them more intensely and they flee from them with great fear, and they say what they used to say upon the descent of a dreadful calamity and the arrival of a terrible force. It was also said: the pronoun in "*yaqulun*" refers to the angels. This was related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, al-Dahhak, Qatada, Ata, and Mujahid, as in *al-Durr al-Manthur*. They said: The angels say to the disbelievers: "*Ḥijran maḥjuran*," meaning: forbidden, prohibited upon you is good tidings; that is, Allah, Exalted is He, has made it forbidden for you. [p. 7] In some reports, they ask the angels, peace be upon them, for good tidings, and they say this to them.

Some said: They mean: "Forbidden, prohibited upon you is Paradise." This was related in *Majma' al-Bayan* from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them). It was also said: it is forgiveness. The making of ﴿حِجْرًا﴾ in the accusative as an object of an implied *ja'ala* (made) is a point of research, as indicated. The apparent meaning, as mentioned, is that this word is used for refusal, which is the first of the two meanings mentioned by al-Farisi. According to this view, "*wa-yaqulun*" is said to be coordinated with what it was coordinated with, on the view that its pronoun refers to the disbelievers. It was also said: it is coordinated with the implied clause *yaqulun* before *la bushra*, which occurs as a circumstantial clause.

Al-Tibi said: It is a circumstantial clause from "*al-mala'ika*" (*the angels*), with the implied "*wa-hum yaqulun*" (*while they say*), like the saying: "I came while I was slapping his face." And on the first view, it is coordinated with "*yarawna*" (*they see*).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 23:**

﴿And We shall turn﴾ means We shall intend and aim, as related from Ibn Abbas. It was also transmitted by Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim, from Mujahid. ﴿To what they did﴾ in the world ﴿of deeds﴾ that are grand, such as maintaining family ties, relieving the distressed, hospitality to the weak, showing kindness to a captive, and other noble and good qualities of theirs, which, had they done them along with faith, they would have obtained their reward for. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa-al-majrur) is an explanatory apposition (bayan) for "ma" (what). The validity of this explanation depends on the indefiniteness (tankir) of the noun, just as the validity of the exception (istithna') in ﴿they assume only a supposition﴾ depends on it. However, the indefiniteness here is for magnification (tafkhim), as we have indicated.

It is also permissible that the phrase be for generalization (ta'mim) and to remove the supposition of a specific reference (ahd) in the relative pronoun. That is, We shall intend every deed they did that was devoid of faith. The first, however, is more suitable to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We shall make it scattered dust﴾, like dust (haba') in its insignificance and its lack of benefit. This, according to what Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, is the glimmer of dust that rises and then vanishes.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it is the spark that flies from the fire when it blazes. In another narration from him, it is the water that is poured out.

From Ya'la ibn Ubayd, it is the ash.

A group transmitted from Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Abu Malik and Amir that it is the ray of the sun in a window (kuwwa), and it seems they meant what is seen in it of dust, as is well known among the lexicographers. Al-Raghib said: "Haba' is the fine particles of dust and whatever is scattered in the air, which does not appear except within the rays of sunlight through a window. It is said: 'The dust haba' yahbu' when it stirs and rises." It is described by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿scattered﴾, as an intensification in nullifying their deeds. For you see dust haba' arranged with the light, but when the wind moves it, it scatters and goes every way. So it was not enough that their deeds were likened to haba', until He made it scattered, unable to be gathered or benefited from at all. A sequence of this kind is called in rhetoric (al-badi') "tatmim" (completion) and "iygal" (overreaching). From it is the saying of al-Khansa:

A bright, radiant one, the guided take him as their model,
as if on his head is a banner of fire.

Here she did not suffice with making him a banner of guidance, until she made fire upon his head.

It has also been said that it was described as scattered (mansur), that is, dispersed, because their aims in their deeds are dispersed. Thus making their deeds into scattered dust is a recompense of the same kind as the deed. It is also permissible that it be a second object after a first object of (ja'ala), and this is the meaning intended by one who said: "a third object for it," meaning: We made it combining the insignificance of dust and dispersal. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾, that is: combining transformation and expulsion. Ibn Durustawayh disagreed with this, as he did not permit that it be the predicate of "inna" (kana being the predicate of inna), and by analogy to his position, one must prohibit that ja'ala have a third object. Nevertheless, the apparent reading is that it is a descriptor (wasfiyya). In the statement there is a figurative metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), in which the state of these disbelievers and the state of their deeds that they did in their disbelief are depicted by the state of a people who opposed their ruler and rebelled against him. So he (the ruler) advanced toward their possessions and aimed at what was under their control, corrupted them, and made them shattered and scattered, leaving nothing of them, no trace or sign. The borrowed word in it is used as "qadima" (advanced) with the meaning of "amada" and "qasada" (intended and aimed), due to its common usage in that sense, although it is a metaphor, as the statement of al-Asas indicates. The aim that reaches its destination is called "qudum" (arrival), because it is its precursor. The depiction included the comparison of their nullified deeds to scattered dust without metaphor, so there is no difficulty according to what has been said. The discussion on this is lengthy, so it should be sought in its proper place.

Some scholars took the "qudum" (coming) regarding Him, Mighty and Majestic, to be an expression for His judgment. It has also been said that the statement has an elided modifier, that is: "Our angels advanced," and that this was attributed to Him, Mighty and Majestic, because it was by His command, Glorified is He. It was reported from some of the early scholars (salaf) that it should not be interpreted in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾, and His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾, as is their habit regarding the ambiguous attributes. By analogy, this indicates that the verse should not be interpreted. Perhaps it is from here that it was said: the interpretation of Zamakhshari of these verses is based on his creed of denying the attributes, and inclination toward interpretation in them is more appealing.

If you do not interpret the "qudum," then you must interpret their being made into scattered dust by showing their complete nullity and removing them from any level of consideration in any respect. The early scholars do not object to that.

[p. 8]

The companions of the Garden (﴿Aṣḥāb al-Janna﴾) are the believers referred to in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised?"﴾ ﴿On that day﴾, meaning the day on which what was mentioned will occur, namely their coming to their deeds and making them ﴿scattered dust﴾, or, alternatively, [it refers to] this [day] and the absence of glad tidings and their saying: ﴿a forbidding, forbidden [barrier]﴾. ﴿Better in resting place (mustaqarr)﴾: the mustaqarr is the place in which one settles for most of the time, for sitting together and conversing. ﴿And finer in place of repose (maqīl)﴾: the maqīl is the place to which one retires for relaxation, for [enjoyment of] wives and delighting in their companionship. It was so named because enjoyment in it usually occurs at the time of the qaylūla (the midday nap). It has been said that it is originally the place of the qaylūla, which is sleeping at midday, and it was transferred from that to the place of enjoying wives, because it resembles it in that each of them is a place of seclusion and rest. Thus it is a metaphor (istiʿāra). It has also been said that it is intended to mean a place of repose in general, using the restricted term for the general, so it is a figurative usage of the metonymic type (majāz mursal). It did not remain on its original sense because there is no sleep in the Garden at all.

Ibn al-Mubārak in al-Zuhd, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Ḥākim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "The middle of the day will not reach its midpoint on the Day of Resurrection until these and those have taken their qaylūla." Then he recited: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in resting place and finer in place of repose﴾, and he recited: "Indeed their maqīl is toward the Blazing Fire." Some of them drew from this that what is meant by al-mustaqarr is the place of reckoning, and by al-maqīl the place of rest after finishing from it. The meaning of "takes his qaylūla" is that the companions of the Garden are transported to it at the time of the qaylūla. It has also been said that al-mustaqarr and al-maqīl refer to the place of gathering before entering the Garden, or that al-mustaqarr is within it and al-maqīl is also within it.

Ibn Jarīr related from Saʿīd al-Ṣawwāf who said: "It reached me that on the Day of Resurrection [the day] will be shortened for the believer until it is like the period between the afternoon prayer and sunset, and they will take their qaylūla in gardens until the people finish from the reckoning." This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in resting place and finer in place of repose﴾. The description of it with added fineness, while being better, by coupling it with al-mustaqarr, is a symbol that for them is what they are adorned with of beauty of forms and other embellishments. For the fineness of a dwelling, if it is not considered in relation to its occupant, the pleasure in it is not complete. The preference considered in both is pleasure, either intending excess in absolute terms, meaning they are at the utmost of goodness of resting place and fineness of repose, or relative to what the disbelieving people enjoying luxury in this world have, [page 9] or relative to what they have in the Hereafter by way of mockery toward them.

This, and explaining al-mustaqarr and al-maqīl as two places, as you have heard, is the well-known view, and it is one of nine possibilities. This is because they permitted that each of the two be a noun of place, or a noun of time, or a verbal noun, and that the first be a noun of place while the second is a noun of time or a verbal noun, and that the first be a noun of time while the second is a noun of place or a verbal noun, and that the first be a verbal noun while the second is a noun of place or a noun of time. Imagine whatever you wish regarding the goodness of the time of the companions of the Garden and its finest quality, and likewise regarding the goodness of their settling and the finest quality of their rest on that day.

The verb governing "on the day" (yawma) is either "remember" (udhkur), or it is the exclusive sovereignty of God, the Most High, indicated by His saying: ﴿The sovereignty on that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾. It has also been said that the governing verb is that same expression in its previously mentioned sense. It has further been said that it is in apposition to "on that day" (yawma'idhin) or to "the day they see" (yawma yarawna). "Tashaqqaqu" means "is split open." The use of this form rather than a simpler one is for the sake of awe-inspiring terror. Its original form is "tatashaqqaqu," and one of the two tā' letters was dropped, as in ﴿a blazing fire (talaẓẓā)﴾. The two Ḥaramayn (the scholars of Makkah and Madinah) and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with the tā' assimilated into the shīn, because of the closeness between them. The apparent meaning is that "the sky" refers to what shades us, and "the cloud" refers to the well-known clouds. The bāʾ that precedes it is the bāʾ of causation, meaning: the sky is split open because of the emergence of the clouds from it. There is no obstacle to its being split by them, just as a camel's hump is cut with a knife. God is capable of all things. The notion that the sky cannot be pierced is a fable.

It has been said that the bāʾ is the bāʾ of circumstance, which is the bāʾ of accompaniment, and some of them preferred this view. The meaning is: the sky is split open while being overcast.

It has been said that it means "from" (ʿan), and al-Farrāʾ held this view.

The difference between your saying "the earth split open with the plants" (inshaqqat al-arḍu bi-l-nabāt) and "the earth split open from it" (inshaqqat ʿanhu) is that the meaning of the first is that God split it by the emergence of the plants, so it was split by them, while the meaning of the second is that the soil rose up from it when it emerged.

It has been said that the cloud here means a white, thin cloud like mist, and that it was only for the Children of Israel during their wandering (tīh).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted, on the authority of Mujāhid, that it is the cloud in which God will come on the Day of Resurrection, the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them in canopies of cloud?﴾ Ibn Jurayj said: "It is a cloud which they claim is in Paradise."

On the authority of Muqatil, the meaning of "the sky" is that which includes all the heavens, and "the sky is split open" means heaven by heaven. This was also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in al-Ahwāl, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim all transmitted from him (may God be pleased with him) that he recited this verse up to His saying: ﴿and the angels are sent down in a sending down﴾, meaning a marvelous sending down, unlike anything known. He said: God will gather creation on the Day of Resurrection in one plain: the jinn, humankind, the beasts, the predators, the birds, and all creation. Then the lowest heaven will be split open and its inhabitants will descend, and they will be more numerous than those on the earth of jinn, humankind, and all creation. They will surround all of them, and the people of the earth will say: "Is our Lord among you?" They will say: "No." Then the second heaven will be split open and its inhabitants will descend, and they will be more numerous than the people of the lowest heaven, the jinn, humankind, and all creation. They will surround the angels who descended before them, and the jinn, humankind, and all creation. Then the third heaven will be split open and its inhabitants will descend, and they will be more numerous than the people of the second heaven, the lowest, and all creation. They will surround the angels who descended before them, and the jinn, humankind, and all creation. Then the people of the fourth heaven will descend, and they will be more numerous than the people of the third, second, and first heavens and the people of the earth. Then the people of the fifth heaven will descend, and they will be more numerous than those who preceded them. Then the people of the sixth heaven likewise, then the people of the seventh heaven, and they will be more numerous than the people of the heavens and the people of the earth. Then our Lord will descend in canopies of cloud, and around Him will be the Karūbiyyūn (cherubim), and they will be more numerous than the people of the seven heavens, humankind, the jinn, and all creation. They have horns like the knots of spears, and they are beneath the Throne. They have a loud chanting of glorification, declaration of God's oneness, and sanctification of God, the Most High. The distance between the sole of one of them and his ankle is a five-hundred-year journey, and from his thigh to his collarbone is a five-hundred-year journey, and from his collarbone to the place of the earring is a five-hundred-year journey, and what is above that is five hundred years.

[page 10]

The descent of the Lord, majestic and exalted, is among the mutashābih (ambiguous verses whose meaning is not to be taken literally). Likewise His saying: "And around Him are the Karūbiyyūn." The people of ta'wīl (figurative interpretation) say: what is meant by this is the descent of His command and decree, as if it were said: "Then the command of the Lord will descend, and around Him are the Karūbiyyūn," meaning with Him. As for the descent of the angels, despite their great number and the magnitude of their bodies, it is not prevented by what is observed of the smallness of the earth, because on that day the earth will expand so that it contains its inhabitants and the inhabitants of all the heavens. Glory be to Him, whom nothing can overpower.

Then the report clearly indicates that the angels, peace be upon them, do not descend within the cloud. Some of them mentioned in the verse that the sky will open with a cloud that comes out of it, and within the cloud the angels will descend, and in their hands will be the scrolls of deeds.

Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Rajāʾ read ﴿wa-nazzala﴾ as a past-tense verb, active, with doubled zāy. It is also narrated from him: ﴿wa-anzala﴾ as an active verb. Its verbal noun is "tanzīlan," whereas its regular form would be "inzālan." However, since "anzala" and "nazzala" have the same meaning, the verbal noun of one was used for the other, as the poet said:

Until I folded myself in the folding of the ... (khiṣb)
As if he said: "until I was folded up."

Al-Aʿmash and ʿAbd Allāh, according to Ibn ʿAṭiyya's transmission, read ﴿wa-unzila﴾ as a past-tense, four-letter-root verb in the passive voice. Jināḥ ibn Ḥubaysh and al-Khaffāf on the authority of Abū ʿAmr read ﴿wa-nazala﴾ as a three-letter, unstressed verb in the active voice. Abū Muʿādh and Kharija, on the authority of Abū ʿAmr, read ﴿wa-nuzzila﴾ with a damma on the nūn, a shadda on the zāy, and a kasra or fatḥa variant, with "al-malāʾikatu" in the accusative. Ibn Jinnī attributed this reading to Ibn Kathīr and the people of Makkah, and explained it on the basis that the original was "nunazzilu," as found in some copies of the Qurʾān. The nūn that is the first radical of the verb was dropped for ease, to avoid the meeting of two nūns. Ubayy read ﴿wa-nuzzilat﴾ as a past-tense, doubled, passive verb with a feminine tā'. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said, on the authority of al-Khaffāf on the authority of Abū ʿAmr: ﴿wa-nuzila﴾ unstressed and passive, with "al-malāʾikatu" in the nominative. If this reading is sound, then the genitive-governed noun has been dropped from it, and the noun in the genitive has been placed in its position. The estimate is: "and there was a descent of the descending of the angels," so the "descending" was dropped and its grammatical case was transferred to "the angels," meaning "the descender of the angels was made to descend," since a verbal noun can have the meaning of a noun. End of quotation.

Al-Ṭībī said: Ibn Jinnī said: "nuzila" in the passive is not known, because "nuzila" does not take a direct object, and it cannot be analogized to "junna" (which is intransitive, so one does not say "Allah junnahu," but rather "ajannahu Allāh"). It has been used in the passive because it is anomalous, and analogy based on it is rejected. Either this is a rare dialectal usage, or it is an omission of a genitive-governed noun, meaning: "there was a descent of the descending of the angels," so the noun was dropped and the noun in the genitive placed in its position. Al-ʿAjjāj said:

Until, when they lined up before him in caution (ḥidhāran)
Here "ḥidhāran" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, not as a direct object, meaning: "they lined up before him in a lining-up made from caution." And "nuzila nuzūla al-malāʾikati" is like your saying: "this is a descent that is descended," "an ascent that is ascended," and "a striking that is struck," and similar to it. It has been said "a saying was said" and "a fear was feared from it." Understand this, for it is the best thing used to argue for this reading. End of quotation.

This is better than the words of the author of al-Lawāmiḥ. Also from Abū ʿAmr, it is narrated that he read ﴿wa-tanazzalati al-malāʾikatu﴾ (and the angels descended). These, together with the reading of the majority and what appears in some copies, make ten readings. As for those that have the imperfect form, their basis is clear. As for those in the past tense, their basis, as has been said, is an indication of the swiftness of the action.

﴿The dominion on that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾. That is, the overpowering sovereignty and the comprehensive, general control, established in form and in meaning, outwardly and inwardly, such that it never ceases, belongs to the Most Merciful on the Day when the heaven splits open and the angels descend. So *al-mulk* is the *mubtada'* (subject), *al-haqq* is its *sifa* (attribute), *li-l-Rahman* is its *khabar* (predicate), and *yawma'idhin* is a *zarf* (adverbial complement) for the establishment of the predicate of the subject. The benefit of the restriction is that the dominion's belonging to Him, Exalted is He, is specific to that Day. As for the other days of the world, others also have some nominal disposition in some respect. Some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqin*) chose this view. Perhaps the matter of separating the attribute from the qualified noun by the mentioned adverbial complement is easy.

It was said: *al-malik* is the subject, *yawma'idhin* is related to it, and it has the meaning of ownership (*al-malikiyya*), *al-haqq* is its predicate, and *li-l-Rahman* is related to *al-haqq*. This was criticized: then the point of presenting the predicate in definite form does not appear, for the apparent wording would be: "The dominion on that Day is a truth belonging to the Most Merciful." It was answered: in its being related to what was mentioned there is emphasis for what conveys the definiteness of both parts. It was said: it is related to a deleted element, as an explanation (*tabyin*), as in *saqyan laka* (سَقْيًا لَكَ), and the explained element is "for whom the dominion is." It was said: it is related to a deleted element that occurred as an attribute of *al-haqq*, and this is, as you see, [weak]. It was said: *yawma'idhin* is the predicate and *al-haqq* is an adjective of *al-mulk*, and *li-l-Rahman* is related to it. In this there is a separation between the attribute and the qualified noun by the predicate, so do not be heedless.

They prohibited relating *yawma'idhin*, when it is not the predicate, to *al-haqq*, and justified this by saying that it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and the complement of a *masdar* may not precede it even if it is an adverbial complement. In this there is room for discussion. The sentence, according to most of the earlier possibilities concerning the governing element of *yawm* (يَوْم), is an independent resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) brought to explain the conditions of that Day and its terrors. His mention by the title of *al-Rahmaniyya* is to signal that His being characterized by utmost mercy does not make the matter easy for the disbelievers, to which He refers by His saying: ﴿and it was a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾. That is: that Day was severe for the disbelievers, despite the dominion being His, the One who exceeds in mercy toward His servants. The intended meaning is the severity of the terrors in it. Al-Rāghib (الراغب) explained *'asir* (عَسِير) as that in which nothing is made easy. The sentence is a concluding parenthetical (*i'tiradh tadhyili*) that confirms what precedes it, and in it there is an indication that the Day is easy for the believers. In a hadith: "It will be made light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer that he prayed in the world."

Page 11

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 27:

﴿And on the Day when the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾ Al-Tabarsi said: The governing element (al-'amil) of "yawma" (on the day) is an omitted verb, "remember" (udhkur). It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with what precedes it. The apparent reading is that the definite article in "al-zalim" (the wrongdoer) is generic (li-l-jins), so it encompasses every wrongdoer. Abu Hayyan related this from Mujahid and Abu Raja'. It is also mentioned that what is meant by "fulan" (so-and-so), in what follows, is Satan. It has also been said that the article is for specific reference (li-ta'rif al-'ahd), and that what is meant by "the wrongdoer" is 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, may Allah curse him, and by "so-and-so" Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It has been narrated that 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt would not arrive from a journey without preparing a meal and inviting all the people of Makkah to it. He used to frequently sit with the Prophet ﷺ and was pleased with his speech, but wretchedness overcame him. One day he arrived from a journey, prepared a meal, then invited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to his food. He said: "I will not eat of your food until you bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah." He said: "Eat, O son of my brother." The Prophet ﷺ said: "I will not do it until you say it." So he bore witness to that, and the Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him, ate of his food. This news reached Ubayy ibn Khalaf, so he came to him and said: "Have you turned away, O 'Uqba?!" He was his close friend. 'Uqba said: "By Allah, I have not turned away, but a man entered my house and refused to eat of my food unless I bore witness for him. I was ashamed that he should leave my house before eating, so I bore witness for him, and he ate." Ubayy said: "I will not be pleased with you until you go to him and do such-and-such," and he mentioned an act that befits only the accursed speaker. So 'Uqba did it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "If I meet you outside Makkah, I will strike your head with the sword."

In another narration: "If I find you outside the mountains of Makkah, I will strike your neck in cold blood." When the day of Badr came and his companions went out, he refused to go out. His companions said to him: "Come out with us." He said: "This man has promised me that if he finds me outside the mountains of Makkah, he will strike my neck in cold blood." They said: "You have a red camel that cannot be overtaken; if there is a defeat, you can fly away on it." So he went out with them. When Allah the Exalted routed the polytheists, his camel carried him off into the rough terrain, and he was taken captive along with seventy men from Quraysh. He was brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he ordered 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, to strike his neck.

Page 12

In the narration of Thabit ibn Abi al-Aflah, [it says] that he should strike his neck. He said: "Will you kill me from among these people?" He said: "Yes." He said: "For what?" He said: "For your disbelief, your wickedness, and your arrogance against Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace." In another narration, the Prophet ﷺ explicitly told him what he had done to him, and then his neck was struck.

As for Ubayy ibn Khalaf, despite his doing that, he said: "By Allah, I will surely kill Muhammad ﷺ." This news reached the Messenger of Allah, upon him be blessings and peace, and he said: "Rather, I will kill him, God willing." That frightened him, and he said to the one who informed him: "I adjure you by Allah the Exalted, did you hear him say that?" He said: "Yes." So it struck his heart, since they knew that the Messenger of Allah ṣallā Allāh ta'ālā 'alayhi wa sallam never said a word except that it was true. When the day of Uhud came, he went out with the polytheists and began seeking the Prophet's inattention in order to attack him. A man from the Muslims came between the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, and him. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw that, he said to his companions: "Leave him alone." So he took a spear and threw it at him, and it struck his collarbone. Not much blood came out of him, but the blood gathered inside his body, and he fell bellowing like a bull. His companions came and carried him while he was bellowing. They said: "What is this? By Allah, there is nothing wrong with you but a scratch." He said: "By Allah, if he had struck me only with his spittle, it would have killed me. Did he not say: 'I will kill him'? By Allah, if what is in me were distributed among the people of Dhu al-Majaz, it would kill them all." He did not remain more than a day or so until he went to the Fire. Then Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. This statement is also related from Ibn 'Abbas and a group.

In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, the wrongdoer is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and "so-and-so" is 'Uqba. As for biting the hands, it is either on its apparent sense, and this is related from al-Dahhak and a group who said: he eats his hands up to the elbow, then they grow back, and he continues thus, each time he eats them they regrow. Or it is a metaphor for extreme regret and remorse. Likewise biting the fingertips, falling into one's hands (remorse), gnashing the teeth and gnawing the lips, and the like, because these are in custom and convention accompaniments of that. In the proverb: "He eats his hands in regret, and his tears flow as blood." The poet said:

He refused humiliation while al-Nu'man burns his tooth against him, so he was brought low while the swords were his refuge.

The verb "'add" (bite) follows the pattern fa'ila with a kasra on the 'ayn, and al-Kisa'i related "'adadtu" with a fatha on the 'ayn.

﴿He will say: "Oh, would that I had taken a way with the Messenger!"﴾ The sentence "with the Messenger" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the wrongdoer," or it is a resumptive sentence, or it explains what precedes it. And "Oh, would that I..." etc. is the content of the saying. "Ya" is either merely for alerting, without intending to specify the one alerted, or the addressee is omitted: "Oh my people, would that I..." The article in "al-Rasul" (the Messenger) is either generic, encompassing every messenger, or for specific reference, so that it means the Messenger of this community, Muhammad ﷺ. The first applies when the article in "al-zalim" is generic, and the second when it is for specific reference. The indefiniteness of "sabilan" (a way) is either for generality or for unity. Leaving it undefined implies that its identity is fixed: that is, "Oh, would that I had taken a path to salvation, whatever path it was, or a single path, which is the path of truth, and the paths of error had not scattered me."

﴿Woe is me!﴾ With the ya' of the first person changed to an alif, as in ṣaḥārā (in the pronunciation "yā waylatā"). Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Quṭayb read it as (yā waylatī) with a kasra on the tā' and the yā', in accordance with the original form. A group read it with imālah (inclination of the vowel toward i). Abū ʿAlī said: "Leaving out the imālah is better, because the original form of this word is with a yā'. The kasra was changed to a fatḥah and the yā' to an alif in order to flee from the yā'. Whoever uses imālah returns to what he first fled from." In any case, the meaning is: "O my destruction! Come, and be present, for this is your time."

﴿Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend.﴾ By "so-and-so" (fulān) he meant Satan, or whoever led him astray in this world, whoever he may be; or Ubayy if the wrongdoer was ʿUqbah, or ʿUqbah if the wrongdoer was Ubayy. It is a kināyah (a pronoun-like reference) for a masculine proper name, and fulānah for a feminine proper name. Ibn al-Ḥājib stipulated that fulān must be quoted speech, as it is here. Ibn Hishām in Sharḥ al-Tashīl refuted this, saying that it is frequently heard otherwise, as in the words of the poet:

"And when so-and-so dies, leaving a noble deed,
they have relieved the needs of his poverty through so-and-so."

The implied saying in it is not clear. Fulān and fulānah are a kināyah for a non-rational being among animals, as al-Rāghib said. Full (fulluh) and fullah are a kināyah for an indefinite rational being: the first means "a man" and the second means "a woman." Ibn ʿUṣfūr, Ibn Mālik, and the author of al-Basīṭ made a mistake, as is mentioned in al-Baḥr, in their saying that full is a kināyah for a proper name like fulān. It is specific to vocative use except in cases of necessity, as in the words of the poet:

"In a deep sea, so-and-so withheld from full."

The diminutive form (murakhkham) of fulān is not used, contrary to al-Farrāʾ. They disagreed about the final letter of full and fulān: it was said to be a wāw, and it was said to be a yā'. They used hann, with a fatḥah on the hā' and a light nūn, as a kināyah for common nouns very frequently. It has also been used as a kināyah for proper names, as in the words of the poet:

"God has given you grace beyond His gift
upon hann and hann, in the past and hann."

According to what al-Khafājī said, he meant ʿAbd Allāh, Ibrāhīm, and Ḥasan. The khalīl (close friend) is from al-khullah, with a ḍammah on the khā', meaning affection. This term was applied to it either because it penetrates (yatakhallalu) the soul, that is, enters into its midst, and the poet recited:

"You have penetrated the path of the spirit within me,
and by this the khalīl was named khalīl."

Or because it pierces it and affects it like an arrow affects its target. Or because of the extreme need for it. This wish, though it is brought forth to express regret and grief, nevertheless contains a kind of excuse and justification by shifting the blame for his offence onto another.

And His Exalted saying

[Page 13]

The explanation of his stated wish mentioned above, and a clarification of his excuse. Beginning it with the oath particle *al-lam al-qasamiyya* (the lam of swearing) emphasises the extent of his error and displays his regret and anguish. The meaning is: "By Allah, indeed so-and-so has led me astray from the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, or from the admonition of the Messenger (ﷺ), or from the word of testimony (*kalimat al-shahada*), or from the Qur'an, ﴿after it had come to me﴾," i.e., after it reached me and I came to know it, or after I had become firmly acquainted with it. Therefore the verse contains no evidence for the faith of the one about whom it was revealed followed by his apostasy. ﴿And Satan is ever a deserter of man﴾, exaggerating in *khudhlan* (abandonment), which is withholding help and support at a time of need from one who is expected to give it. This sentence is a parenthetical statement (*i'tiraD*) confirming the meaning of what precedes it, either from Allah's side, or as part of the speech of the wrongdoer himself, in which he calls his close friend "Satan" after describing him with misguidance (*al-idlal*), which is the most specific of the satanic attributes. Alternatively, he meant by "Satan" Iblis, because he is the one who drove him to sit with the misguiders and to oppose the Guiding Messenger (ﷺ), through his whispering and seduction. The description of him with *khudhlan* indicates that he used to promise him in this world and hold out hopes to him that he would benefit him in the Hereafter, and this is more fitting to the condition of Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him.

﴿And the Messenger says﴾ is in ʿaṭf (coordination, grammatically linked to) his saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say﴾ and so on. What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) brought to magnify what they said and to explain the terrors and calamities that will befall them. By "the Messenger" is meant our Prophet (ﷺ), may Allah exalt, honour, glorify and ennoble him. Mentioning him (peace be upon him) by the title of messengerhood serves to establish the truth and to refute them, since what is reported of them amounted to a disparagement of his messengerhood (ﷺ). That is, they said such-and-such things, and the Messenger, upon witnessing from them the utmost arrogance and the extreme of transgression, complained to his Lord, mighty and majestic, and lodged his grievance against them, saying: ﴿My Lord, indeed my people﴾, those whom He has reported as making the shameful statements He has recounted, ﴿have taken this Qur'an﴾, the one of exalted station that contains what is good for their livelihood and their hereafter, ﴿as something abandoned﴾, that is, completely forsaken. They did not believe in it, they did not pay it any attention, and they were not affected by its threat or its promise. So "mahjūran" (abandoned) is from hajr, with the hā' vowelled with a fatḥa, meaning abandonment; this is the apparent sense. This was reported from Mujahid, al-Nakhaʿi and others. Ibn al-Faras took this verse as evidence for the disapproval of leaving the copy of the Qur'an (muṣḥaf) unattended and not regularly reading in it. That is so that whoever does not regularly read in it is not included under the apparent meaning of the noble wording, for its apparent sense is condemnation of abandonment in every form. Even if what is meant is non-acceptance and not mere neglect while accepting, the verse does not cover both. If such a thing suffices as evidence, well and good; otherwise another proof for the disapproval must be sought.

Some have cited a report which says: "Whoever learns the Qur'an and hangs its copy, not regularly consulting it or looking into it, will come on the Day of Resurrection clinging to it, saying: 'O Lord, this servant of Yours has taken me as abandoned; judge between me and him.'" Al-ʿIraqi criticized this report, saying that it was narrated from Abu Hudba, who was a liar. The truth is that whenever that act undermines reverence for the Qur'an and care for it, it is disapproved, indeed prohibited; otherwise it is not.

It has also been said that "mahjūran" is from hujr (with a ḍamma, which is the well-known vowelling), meaning idle talk and foul speech. The sentence then involves ellipsis (ḥadhf) and transitivity by a preposition (īṣāl), meaning: they made it a thing of idle talk regarding it, either by their false claim, as in their saying that it is "the fables of the ancients which he has written down," or by their raising their voices with idle talk while it was being recited, so that it would not be heard, as they said: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it﴾. It is also permissible that it be a verbal noun (maṣdar) from hujr with a ḍamma, like "al-maʿqūl" meaning reason and "al-majlūd" meaning endurance, that is: they took it as sheer idle talk and nonsense. The use of a passive form (mafʿūl) as a verbal noun is affirmed by the Kufans, but it is rare. In this complaint there is considerable warning and admonition that is not hidden, for when the prophets (peace be upon them) complained to Allah the Exalted about their peoples, the punishment was hastened upon them and they were not given respite.

It has also been said that "qāla" (said) and what follows is coordinated with ﴿the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾, and the meaning is: "and the Messenger will say." However, the past tense was used to express certainty of occurrence, while not intending the renewed, continuous sense, which is indicated by the context in some respects, although this is information about the Hereafter.

As for its coordination with ﴿and Satan has been a betrayer to man﴾ and so on, on the basis that it is part of His speech, exalted is He, its status is not hidden. The Messenger's saying this on the Day of Resurrection is like a testimony against those disbelievers and is not a warning. A group, among them Abu Muslim, held this view, but the first is more fitting with His saying, exalted is He:

[Page 14]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 31:

﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals.﴾ This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and an encouragement for him to follow the example of the prophets before him, peace be upon them. Calamity, when it is widespread, becomes easier to bear. The word "enemy" (ʿaduww) may be singular or plural. That is, just as We have made for you enemies from among the polytheists, who say what they say and do what they do of falsehoods, so We have made for every prophet among the prophets, who are the bearers of the Sharia (sharīʿa, sacred law) and the callers to it, an enemy from among the perpetrators of crimes and sins. This includes Adam (peace be upon him), since the satans are included, and Qabil (Cain) is included among the criminals. It suffices to include Qabil if by "the criminals" is meant the criminals of mankind or the criminals of the Prophet's community. It has also been said that the universality (of "every") is intended to mean abundance. By "making enemies" is meant making their enmity and creating it, and what arises from it in them, not making their essences (enemies). In this there is a refutation of the Mu'tazila, who claim that the creator of evil is other than Him, exalted is His majesty.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a guide and a helper.﴾ This is a generous promise to him, upon him be prayers and peace, of guidance to all his aims and of victory over his enemies. That is, your Lord, the Master of your affair and the one who brings you to perfection, is sufficient as a guide to you toward what leads you to the ultimate goal, among which is conveying what has been revealed to you and implementing its rulings throughout the world until the Book reaches its appointed term; and (sufficient as) a helper to you against them in the most eloquent manner.

Some have construed the complement of ﴿guide﴾ as "to the path of subduing them." It has also been said: the meaning is a guide for those among them who believe, and a helper for you against others. It has also been said: a guide for the prophets to avoid the enmity of the criminals by holding fast to His rope, and a helper for them against them; but this, as you see, is (weak). The two descriptive words are in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or as a specification (tamyīz).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 32:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾ This is a report of another kind of their falsehoods. By "those who disbelieve" are meant the polytheists, as is authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas, and they are the ones who said this earlier. Describing them by the title of disbelief serves to censure them for it and to indicate the reason for the ruling. It is also said that those meant are a group of the Jews. ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down upon him﴾ means: why was it not revealed to him, with "was sent down" (nuzzila) being in the sense of "was informed" (ukhbira)? So there is no intention in it of gradualness, because of ﴿all at once﴾. For if that were intended, the two would contradict each other, since the meaning would become "why was the Qur'an not divided all at once," and division contradicts "all at once." It is also said: it was expressed in this way to indicate the great quantity of what was revealed in itself. ﴿Jumlatan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and ﴿wahidatan﴾ is an emphasizing attribute of it. The meaning is: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, in one go, undivided, just as the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms were sent down," as the hadiths and reports indicate, to the point that it nearly amounts to a consensus, as al-Suyuti said. He refuted those among the eminent scholars of his age who denied this. Thus the statement of Ibn al-Kamal, that the Torah was sent down in installments over eighteen years, and that the texts of the Torah indicate this with no definitive proof to the contrary from the Book or the Sunnah, arises from a lack of knowledge.

This objection is of no benefit, because miraculousness is not affected by whether it is revealed all at once or in parts. Moreover, gradual revelation has benefits, among them what Allah the Exalted mentions after this. It has also been said: the evidence for the authenticity of the Qur'an is its miraculousness, and that is through its eloquence, and its eloquence lies in its conformity to the requirement of the situation in every sentence of it. This cannot be easily achieved in its being sent down all at once, so it cannot be compared with the other books, for the evidence for the authenticity of those is not miraculousness. Yet in this there is an objection: his saying "cannot be easily achieved" and so on is disputed, for it is possible that it be sent down all at once while observing the stated conformity in every sentence to the events that occur which match it and indicate its rulings.

It is authentically established that it descended in this way to the lowest heaven. Had this not been so, it would follow that it would not be miraculous there, and no one holds this. Indeed, it may be said that this is stronger for its miraculousness. The eloquent person understands from the context of the speech what the situation requires, so understand.

﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾: this is a resumptive statement coming from Him, the Exalted, to refute their false claim and to explain some of the wisdoms in its being sent down gradually. The place of the kaf is in the accusative, being an attribute of an emphasizing verbal noun for an implied verb, which is causally linked to what follows it. It is also permitted for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state. "Thus" (dhalika) is a reference to what is understood from their speech, meaning: a revelation like that revelation which they criticized and whose opposite they proposed, We sent it down, not a revelation different from it; or, We sent it down similar to that revelation, so that We might strengthen your heart by it. For in its being sent down in parts there is facilitation for memorizing the arrangement, understanding the meanings, mastering the speech, and grasping the details of the wisdoms and interests taken into account in it, and in the multiplicity of Jibril's descents, and in the renewed challenge to its detractors in each sentence, equal to the length of the shortest surah that descends from it. There are also benefits other than those mentioned: among them is knowing the abrogating text that was revealed later from the abrogated text that was revealed earlier and contradicts its ruling; and among them is the combining of contextual indicators with verbal indications, for this helps in recognizing eloquence, since by looking at the situation the listener becomes alert to what agrees with and matches it, and to other things besides.

It is also said that the statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Thus﴾, is part of the speech of the disbelievers, and the kaf is in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the Qur'an, or as an attribute of the verbal noun of the mentioned verb "was sent down," or of "jumlatan." The reference is to the sending down of the earlier books. The lam in ﴿that We may strengthen﴾ is the lam of causation, and the thing caused is omitted, like what you heard at the beginning, meaning: We sent it down in parts so that We may strengthen, and so on. Abu Hatim said: it is the lam of oath, and the estimate is: "By Allah, We will surely strengthen," so the nun was dropped and the lam was given a kasra. Abu Hayyan related this from him, and the apparent meaning is that it is according to him in both views regarding "thus." He criticized this, saying it is a view of extreme weakness. It seems he leans toward the school of al-Akhfash, that the answer to an oath may be introduced by the lam of kay, and he cited from it "and that the hearts may incline to it" and so on, but this is a weaker view. 'Abdullah recited "li-yuthabbita" with the ya, meaning: that Allah the Exalted may strengthen.

The statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And We have arranged it in arrangement﴾, is coordinated with the omitted verb which is causally linked to what has been mentioned. The indefiniteness of "tartilan" is for exaltation, meaning: thus We sent it down and arranged it in a wondrous arrangement whose measure cannot be estimated. Its tartil is its separation verse after verse. This was said by al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan and Qatadah. Ibn 'Abbas said: We clarified it with a clarification that has deliberateness in it. al-Suddi said: We detailed it in detail. Mujahid said: We made some of it follow upon some. It has also been said: it is the command to recite it with measured recitation, by the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾. It has also been said: We recited it to you through the tongue of Jibril, peace be upon him, little by little, over twenty or twenty-three years, with deliberation and unhurried pace. It is derived from the saying of them: "a measured thaghr," meaning one whose teeth are spaced apart and not pressed together.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 33:

﴿And they do not bring you any similitude﴾ from among the similitudes, of which are their ugly proposals that lie outside the sphere of sound reason and are treated in that way as similitudes. That is: they do not bring you any strange speech that is a similitude in falsehood, which they intend as a means of discrediting your prophethood and which they display to you, ﴿but We bring you﴾ in response to it ﴿with the truth﴾, that is, with the true and established answer by which it is refuted, which cuts off the matter of idle talk, as has passed concerning the sound answers that uproot their vile questions and completely demolish them. His words, exalted is He, ﴿and a better explanation﴾ (ahsan tafsiran) are coordinated with "the truth" (al-haqq), meaning: We bring you with a better explanation, that is, with what is better. Or they are coordinated with the position of "with the truth" (bi-al-haqq), meaning: We have brought to you and sent down to you the truth and a better explanation (tafsir, here meaning disclosure and clarification), in the sense that it is at the utmost of goodness in itself, not that what they bring has some goodness while this is better than it. This is like their saying "Allah is greatest" (Allahu akbar), meaning He has the utmost of greatness in Himself. Some supplied a comparative object, saying: that is, and a better explanation than their similitude and its goodness according to their claim. Or it is mockery (tahakkum). The first view has been criticized on the ground that it loses the sense of consolation, because the intended meaning is: what they propose, such as their saying ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ does not harm you, for its being sent down gradually is better than what they propose, for various benefits. In this there is clear objection. It has also been said: the intended meaning of tafsir is meaning (ma'na), and the intended sense is: and a better meaning, because it is said "the tafsir of such-and-such is such-and-such," meaning its meaning. So it is a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle, since the meaning is explained (mufassar), like "a dirham of the amir's minting." This has been rebutted on the ground that the mufassar, as a passive participle, is the speech itself, not the meaning, since one says "I explained the speech" (fassartu al-kalam), not "I explained its meaning."

Al-Tayyibi said: tafsir was placed in the position of meaning, by the figure of putting the cause in place of the effect, because tafsir is the cause of the manifestation and disclosure of the meaning. It has been objected to this that there is a difference between the meaning and its manifestation, so the approximation does not hold. But it may suffice to consider it a cause of it in general.

Whatever the case, it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The exception is an exceptive construction lacking its object (mustathna mufarragh) from the most general of states, so the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial (hal). That is: they do not bring you any similitude in any state, except the state of Our sending down to you and bringing to you the truth and a better explanation. This state was made concurrent with their coming, though it comes after it, to indicate haste in nullifying what they brought, in order to strengthen his heart, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is also permitted that the similitude is an expression for the strange attribute that they used to propose that he, upon him be blessings and peace, be characterized by, such as independence from eating and drinking, possession of a treasure, a garden, and the sending down of the Qur'an upon him all at once. The meaning is: they do not come to you with a strange condition whose attribution to you they propose, saying: "Why was he not in this state?" Except that We give you, from among the possible states, what it is fitting for you to be given in Our wisdom and will, and what is better. This has been objected to on the ground that the stated exception rejects it, since what is immediately understood from it is that what Allah, exalted is He, gave him of truth is consequent upon what they brought of falsehoods, demolishing them. There is no doubt that what Allah, exalted is He, gave him of the noble qualities befitting the message was given to him from the very beginning, not in exchange for the proposals reported of them, in order to demolish and nullify them.

It has been answered that the meaning of "except that We bring you" and so on, according to that view, is: except that We manifest in you what discloses the falsehood of what they brought. But this, as you see, is weak. So the reliance is on the first view.

It is well known that coming (ityan) and arrival (majiy') have the same meaning, but the former was expressed first and the latter second for variety of style, and out of dislike that what is attributed to Him, mighty and majestic, and what is attributed to them should share the same wording, although what they brought is in the utmost of ugliness and falsehood, and what He, glorified is He, brought is in the utmost of truth and goodness.

Al-Raghib distinguished between them, saying: majiy' is like ityan, but majiy' is more general, because ityan is arrival with ease. From this it is said of a flood passing over its surface: utan and ataw. Ityan may be said with regard to intention even if the arrival (husul) did not come from him, while majiy' is said with regard to arrival. Perhaps in the expression ityan first and majiy' second, according to this, there is an indication that what they bring of similitudes is in itself among matters that are imagined with ease and do not need the exercise of thought, unlike what stands in opposition to it, for that is in itself among rational matters that thought has polished, so no one finds a way to reject or challenge them. Or it indicates that their action, because it has gone out of the realm of acceptance, is treated as nonexistent, so that it is as if the intention from them was not realized, rather than their arrival, unlike what came from Him, mighty and majestic. So reflect. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His Book.

Page 17

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 34:

﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell﴾ — that is, they will be gathered walking upon their faces.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three categories: one category walking, one category riding, and one category upon their faces." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, how will they walk upon their faces?" He said: "The One who made them walk upon their feet is able to make them walk upon their faces. Indeed, they will protect their faces from every rough ground and thorn."

This may mean that their faces, and what is on the same side of them, such as their chests, bellies and the like, touch the ground; or it may mean that they are turned over on their heads, with their faces toward the ground, their feet raised and the rest of their bodies lifted. The hadith is perhaps more apparent regarding the first.

It was said: the angels — peace be upon them — drag them and pull them upon their faces to Hell; the matter according to this is clear and there is no strangeness in it. It was said: gathering upon the face is a metaphor for extreme humiliation, disgrace and abasement. It was said: it derives from the saying of the Arabs, "So-and-so passed upon his face," when it is not known where he went. It was said: the statement is a kinaya (allusion) or a metaphorical image (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), and the meaning is that they will be gathered with their hearts attached to the lowly things of the world and its adornments, and their faces turned toward them. Perhaps this state in the gathering is by consideration of the lingering of its traces; otherwise they will be there in a preoccupation that distracts them from turning to the world and its adornments and from their hearts being attached to it.

As for the place of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), it was said that it is either in the accusative by the implied "I dispraise" (adhummu) or "I mean" (a'nI), or in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are those who," or as a subject, and His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Those﴾ is a substitute for it or an explanatory apposition to it.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿worse in place and further astray in way﴾ is its predicate; or the demonstrative is a second subject, and "worse" is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the relative pronoun. The author of al-Fara'id said: it is possible that the relative pronoun is a substitute for the pronoun in "they come to you," and "those are worse in place" is a resumed independent statement. Yet the closest view is that the relative pronoun is the subject and what follows it is its predicate. Al-Tibi said: this is from the manner of the just speaker and of giving free rein. "Those who will be gathered" is separated from what precedes it as a resumed statement, because the preceding consolation stirred in the Prophet (ﷺ) a question: "Then with what shall I answer them, and what shall my word to them be?" So it was said: "Say to them: those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell, etc.," meaning: your aim in this obstinacy is a locational disparagement and a misguidance of way, but I do not say this of you; rather I say: those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell are worse in place and further astray in way. So look with an eye of fairness and reflect on who is more deserving of this description, us or you, so that you may know that your place is worse than our place and your way is more astray than our way. Upon this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance or in manifest error﴾. So "place" means rank and station, and it is permissible that it means dwelling and abode. "Worse" and "further astray" are taken in the comparative sense, in the manner of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Shall I inform you of something worse than that as recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry﴾.

The author of al-Fara'id took this to establish all evil for their place and all error for their way. Describing the way as astray is a figurative attribution for emphasis. The verse, as you have heard, is connected to what precedes it, His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and they do not come to you﴾, etc. Al-Kirmani said: it is connected to His statement, exalted is He, ﴿the companions of the Garden on that day﴾, the verse. It was said: it is permissible that it be connected to His statement, glorified is He, ﴿And thus We appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, concluded. What was mentioned first is further removed in purpose.

And His statement, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 35:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ etc. This is a resumptive sentence (jumla musta'nafa), brought in to confirm what preceded it of consolation and the promise of guidance and victory in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord suffices as a guide and a helper﴾, as we have set forth, by relating what took place between the prophets mentioned - peace be upon them - and their peoples, in a summary account that is sufficient for the purpose intended.

The lam (al-lam) falls in the answer to an oath (jawab al-qasam), meaning: by God, exalted is He, We certainly gave Moses the Torah, that is, We sent it down to him at once (bi-al-akhira). It has been said that by "the Book" is meant judgment (al-hukm) and prophethood, but its remoteness is not hidden. ﴿And We made with him﴾: the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to "We made" (ja'alna). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿his brother﴾ is the first object of it (maf'ul awwal). His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Harun﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "his brother" or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to it. His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿a minister (wazir)﴾ is the second object of it. The meaning of wazir has already been set forth. This is not contradicted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We bestowed upon him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun as a prophet﴾, because he - although he was a prophet - the sharia belonged to Moses, peace be upon him, and he was a follower of it, just as the minister follows his ruler.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 36:

﴿So We said: "Go to the people who denied Our signs."﴾ They are Pharaoh and his people. The apparent reading is that (bi-ayatina, "with Our signs") is connected to (kadhdhabu, "they denied"). What is meant by the signs is the proofs of tawhid (divine oneness) deposited in the souls and in the horizons, or the signs that the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, brought, or the well-known nine signs.

The expression of the denial in the past tense is clear on the first two interpretations. On the last one it has been said that the future is placed in the position of the past because of its certainty; this has been objected to on the grounds that it does not suit the context.

Abu al-Su'ud, the great scholar, said: The people were not described to the two of them, at the time of their being sent to them, with this description, because the denial of the nine signs necessarily came after their manifestation, which came after the going, which came after the command to go. Rather, they were described with it when the narration was relayed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as an explanation of the cause of their deserving what is narrated after it of destruction. He discussed this, and there is room for reflection in what he said.

It has been permitted that the adverbial phrase be connected to (idhhaba, "go"), so the meaning of (kadhdhabu, "they denied") is that they committed denial. ﴿Then We destroyed them with a destruction﴾ extraordinary, terrible, beyond measure in its magnitude and beyond comprehension in its reality. What is meant by it is the most severe ruin; its root is breaking a thing in a way that it cannot be repaired. The fa' (then) is fa' fasihah (an eloquent fa' indicating an omitted intermediate). The underlying sense is: "So We said: Go to the people," and they went to them and called them to faith, but they denied the two of them and persisted in that, "so We destroyed them." The narrative was reduced to its two edges, being satisfied with what is intended. It has also been said: the meaning of "fa-dammarnahum" is "so We decreed their destruction," so the sequence is in terms of the decree, and there is not much benefit in reporting this. It has also been said: the fa' is merely for sequence, and this, as you see, is weak.

(Qad) "We said" is conjoined to (ja'alna, "We made"), which is itself conjoined to (ataina, "We gave") by the wa' (and), which on the correct view does not require sequence. Thus it is permissible for it to precede, together with what follows it, the giving of the Book. It is therefore not objected that the giving of the Book, which is the Torah, came after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, so the sequence would be incorrect, and the mention of this at the opening of the narrative is not out of place, since it has no bearing on the destruction of the people. Rather, it is an announcement from the outset of his, peace be upon him, reaching the utmost perfection, which is the deliverance of the Children of Israel from the dominion of Pharaoh and guiding them to the path of truth through the laws in the Torah, for through it the promise of guidance is affirmed in the manner mentioned earlier.

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and al-Hasan and Maslamah ibn Muharib read: (fa-dammiraahum, "so destroy them") as a command to Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both. It is also narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, the same, except that it is emphasized with the heavy nun. Also from him, may Allah ennoble his face: "fa-dammira" as a command to the two of them concerning them, with the preposition bi (bihim). It seems this is of the type of:

"tajrahu fi 'araqibiha nasli" (it wounds at its hamstrings with my blade)

It is related in al-Kashshaf from him as well, may Allah ennoble his face: "fa-dammartuhum" with the pronoun's tā' (first person).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 37:

﴿And the people of Noah﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb indicated by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿We destroyed them﴾. That is: and We destroyed the people of Noah. Al-Hawfi and Abu Hayyan permitted that it be in the accusative as a conjunct (ma'tuf) of the object of (﴿We destroyed them﴾). It was rejected on the grounds that the destruction of the people of Noah is not consequent upon the denial of Pharaoh and his people, so its being conjoined to it is not valid.

It was answered that it is not a necessary requirement of the consequence of their destruction upon what precedes it that the destruction of these people is consequent upon it, especially since its cause has been explained by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿when they denied the messengers﴾, that is, Noah and those messengers before him, peace be upon them, or Noah alone, for his denial, peace be upon him, is a denial of all of them, since they agree on monotheism, or they denied the permissibility of sending messengers in general. The definiteness of "the messengers" is, according to the first view, the definiteness of previous reference (ahd); it may be for comprehensiveness (istighraq) since no one other than them existed at the time of their denial; according to the second view it is comprehensive but by way of resemblance and claim; and according to the third view it is for the genus or for true comprehensiveness. It seems that the one who answered intended that the conjunction is considered before the sequence, so the thing sequenced is the whole of the two conjoined items, and the sequence of part of them suffices for it.

It was also said: the purpose of the conjunction is equating and making a comparison, as if it were said: "We destroyed them like the people of Noah," so the pronouns refer to them, and the messengers are Noah, Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them. What is problematic in this is not hidden.

A group chose that it is in the accusative governed by an implied (uthkur, "mention"), and it was said: it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb which is explained by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿We drowned them﴾. It is preferred over the nominative by the precedence of verbal clauses. It is not hidden that this is only feasible according to the view of al-Farisi that (lamma) is a temporal adverb (zarf zaman). As for when it is a particle of existence for existence (harf wujud li-wujud), then no, because ﴿We drowned them﴾ would then be its answer (jawab), so it cannot explain a governing verb. Perhaps the most preferred of the possibilities is the first, and ﴿We drowned them﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of their destruction, as if it were said: "How was their destruction?" So it was said: "We drowned them by the flood." ﴿And We made them﴾, that is, We made their drowning or their story, ﴿a sign for the people﴾, that is, a great sign by which whoever witnessed it or heard of it takes a lesson. It is the second object of (We made), and "for the people" is related to it, or related to an implied word that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of (sign), for if it came after it, it would be a qualifier of it. ﴿And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment﴾, that is, We made it prepared for them in the Hereafter, or in the barzakh, or in both. By "the wrongdoers" is meant the people mentioned, and the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to signal their exceeding the limit in disbelief and denial. Or it means all wrongdoers who did not take heed from what befell them of punishment, so the Quraysh enter among them in the first place. The punishment may be worldly or otherwise.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 38:**

﴿And 'Ad﴾ is coordinated with (*qawm Nuh*, "the people of Nuh"). That is, "and We destroyed 'Ad," or "mention 'Ad," according to what has been said. It cannot be coordinated if it is in the accusative through *al-ishtighal* (the construction in which a verb is governed by a pronoun-object that refers back to the noun), because they were not drowned.

Abu Ishaq said: it is coordinated with (*hum*, "them") in (*ja'alnahum li-l-nasi ayah*, "We made them a sign for the people"). It may also be coordinated with the place (*mahall*) of (*al-zalimin*, "the wrongdoers"), since the sentence is interpreted (*ta'wil*) as "We promised the wrongdoers." End of quote. The two possibilities are clearly weak. ﴿And Thamud﴾: what is said about it and what follows it is the same as what was said before it.

Abdullah, Amr ibn Maymun, al-Hasan and Isa read (*Thamuda*) without tanwin (*ghayr masrūf*), on the interpretation of the tribe. This is also transmitted from Hamzah and Asim. The majority reads it with tanwin. Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Asim the reading with tanwin with reference to the clan, or that they were named after their greatest ancestor.

﴿And the companions of the Rass﴾. According to Ibn Abbas, they are the people of Thamud. But coordination makes this less likely, since coordination requires difference.

Qatadah said: they are the people of a town in al-Yamamah called al-Rass and al-Falaj. It is said that they killed their prophet and were destroyed. They were the remnant of Thamud and the people of Salih.

Ka'b, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: they are the people of a well called al-Rass at Antioch in Syria. They killed there the companion of Ya-Sin, who was Habib al-Najjar.

It is also said: they are a people who killed their prophet and threw (*rassuhu*, "cast him") into a well, meaning they pushed him into it.

Wahb and al-Kalbi said: the companions of the Rass and the companions of the Thicket (*al-Aykah*) were two peoples to whom Shu'ayb was sent. The companions of the Rass were a people who worshipped idols and owned wells and livestock. He invited them to Islam, but they persisted in their rebellion and in harming him, peace be upon him. While they were around the Rass, which is the well that is not lined with stone, as narrated from Abu Ubaydah, it collapsed on them and on their dwellings.

Ali, may God honour his face, said, as transmitted by al-Tha'labi: they were a people who worshipped a tree called *Shah Darakht*. They threw their prophet into a well they had dug for him, in a long narration.

It is also said: they were the companions of the prophet Hanzalah ibn Safwan. They were afflicted by the *'anqa'* (a legendary bird), which is the largest of birds and had every colour. It was called *'anqa'* because of the length of its neck. It lived on their mountain, which is called Fath, and swooped down on their children and snatched them when it could not find prey. Because of this strange act it was called *maghrib*. It is also said it was named that because it once snatched a bride, or because of its "ghurub" (disappearance), meaning its absence, or because its nest was at the setting place of the sun (*maghrib al-shams*). It is called *'anqa' maghrib*, with the qualifier and the construct form, with both a damma and a fatha on the mim. Hanzalah prayed against it, and a thunderbolt struck it and it perished. Then they killed Hanzalah, and they were destroyed.

It is also said: they were a people to whom a prophet was sent, and they ate him. It is said: a people whose women were lesbians. It is said: a people to whom prophets were sent, and they killed them and threw their bones into a well. It is said: they are the people of the Trench (*al-Ukhdud*), and the Rass is the trench. In a narration from Ibn Abbas, it is the well of Adharbayjan. It is also said that the Rass is the area between Najran and Yemen and as far as Hadramawt. It is said: it is water and palm trees belonging to the Banu Asad. It is said: it is a river in the eastern lands, where God sent a prophet from the descendants of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub to its people.
