They denied him. He remained among them for a time, then complained to God about them. They dug a well for him and cast him into it, saying: "We hope that our gods will be pleased with us." They were around him each day, hearing the groaning of their prophet. He prayed for his soul to be taken quickly, and he died. A black cloud overshadowed them and melted them as lead melts.

Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "The companions of the Rass seized their prophet and threw him into a well and closed it with a rock. There was a black servant who had believed in him, and he would bring food to the well. God would help him lift that rock, and he would give him what nourished him. Then he would return the rock to the mouth of the well. Until God struck the ear of that black man, and he slept for fourteen years. The people of the town then brought out their prophet and they believed in him," in a long narration, in which it is mentioned that this black man was the first to enter Paradise. If this is authentic, it would be the view that cannot be disputed. However, their mention here causes a difficulty, and al-Tabari answered it by saying that it is possible they disbelieved after that and were destroyed, so God mentioned them together with those who were destroyed. The summary of the opinions is that they are a people whom God destroyed for denying the one who was sent to them.

﴿And generations﴾: that is, people of generations. The discussion of *qarn* (generation) has already passed. ﴿Between those﴾: that is, between the nations mentioned. Enumerating them without conjunction has clear elegance. ﴿Many﴾: whose stories would make the discourse very long if mentioned. It is not far-fetched that the Messenger of God ﷺ knew their number. The words of God, ﴿And among them are those We have not related to you﴾, are not an explicit denial of knowledge of their number, as is not hidden.

In *Irshad al-Aql al-Salim*: perhaps the sufficiency in the affairs of those generations with this general account is because each of those generations was not as famous or as striking in its story as the nations mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 39:

﴿And each﴾ is in the accusative (manṣūb) by an implied verb (muḍmar) indicated by what follows it, since the setting forth of parables (ḍarb al-mathal) carries the sense of admonition and warning. The omitted element for which the tanwin (nunation) compensates is either a reference to the nations whose causes of destruction were not mentioned, or a reference to all of them. What is related about Pharaoh and his people, and about the people of Noah, peace be upon him, is their denial of the signs and the messengers, not a lack of influence from the parables that were set forth. The meaning is: We warned and admonished each one of those mentioned. ﴿We set forth parables for him﴾, that is, We made clear to each of them the wondrous stories that restrain them from the disbelief and sins they were engaged in, through the messengers, peace be upon them. It has also been said that the pronoun in "for him" refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the meaning would be: We set forth for the Messenger all the parables, so that "kullan" is in the accusative governed by "ḍarabnā" (We set forth), and "al-amthāl" (the parables) is a substitute (badal) for it, according to what is found in al-Bahr. In this there is the objection that whoever holds this view is too distant, and in my opinion this is something that the speech of Allah the Exalted should not be interpreted by.

As for the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And each﴾ is a fronted direct object (mafʿūl muqaddam) of His words, glorified is He, ﴿We utterly destroyed [them] with complete destruction﴾. Its fronting is for the sake of the verse-ending (fāṣila). It has also been said that it is for the purpose of restriction (qaṣr), meaning "each one, not some." This was objected to on the grounds that the word "kull" (each) already conveys that, and it may be justified as a matter of emphasis (ʿināya).

The original meaning of tatbīr is pulverizing and breaking into fragments. Al-Zajjaj said: "Everything you break and crush into pieces, you have made tabbar." From this comes tibr, meaning the fragments of gold and silver. What is meant here is tearing apart and destruction, that is: We destroyed each one of them with a wondrous, terrifying destruction, because they were not affected by that and did not lift their heads to it, and they persisted in the disbelief and transgression they were upon.

And they have certainly passed by it: this is a resumed clause, brought to explain that the Quraysh unbelievers witnessed the traces of the destruction of some of the overturned nations, and yet were not admonished by them. It is introduced with an oath to affirm its content and to give it emphasis. The verb *ataw* (أتى, "to come") is used here with the implicit meaning of *marra* (مَرَّ, "to pass by"), since it takes *ʿalā* ("upon/by"). The meaning is: "By Allah, the Quraysh certainly passed by [it] on their trade journeys to Syria."

﴿upon the town that was rained upon with a rain of evil﴾. This is Sodom (Sadhum), the greatest of the towns of the people of Lot. It was named after its judge, Sadhum, spelled with a dhal (ذ), as al-Azhari corrected it and as al-Zamakhshari adopted it in al-Kashshaf. There is a proverb: "More unjust than Sodom." Allah destroyed it with stones, and this is what is meant by "a rain of evil." He likewise destroyed the rest of its towns, which were five, except for one town, Zughar, which He did not destroy, because its people did not commit the vile deed, as is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

The town is mentioned singly for the reason we have pointed out. The word *maṭar* (مَطَرَ, "rain") is in the accusative as a second object (*mafʿūl thānin*) of *umṭirat* (أُمْطِرَتْ, "was rained upon"), in the sense of "was given" or "was bestowed." Alternatively, it is a cognate object (*maṣdar muʾakkad*) with the augmenting elements omitted, meaning *imṭār al-sūʾ* (إمْطارَ السَّوْءِ, "a rain of evil"), as is said regarding ﴿And He caused you to grow from the earth, a growth﴾. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning "a rain like the rain of evil," but this is not worthwhile.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read *muṭirat* (مُطِرَتْ) in the triliteral passive form, and *muṭira* is among the verbs that are transitive by themselves. Abu al-Sammal read *maṭara al-suʾ* (مَطَرَ السُّوءِ) with a damma on the sin.

﴿Had they not been seeing it?﴾ This is a rebuke for their neglect of reflection when they witnessed what necessitates it. The interrogative particle *a-* (الهَمْزَةُ) is used to deny the denial of the continuity of their seeing it, and to affirm the continuity of their seeing it in accordance with the continuity of what necessitates it, namely their passing by it. It is not a denial of the continuity of their non-seeing and an affirmation of their seeing it. The particle *fa-* (الفاءُ) conjoins what follows it to an implied element required by the context, meaning: "Did they not look at it, so that they did not see it?" Or: "They used to look at it, yet they did not see it on their many passages, so that they might take warning from what they were witnessing of the traces of punishment."

In the first case, what is denied is both looking and not seeing together. In the second, what is denied is not seeing despite the looking which normally necessitates seeing. So it is stated in Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim (Abu al-Suʿud's commentary).

He did not say *a-falam yarawnaha* (أفَلَمْ يَرَوْنَها), even though it is shorter and clearer in purpose, in order to convey repetition together with continuity. And at the beginning of the verse He did not state explicitly something like "Indeed they used to come [to it]" (*wa-laqad kanu yaʾtūna*) in place of "And they have certainly passed by," to indicate that passing by, even once, is sufficient for admonition. So reflect.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they did not expect a resurrection.﴾ This is either a turning away (*iḍrāb*, "a transition away") from what precedes it, namely their not seeing the traces of the punishment that befell the people of the towns, and an explanation that their failure to be admonished was due to their denial that this was a punishment for their sins, not due to their not seeing its traces. However, the explicit statement of their denial of this is omitted, and instead what necessarily implies it is mentioned, namely the denial of the otherworldly recompense. This is expressed indirectly by not expecting resurrection. The word "expectation" (*rajāʾ*) is used figuratively to mean anticipation. It is as if it were said: "Rather, they did not anticipate the resurrection which entails the otherworldly recompense, and they denied it, and they did not regard any soul as having a resurrection at all, though its occurrence is certain, its encompassing of people is general, and its happening is constant. How then would they acknowledge the worldly recompense for a particular group, when there is no regularity or necessary connection between it and sins, so that they would remember and take warning from what they witnessed of the traces of destruction? Rather, they attribute it to coincidence." Or it is a transition from the rebuke for not remembering to a greater rebuke, namely for not expecting resurrection. Taking *rajāʾ* to mean anticipation and resurrection in its general sense is more fitting to the context.

It has been said that it has its literal meaning, namely hoping for good, and that by resurrection is meant a resurrection in which there is good, like the resurrection of the Muslims.

It is also permitted that *rajāʾ* means fear, according to the dialect of Tihama, and that by resurrection is meant their resurrection. All of these, as you see, [are weak].

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 25, verse 41:**

﴿And when they see you, they take you not except as a mockery﴾. That is: they do not take you except as a mockery, in the sense that they do nothing with him except make him an object of mockery (*huzu*), i.e., a place of mockery or one mocked. Thus, هُزُوًا (*huzuwan*, "mockery") is either a *maṣdar* (verbal noun, *maṣdar*: the verbal noun of an action) used in the sense of the passive participle for emphasis, or it stands with an implied *muḍāf* (an omitted noun in a construction of possession, *muḍāf*). The clause ﴿they take you﴾ is the answer (*jawāb*) of إذا (*idhā*, "when"). It is, as Abu Hayyan and others said, distinctive in that its negated answer occurs with *in* and *lā* and *mā* without a *fā'* (the particle *fa*), unlike other conditional particles.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ is a *maqūl qawl* (the object of an implied speech verb), meaning: they say, "Is this...?" and so on. The clause is either in a position of circumstance (*ḥāl*) relative to the subject of (يَتَّخِذُونَكَ, "they take you"), or it is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafah*) answering the question "What do they say?"

It is permitted that it be the answer, with the clause ﴿they take you﴾ as a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtirāḍ*). The one who says this is Abu Jahl and those with him, and it is related that the verse was revealed concerning him. The demonstrative (*ishārah*, "this") is for belittling, as in the phrase: "O wonder at this son of ʿAmr!" The relative pronoun's returning reference (*ʿāʾid*) is omitted, meaning: "whom God sent [him]." The word رَسُولًا (*rasūlan*, "messenger") is a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) from it, and it has the meaning of *mursal* (one sent). Abu al-Baqa permitted that it be a *maṣdar* from which the *muḍāf* has been omitted, meaning: "one of a messenger," i.e., of a message (*risālah*), but this is a strained interpretation that is unnecessary.

Placing "God sent him (ﷺ) as a messenger" as a relative clause (*ṣilah*), while they are in utmost denial, is sarcasm and mockery. Otherwise they would have said: "Has God sent this one as a messenger?" It has been said that this is with an implied phrase: "Is this the one whom God sent as a messenger, in his claim?" But what preceded is more fitting to the state of those disbelievers, and it is free of the need for an implied element.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 42:

﴿In kada﴾ (in is a lightened form of inna, and its noun, according to some, is an omitted pronoun of the matter/situation, meaning: "indeed he nearly..."). ﴿Layudillana 'an alihatina﴾ means: he would turn us away from their worship with a complete turning, such that he would distance us from them, not merely from worshipping them. The shift to "misguide" (idlal) is for the extreme of their own misguidance, in claiming that worshipping them is a straight path.

﴿Lawla an sabarna 'alayha﴾ means: we remained steadfast in them and held firm in worshipping them. "Lawla" in such statements functions as a restriction of an absolute judgment in meaning, not in wording. This is an acknowledgment from them that he ﷺ had exerted such effort in calling to monotheism, showing the miracles, and establishing proofs and clear evidences, that they came close to abandoning their religion, were it not for their excessive obstinacy and utmost stubbornness. This does not contradict their earlier mockery and derision, because this is from one aspect and that is from another aspect, which they claimed as a reason for it. May God Most High curse them.

It is said: their speech contradicts itself due to their confusion and bewilderment, for the earlier interrogative indicates contempt, while this indicates the strength of his argument and the perfection of his intellect ﷺ. Thus, in what God Most High related of them there is a reproach to them and a showing of their ignorance in mocking what they had magnified.

It is said against this: it is not explicit in their admission of what was mentioned; rather, the apparent meaning is that it was produced in the form of concession, mockingly, as in their saying: "God has sent a messenger." This is an evident objection, and the contradiction is dispelled, as is not hidden.

﴿And they will know, when they see the punishment﴾ which their disbelief and obstinacy deserve, ﴿who is more astray in way﴾, meaning: they will know the answer to this. The interrogative "man" is an interrogative, subject, and "adallu" its predicate, and the clause is in the position of the two objects of "ya'lamuna" if it is transitive to two objects, or in the position of one object if it is transitive to one; or "ya'lamuna" means "the one who is more astray," with "man" as a relative pronoun, object of "ya'lamuna," and "adallu" the predicate of an omitted subject, the clause being the relative clause, with the initial element of the relative clause (the returning pronoun) omitted because the clause is long, by the specifier. When those disbelievers made his ﷺ call to monotheism into misguidance, saying: "He nearly misguided us from our gods," and the one who misguides others must himself be astray, this sentence was brought as a response to them, explaining that he, upon him be prayers and peace, is a guide and not a misguider in the most eloquent manner, for it indicates the negation of misguidance from him ﷺ, since what is meant is that they know they are in the utmost misguidance and not he, and the negation of the consequent necessitates the negation of its antecedent, so it follows that he, upon him be prayers and peace, is a guide and not a misguider. In restricting knowledge to the time of seeing the punishment, there is a warning to them and an alert that He, Most High, does not neglect them, even if He gives them respite.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 43:

﴿Have you seen him who takes his own desire as his god?﴾ It is an expression of wonder addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the monstrousness of their condition, after relating their vile sayings and deeds, and drawing attention to the end and final destiny that awaits them. It also alerts that this matter is so strange that it ought to be seen and wondered at. The apparent reading is that "ra'a" (raʾā, to see) is visual, and "man" (who) is its object; it is a relative pronoun, and the clause after it is its relative clause. "Ittakhadha" (took) is transitive to two objects: the first is "hawāhu" (his desire) and the second is "ilāhahu" (his god). The second was placed before the first for emphasis upon it, in that it is the thing on which the matter of wonder turns, not because a god deserves exaltation and precedence, as has been said. That is: Have you seen the one who made his desire a god for himself, by obeying it and building upon it the matter of his religion, turning away entirely from listening to the dazzling proof and from observing the luminous evidence? The meaning is: look at him and wonder at him.

Ibn al-Munir said: in the placing of the second object first here there is a fine subtlety, which is the conveying of restriction (ḥaṣr). Before the entry of "ra'ayta" (have you seen), the sentence with "ittakhadha" originally was "hawāhu ilāhuhu" (his desire is his god), with "hawāhu" as the subject and "ilāhuhu" as its predicate. So when it is said "ilāhuhu hawāhu," it is the predicate placed before the subject, and this conveys restriction. The meaning of the verse then becomes: Have you seen the one who has taken as his worshipped deity nothing but his desire? And this is more eloquent in censuring and rebuking him.

The author of al-Fara'id said: placing the second object first is possible wherever placing the predicate before the subject is possible, and when two definites occur as subject and predicate, the one placed first is the subject. So whoever makes what is here the parallel of your saying "ʿalimtu muntaliqan Zaydan" has overlooked this. It may be said: the one placed first here indicates permanence, unlike the one placed later, so placing "ilāhahu" first indicates that there must be a god; it is like your saying "ittakhadha ibnahu ghulāmahu" (he took his son as his servant), for it indicates that he has a son but does not indicate that he has a servant. This is the benefit of placing "ilāhihi" before "hawāhu."

al-Tibi criticised this, saying: there is no doubt that the proper position of the subject is first, and that of two definites whichever is placed first is the subject. But the rhetorician does not abandon consideration of the original meaning. When it is said "Zaydun al-asad" (Zayd is the lion), "al-asad" is originally the thing compared-to (the likened-to), and its proper place is after the thing compared, without dispute. When you make it the subject in your saying "al-asadu Zaydun" (the lion is Zayd), you have removed it from its original station for the sake of hyperbole, and by "the one placed first" we mean only the one displaced from its place, not the one settled in it. So here the thing likened-to is "the god" and the thing being likened is "the desire," because they had given their desires in following them the rank of a god. Thus the original likened-to was placed first and was made the thing being likened, to indicate that desire, in the matter of deserving worship, is in their view stronger than the Mighty and Majestic God, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: trade is only like usury﴾. The author of al-Miftah alluded to this meaning in his book.

As for the example given by the author of al-Fara'id, the meaning of his saying "ittakhadha ibnahu ghulāmahu" is: he made his son like a servant who serves him in the work of his household; and his saying "ittakhadha ghulāmahu ibnahu" is: he made his servant like his son, honoured and pampered. End of quotation. You know what is in his saying "whichever of the two definites is placed first is the subject," for the truth is that the matter turns on the indicator (qarīnah), and the indicator here is established that "ilāhahu" is the predicate; and it is an intellectual indicator, for the meaning requires it, so there is no need to make this a case of semantic placing-first.

Shaykh al-Islam said: whoever imagines that the two are in order, on the basis of their equality in definiteness, has slipped past the point that the second object in this construction is the one that is bound to the newly arising state, and in this is a refutation of Abu Hayyan, in that he required that they be in order.

It is reported from some Medinan readers that he read "ālihatan" (gods) with tanwin, in the plural, and made this a case of hyperbole and inversion, the meaning being: he made every kind of his desire a god. It is also mentioned that Ibn Hurmuz read "ilihatan" on the pattern of "fiʿālah," and this too is a case of inversion: he made his desire a worshipped god (ilihah, in the sense of ma'lūhah), that is, an object of worship, and the ta' is for intensification, which is why it is given tanwin. It was also said: rather, "al-ilahah" is the sun, and it is said "ulāhah" with a damma on the hamzah, and it is not diptoted for being a proper name and feminine; but since it is among those that take the definite article in some dialects, it became like what had the article, then the article was removed, and therefore it takes tanwin and becomes like the indefinite after definiteness. This was stated by the author of al-Lawami', and it is as you see.

The verse was revealed, as has been said, concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, who whenever he desired a stone, worshipped it. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: a man would worship a white stone for a time in the Age of Ignorance, and when he found something better than it he would cast it away and worship the other. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed ﴿Have you seen﴾ ... and so on. Some have claimed, for this and similar cases, that "hawāhu" means "mahwiyyuhu" (the object of his desire), but this is not necessary, as is not hidden.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said concerning the verse: whenever he desired something he mounted it, and whenever he craved something he went to it, and no piety or God-fearing restrained him from that. So the verse includes whoever worships other than Allah according to his desire, and whoever obeys desire in all sins. This is what the words of al-Hasan imply, for ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from him that it was said to him: is there shirk among the people of the qiblah? He said: yes, the hypocrite is a polytheist. The polytheist prostrates to the sun and the moon besides Allah, exalted is He, and the hypocrite worships his desire; then he recited this verse. And the hypocrite, according to al-Hasan, is the one who commits sins, as more than one of the eminent scholars has mentioned.

Al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah reported from Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Under the shade of the sky there is no god worshipped besides Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, greater in the sight of Allah than a desire that is followed." Yet it is hardly safe, on this, from the generality of the verse except for one who follows what Allah, exalted is He, has chosen for His servants and legislated for them in everything they do and forsake; and upon this the disbeliever enters what has been mentioned by primary entry. ﴿Then would you be a guardian over him?﴾ This is a resumptive sentence brought to express the improbability that he (ﷺ) would be a keeper over this one who takes his desire as god, restraining him from the error he is upon and guiding him to the truth willingly or unwillingly; and it is a denial of this. The "fa" (then) is for ordering the denial upon what precedes it, the state that necessitates it. It is as if it were said: after you have witnessed his excess in obeying desire, would you make him hard to lead to guidance, whether he wills it or refuses? It was also permitted that "ra'a" be cognitive (ʿilmiyyah), and that this clause be in the position of the second object, but that is not the case.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 44:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or understand?﴾ is a turning away (idrab) and a transition (intiqal) from the previous denunciation to a denunciation of the Prophet's (ﷺ) presumption that they were among those who hear or understand. This is in line with what his earnest effort (jadd) in the call (da'wah) and his concern for guidance and admonition indicate, meaning that it should not happen. That is: "Rather, do you think that most of them hear the recitation of the Qur'anic verses that you recite to them with true hearing, or understand the manifest signs of the horizons and of the souls that are displayed to them, so that you take care of them and hope for their faith?" Since transmitted evidence (al-dalil al-sam'i) is more important for the context than rational evidence (al-dalil al-'aqli), it says "hear or understand." It was also said that the meaning is: "Rather, do you think that most of them hear the verses you recite with true hearing, or understand the admonitions within them that restrain from vices and call to virtues, so that you strive in calling them and take care in admonishing them?" The first view is more likely, so reflect on it.

Whatever the case, the pronoun in (akthara-hum) refers to "man" (in terms of its meaning), and the pronoun in (alayhi) also refers to "man" in terms of its wording. The plural was chosen here to match the attachment of "most" to "them." It was used in the singular before this, because they are treated, in their agreement upon desire, as one thing. It was also said that the pronoun in (akthara-hum) refers to the disbelievers and not to "man," because the Exalted's saying "upon him" (alayhi) rejects this, but this view is worthless. The pronouns of the two verbs refer to "most," not to what is attached to it. The restriction to "most" is because among them are those for whom the eternal providence had already preceded faith after the aforementioned taking, and among them are those who heard or understood but were arrogantly stubborn, out of fear for their leadership.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are only like livestock﴾ ... etc., is a resumed sentence (jumlah mustanifah) for the repetition and emphasis of the denunciation, and for cutting off the root of presumption entirely. The pronoun refers to "most" or to "man." Mention of "most" is dispensed with because of what precedes it. That is: they are not benefiting from what strikes their ears of the striking verses, and there is no reflection on what they see of the clear proofs, except as the beasts, which are a proverb for heedlessness and a sign of error, ﴿Rather, they are more astray﴾ than them ﴿in way﴾, because the beasts submit to their owner who looks after them, they recognize who is good to them and who is bad to them, they seek what benefits them and avoid what harms them, they find their way to their pastures and watering places, and they return to their resting places and enclosures. But these people do not submit to their Lord, Glorified is He, their Creator and Provider, nor do they recognize His, the Exalted's, kindness to them from the harm of Satan, who adorns for them the following of desires and who is a clear enemy. They do not seek the reward, which is the greatest of benefits, nor do they guard against punishment, which is the greatest of harms and destructions, nor do they find the way to the truth, which is the sweet watering place and the pleasant, flowing source. Also, if the beast does not believe in a truth that leads to gaining good, it does not believe in a falsehood that requires committing evil, unlike these people, who have laid the foundations of falsehood and built upon them the rulings of evils. Also, the rulings of the beast's ignorance and error are confined to itself and do not extend to anyone, whereas the ignorance of these people leads to the rising of strife and corruption, the turning of people away from the paths of rectitude, and the outbreak of chaos and confusion among the servants. Also, the beast does not leave idle any power of the powers deposited in it, but directs them to what it was created for, so there is no shortcoming on its part in seeking perfection. As for these people, they leave idle their rational powers and waste the original nature (al-fitrah) upon which people were created.

It has been inferred from the verse that beasts do not know their Lord, Mighty and Majestic. As for whoever holds that they know Him, Glorified is He, and glorify Him, as is the view of the Sufis (al-Sufiyyah) and a group of people, he said: "This comes out in the outward sense." It was also said: the meaning is: "They are only like livestock in not benefiting from the Qur'anic verses and the signs of the souls and the horizons, for livestock is likewise. The knowledge of God, the Exalted, that is attained by them is not inferential but innate (fitri). Their being more astray in way than livestock is because livestock has been given knowledge of its Lord, the Exalted, so it glorifies Him, Mighty and Majestic, by it, whereas these people have not been given that, so they are in utmost error."

[p. 26]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade?﴾ ... and so on, is an illustration of some of the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), following a description of the ignorance and error of those who turn away from them. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The hamza (the interrogative particle) is for affirmation (taqrir, confirming what the listener already knows), and the seeing (ru'yah) is visual, because it is the kind that takes "ila" (to). In the speech there is an implied omitted noun: the genitive noun was dropped and the noun that depends on it was put in its place. That is: "Have you not looked at the handiwork of your Lord?" The reason is that the intended meaning is not seeing the essence of God, Exalted and Majestic. Taking "ila" to mean a noun meaning "bounties," which are blessings, is very far-fetched.

It is also permissible that the seeing be intellectual ('ilmiyyah, knowing), with no implied noun. Its construction with "ila" would then be by including the meaning of reaching (tadmin, implying a verb with a different meaning). That is: "Has your knowledge not reached the point that your Lord how He extends the shade?" The first reading is preferable.

Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that the proper expression might have been: "Have you not considered the shade, how your Lord extended it?" but this was changed to what is in the sublime wording, to indicate that what is understood from this speech, because its proof is clear, is that its origin and its variation in a beneficial manner through possible causes indicate that this is the act of a wise Creator, like something seen with the eye, so how much more so what is perceived by the senses.

The excellent al-Tibi said: If it were said, "Have you not considered the shade, how your Lord extended it?" the movement would be from effect to cause. But the recitation is the reverse, and the context requires it, because the speech concerns rebuking and reproaching the people for taking their desires as gods despite the clarity of these proofs. For this reason, what indicates the Essence of God, Exalted is He, is placed before His acts throughout His verses: ﴿And He it is who made the night for you﴾, ﴿And He it is who sends the winds﴾, ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised up in every town a warner﴾.

Al-Sulami, in al-Haqa'iq, transmitted from some of them the address to the general person: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ and the address to the elite: ﴿Have you not considered your Lord?﴾ End of quotation.

In al-Irshad (of Abu al-Su'ud): Perhaps directing the seeing to Him, Glorified is He, although the intended purpose is to affirm the Prophet's seeing of the manner in which the shade is extended (may blessings and peace be upon him), is to alert that his seeing (peace be upon him) is not confined to what he observes of traces and works, but rather the aim of his gaze (ﷺ) is knowledge of the affairs of the Glorious Creator, may His majesty be exalted. Perhaps this is the secret of what was narrated from al-Sulami.

It has been said that the expression mentioned is to indicate that the goal is knowledge of the Lord, knowledge resembling seeing. Al-Tabarsi transmitted from al-Zajjaj that he interpreted seeing as knowing, and mentioned that the speech is of the type of inversion (qalb), and the meaning is: "Have you not considered the shade, how your Lord extended it?" But there is no need for that.

The mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah), with its attribution to his pronoun (peace be upon him), is to honor him (ﷺ), and to announce that what follows of the effects of His Lordship, Exalted is He, and His mercy, Majestic is He.

"Kayfa" (how) is in the accusative, governed by "madda" (extended), in the circumstantial position (hal), and it is suspended with respect to "tara" (have you seen), if the sentence is not a resumptive one (isti'naf, a new independent clause). In al-Bahr (of Abu Hayyan): The interrogative clause after which the verb of the heart is suspended does not remain on the true sense of interrogation. There is a discussion about this. Some of the excellent scholars mentioned that "kayfa" is for interrogation, and it may be stripped of interrogation and carry the meaning of a state, as in: "Look at how you do it." Al-Damamini permitted this in this verse as a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for the genitive noun, and this is far-fetched. It is not hidden that one can dispense with this and not consider an implied noun, but this does not counterbalance the distance.

By "the shade," according to what a group narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Hasan, Ayyub ibn Musa, Ibrahim al-Taymi, al-Dahhak, Abu Malik al-Ghifari, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, is what lies between the break of dawn and sunrise. That is the best of times, for pure darkness repels natures and blocks the view, while the rays of the sun heat the air and dazzle the sight. For this reason the shade of Paradise is extended, as He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿And shade extended﴾.

It has been said that it means what results from the opposition of a dense object, such as a mountain, a building, or a tree, to the sun at the beginning of its rising. The extension of the shade is in the category of the narrow mouth of a waterskin. The meaning is: "Have you not looked at the handiwork of your Lord, how He brought forth a shade," that is, a shade which at the beginning of the sunrise is extended as far as God, Mighty and Majestic, wills. Shaykh al-Islam chose this, and he criticized what came before it by saying: "not correct," since there is no doubt that the purpose is to alert people to the great power of God, Mighty and Majestic, and His perfect wisdom, Glorified is He, in what they witness. So the shade must mean what they commonly recognize, a specific condition they witness in a place where a body comes between them and the sun, different from what is around its sides in the places where the sun shines. What was mentioned, although in reality it is a shade of the eastern horizon, they do not count as a shade and do not describe it with its familiar attributes, end of quotation. In this there is a clear objection, and it is more evident according to what Abu Hayyan mentioned in objecting to that, that it is not called a shade. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani), and that suffices as proof in the language, said: "The shade is the opposite of the sunlit, and it is more general than the fay' (shade after noon). It is said: the shade of the night and the shade of Paradise, and every place the sun has not reached is called shade, while fay' is only said of what the sun has left." End of quotation. The apparent meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and shade extended﴾ in describing Paradise, requires that they count the like of what was mentioned as shade.

It has been said that it is what occurs from the setting of the sun to its rising. This was reported from al-Jubba'i and al-Balkhi. It has also been said that it is what existed on the day God created the heaven and made it like a dome, and spread out the earth beneath it, and it cast its shade upon it. This is not correct, even if "tara" (have you seen) is interpreted as "'alima" (have you known), because of the strain and the departure from the apparent meaning in applying to it what follows as the continuation of the verse, and the intended purpose for which the noble wording was brought may be lost. It may occur to some minds that it is permissible to mean by it everything that truly qualifies as a shade, including the shade of the night, the time between dawn and sunrise, and the shade of dense things opposite the sun, such as mountains and others. When one begins to apply the verse to all of that, it is set aside, as is not hidden. The Sufis have a lengthy discussion on this, of which, God willing, we will mention some. Most of the exegetes follow the first view, and the second view is safer from disputes and talk.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And had He willed, He would have made it still﴾ is a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tirashiyyah) between the two coordinated items, to alert from the outset that the ordinary causes, such as the sun's nearness to the eastern horizon according to the first view, or the standing of a dense object according to the second, have no role. Rather, the real influence is the reality of will and power. The object of the will is omitted, and it is the content of the conditional (jaza'), as is the constant rule in such structures. That is: "And had He willed to make it still, He would have made it still," that is, fixed in its condition as a shade forever, as He, Mighty and Majestic, did with the shade of Paradise. Or: He would have made it fixed in its condition of length and extension, by not allowing the sun any path to abrogate it, by making it rise without letting it abrogate it, or by not letting it change it through the variation of its positions after rising.

It has been said: by making it, after rising, remain in a single position. This is not the right view. The reason that this is expressed by "stillness" (sukun) is said to be that its opposite, which is its disappearance, being gradual, is most similar to motion. It has also been said that its opposite, which is the change of its state according to the changing positions between the shade and the sun, appears to the eye as motion and movement.

Al-Zamakhshari noted that the extension of the shade, which is its spreading and lengthening, is paired with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿still﴾. Stillness only opposes motion, so the phrase ﴿the extension of the shade﴾ has been used to mean motion figuratively (majaz), by the naming of a thing with the name of what accompanies it or causes it, as al-Tibi established. He mentioned that "madda" was preferred over "harraka" (moved), although "madda" is less clear than "harraka" in including spreading and lengthening, in order that the purpose of benefit be embedded in it (idmaj, the intended meaning of benefit being included within the expression), namely knowing the times of the prayers, for the shade is considered in them by its lengthening, not its spreading. The embedding meaning is completed by His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 46:

﴿Then We withdrew it to Us, a gradual withdrawal.﴾ That is: gradually and with a respite, so that the hours and times may be known. In it there is a glimpse of the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: They are timekeeping markers for mankind.﴾ End quote.

It is not far-fetched to say: the expression "extended" (madda) is used because the shadow mentioned is the shadow of the eastern horizon. The east and west are regarded as the two ends of the earth's direction in length, and the north and south as its two ends in breadth. Or, because its appearance on the earth and the length of the inhabited part of it, where those who see the shadow dwell, is greater than the breadth of the inhabited part of it. For the former, as is well known, is half a circle, that is, one hundred and eighty degrees, while the latter is less than that according to all the opinions about it. So the shadow, with respect to those who see it in the inhabited part of the earth, extends between its eastern and western directions more than between its northern and southern directions. It may also be said: this is because the beginning of the shadow is the first dawn, and its light is seen extended and elongated like the tail of a wolf, and it is maintained that it does not vanish completely, though this is weak, but remains until the light of the second dawn extends it, so it is seen spread out. And God, Exalted is He, knows best.

As for His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Then We made the sun a guide over it﴾, it is a conjunction upon "extended" and falls under its ruling. That is: then We made the rising of the sun a sign for its manifestation to the senses. For the one who looks at a coloured body while the shadow is upon it sees nothing but the body and its colour. Then, when the sun rises and its light falls upon the body, it becomes apparent to him that the shadow is an additional quality over the body and its colour.

"The opposite reveals the state of its opposite."
Said by al-Razi, al-Tabari and others.

It was also said: that is, then We made it (the sun) a sign of its existence, that is, a cause for it, because its existence comes about by the movement of the sun toward the horizon and its customary nearness to it. But what is in this is not hidden. Or: then We made it a sign by whose changing states one infers the states of the shadow, without there being between them any definite causation or influence, as the conditional clause interposed clearly indicates. Among the strange views, one that should not be applied to the glorious speech of God Most High, is that "ʿalā" means "maʿa" (with), that is: then We made the sun, together with the shadow, a sign of Our oneness, meaning: We made the shadow a sign and We made the sun a sign of Our oneness.

The shift to the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama) serves to announce the great rank of this making, because of the many benefits that follow from it that cannot be counted; or because, in the aforementioned making, which is devoid of influence, together with what is observed between the shadow and the sun of constant alternation indicating causation, there is an increase in the indication of the greatness of power and the precision of wisdom. And "then" (thumma) is either for successive rank, whose meaning is known from what has been mentioned, or for successive time, as is its literal sense, on the basis of the long time between the beginning of dawn and the rising of the sun.

As for His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Then We withdrew it to Us, a gradual withdrawal﴾, it is a conjunction upon "extended" and also falls under its ruling. That is: then We removed it after We had brought it into being extended at the moment the sun's rays fell upon its place, or by causing it to fall thus, and We erased it slowly, little by little, according to the course of the sun. This is evident on the view that the intended shadow is the shadow of an object such as a mountain or the like. As for the view that what is intended is what lies between the two risings, then because when it covers everything it does not disappear all at once with the rising of the sun on one horizon, owing to the sphericity of the earth and the difference of horizons: the sun may rise on one horizon while the shadow among its people vanishes, whereas on another horizon it has not yet risen, and its people are at the edge of that shadow; and when it has risen above the first horizon until it appears from their horizon, the shadow among them disappears. So the disappearance of the shadow after its covering is gradual. Thus it has been said.

It was also said: there is no need for this, for its disappearance is gradual even with regard to a single horizon, on the basis that some of it remains after the sun rises, as long as its rays have not fallen upon its place because of an obstruction such as a mountain or the like; and that is removed gradually according to the movement of the sun and the falling of its rays on what they had not reached at the beginning of its rising. And it seems that the expression of that removal as "withdrawal" (qabḍ), which, as al-Tabrisi said, is the gathering of spread-out parts, is because the coming-into-being is expressed by "extension."

As for His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿to Us﴾, it is to specify that the return of the shadow is to Him, Mighty and Majestic, and none truly shares with Him in its removal, just as its coming into being from Him, Glorified is He, is not truly shared in by anyone. And "then" may be for successive time or for successive rank, as explained above.

As for the one who interprets the shadow as that which existed on the day God Most High created the heaven like a dome and spread out the earth beneath it, so that it cast its shadow upon it, the meaning of "Then We made..." and so on becomes: Then We created the sun and made it dominant over that shadow, and We made it a guide followed, as a guide is followed on the road; so it increases and decreases, extends and contracts. Then We withdrew it with an easy withdrawal, without difficulty.

It is also possible that its withdrawal is at the Hour of Resurrection, by the indication of "to Us" and likewise "easy," and that is by the withdrawal of its causes, which are the bodies that cast the shadow. Thus He has mentioned its annihilation by the annihilation of its causes, just as He mentioned its creation by the creation of its causes. The use of the past tense is for the certainty of its occurrence and for the fitness of what is mentioned with it. And "then" is for successive time, and there is in this what there is, as we have pointed out.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 47:

﴿It is He who made the night for you a garment﴾ is an explanation of some of the wondrous signs of His power, glorious and exalted is He, and the marvelous rulings of His mercy and His bounty overflowing upon creation. The shift in address serves to give the context of bestowing favor its due. The preposition (lam) is connected to (ja'ala, made), and placing it before its two objects is for the sake of emphasizing that what follows is among their benefits. In linking the explanation of the states of the shade with the explanation of the rulings of the night, which is the shade of the earth, there is a gentleness of transition beyond which there is no further refinement. That is: It is He who made the night, for your benefit, like a garment that covers you with its darkness, just as a garment covers you. (And He made sleep), which generally occurs by the overcoming of the faculties by vapors, and it was said: by inhaling a breeze that blows from beneath the Throne, but this hardly holds true.

﴿a rest﴾: a repose for the bodies through cutting off the activities that occur while awake. The root of (sabt) is cutting off. It was said: the day of Saturday (sabt) because it was customary to rest on it, according to what is said; and it was said: because God Most High created nothing in it. It is said of the sick person when he rests from the fatigue of his illness: (masbut), and to this view Abu Muslim went.

Abu Hayyan said: (sabat) is a kind of fainting that afflicts the awake person as an illness, so sleep was likened to it; and (sabt) is remaining in a place, so sleep was a kind of stillness.

﴿And He made the day a resurrection﴾: that is, having resurrection, in which people spread out to seek livelihood. It is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made the day a means of livelihood﴾. In making it the very act of resurrection there is hyperbole. It was said: (nushuran) means (nashiran, spreading), by metaphorical attribution. It is also permissible that (sabat) be intended to mean death, because of the complete cessation of sensation or life in it, and sleep was expressed by it because of the complete resemblance between them in the cessation of the rulings of life. Upon this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who takes you in death by night﴾, and His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died in their sleep﴾. By (nushur) is meant the raising up, that is: and He made the day a time of rising from that sleep, or the very raising up by way of hyperbole.

Al-Zamakhshari rejected the meaning of rest in the explanation of (sabat), and said: the mention of (nushur) in contrast to it contradicts it, as a wild camel shuns a watering place that is turbid. Perhaps this is because (nushur) in the Qur'an is hardly ever found with the meaning of dispersal and movement to seek livelihood. Al-Zamakhshari's rejection was explained in al-Kashf by this reason, and by the fact that the preceding and following verses, along with what they contain of reminder of blessing and power, incorporate an indication of return; so likewise it should not be distinguished between this verse and its counterparts.

It seems he made the making of the night a garment and sleep in it a repose, taken together, the counterpart of making the day a resurrection; and for this reason (ja'ala, made) was repeated in it, because of what resurrection contains of the meaning of manifestation and the active movement, or the meaning of manifestation and raising up. He did not take this path in the verse of surah al-Naba' for reasons that are not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 48:

﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾ Ibn Kathir recited it in the singular (al-Rih), taking it as denoting the genus, with the definite article (bi-Al) or as encompassing all (al-istighraq). So it has the meaning of the plural, in agreement with the recitation of the majority. Ibn 'Atiyyah (Ibn Atiyyah) said: the recitation in the plural is more correct (awjah), because wherever al-rih appears in the Qur'an in the singular, it refers to punishment, and wherever it refers to rain and mercy, it comes in the plural, since the wind of rain disperses, scatters, spreads out, and comes gently from here and there, one after another, whereas the wind of punishment comes as a single mass that does not scatter. Do you not see that it smashes and demolishes whatever it encounters?

Al-Rummani said: the winds of mercy are plural because they are three fertilizing winds: the south wind (al-Janub), the east wind (al-Saba) and the north wind (al-Dabur), while the wind of punishment is singular because it is one wind that does not fertilize, and it is al-Dabur. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when the wind blew: "O Allah, make it winds (riyahan) and do not make it a wind (rihan)" points to what has been mentioned. You know that in the words of Ibn 'Atiyyah there is an oversight regarding the interpretation by which the two recitations agree. It has been mentioned in al-Bahr that it is not permissible to say that this recitation is more correct than the other recitation, since each of them is mutawatir. The alif-lam in al-rih is for the genus and thus generalizes. What has been mentioned regarding the distinction between the singular and the plural is mostly the case, or where there is no indicator, or in the indefinite, as has come in the hadith. What pertains to this topic will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in surah al-Rum.

Page 30
﴿bushran﴾: a lightened form of (bushuran) with two damma, the plural of bashur, in the sense of mubashshir (bringer of good news), meaning: he sent the winds as bringers of good news. It was also read as "nushran" with nun and lightening, the plural of nashur like rasul and rusul, and as "nushuran" with damma on the nun and shin, which is also a plural of that. That is, He sent them as spreaders of the clouds, from al-nashr in the sense of resurrection (ba'th), because they gather it as though they give it life, not from al-nashr in the sense of dispersal, because that is not suitable, unless it is intended as driving (al-sawq) metaphorically. "Nashran" with a fatha on the nun and sukun on the shin is taken as a verbal noun (masdar) described by it for emphasis, and it is permitted that it be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of (arsala), because it has the meaning of nashara. All of these are mutawatir. It is narrated from Ibn al-Sumaiqi that he read "bushra" with the feminine alif.

﴿Before His mercy﴾: that is, in front of the rain. Mercy has been used as a metaphor for it, and the metaphor has been supported in the best manner (rashshahat al-isti'arah ahsan tarshih). It is permitted that there is a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) in the speech, and bushran is a completion of the metaphor, included within it. The turning to the royal "we" (nun al-'azamah) in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We send down from the sky﴾, is to display complete care for the sending down, because it is the result of what was mentioned of the sending of the winds. That is: We sent it down by Our majesty, through what We arranged of sending the winds, from the direction of height that is not the place of water, or from the clouds, or from the known body. The detailed discussion of this has preceded.

﴿pure water﴾: The apparent reading is that it is a qualifier of (water), and on this basis it has been said its meaning is: most perfectly pure, abundant in purity. In al-Bahr the intensification (mubalaghah) was explained as relating to the quality, in the sense that nothing else mixed with it in its place of rest, its course, or what is cast into it, like the waters of the earth. Tha'lab interpreted it as that which is pure in itself and purifying for others. Al-Zamakhshari objected to this, saying: if what he said is an explanation of its eloquence in purity, it is sound; otherwise, fa'ul is not from the form tafil at all. Others said: taking purifying into it is contrary to it, since purity is intrinsic, and intensification in an intransitive verb does not make it transitive.

The author of al-Kashf answered that: since purity in itself does not admit increase, the intensification in it returns to the addition of the meaning of purifying to it, not that the intransitive became transitive. Al-Mawla al-Dawwani objected to this, saying that there is scrutiny in it, since the addition of the meaning of purifying, when it was derived from the intensification with the aid of non-acceptance of increase, the intensification in general was a cause of transitivity. Then he said: it may be escaped by saying that the intransitive meaning remains in its state, and the intensification necessitated the addition of the transitive to it, not the transitivity of that intransitive, and between them there are two differences. Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that the intensification's conveying the verb's connection to another is something neither language nor custom supports, and where is this connection in the words of Jarir:

To the full-buttocked, gazelle-like ones of the gazelles, sweet-toothed, whose saliva is pure (tahur).

Similar to it is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And their Lord gave them to drink a pure (tahuran) drink﴾. From this and similar examples, some chose that the intensification returns to the quality, as you heard from al-Bahr. Some of the verifiers said: here "tahuran" is a noun for that by which one purifies, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Dust is the purifier (tahur) of the believer." And fa'ul, as al-Azhari said in al-Zahir, may be a noun of instrument for what something is done with, like ghasul, wudu', fatur and sahur, and so on, as it may be a qualifier in the sense of an active participle like akul, or a passive one like sabub meaning masbub, and a noun of kind like dhanub, and a verbal noun, which is rare, like qabul. Thus it conveys purifying for others by its lexical form. What was narrated from Tha'lab may be carried upon this, and the consideration that it is pure in itself, because its being purifying for others is a branch of that. On this basis it is taken as a substitute for water or an explanatory apposition to it, not a qualifier, so the construction would be like: I sent to you water, wudu'.

You know that what is apparent in our context is that it is a qualifier. If that is possible on this view by some kind of interpretation, it would be further from disputation and debate. Sibawayh related that tahur came as a verbal noun of tatahhur in the saying: "I purified myself, a good purification (tahuran hasanan)," and he mentioned that among it is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "There is no prayer except with purification (tahur)." To carry what is in the verse upon that is not fitting. Whatever the case, describing water with it conveys the magnitude of the favour, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 49:

﴿That We may give life thereby﴾ i.e., by means of what We sent down of water, pure (ṭahūr), ﴿to a dead land﴾, one in which there is no vegetation, and that is by causing vegetation to grow through it. By "the land" (al-balda) is meant the earth, as in his saying:

They made camp, and she [the camel] cast down a land upon a land, few are the voices in it except its lowing.

It is also permitted that by it is meant its well-known sense (a town or city). Its indefiniteness is for classification (li-l-tanwīʿ), and the masculine form of its adjective is because it carries the meaning of "al-balad." Alternatively, (maytan) is among the intensive patterns (amthila al-mubālaghah) which do not resemble the imperfect in its vowels and quiescences, and it denotes permanence, so it is treated as one of the fixed nouns (al-jawāmid). The lām of ﴿li-nuḥyiya﴾ is connected to (anzalnā), and its connection to (ṭahūran) is nothing.

ʿĪsā and Abū Jaʿfar read (mayyitan) with shaddah (tashdīd). Abū Ḥayyān said: The majority preferred the lightened form (takhfīf), because it resembles a verbal noun (faʿl) from among the infinitives (maṣādir); thus, just as the masculine and feminine are described by the infinitive, so too by what resembles it. In contrast, the shaddah form resembles the active participle (fāʿil) in terms of accepting the tāʾ, except in what is specific to the feminine, such as ṭāmith.

﴿And that We may give drink﴾ i.e., that pure water, and upon its flowing in the valleys or its gathering in the pools, reservoirs and wells, ﴿from what We have created: cattle and many humans﴾, i.e., the people of the deserts who live by the rain-fed waters (al-ḥayāʾ). For this reason, (al-anʿām) and (al-anāsī) are indefinite, so the indefiniteness is for classification.

The singling out of this category for mention is because the people of towns and cities live near rivers and springs, so they and their livestock are self-sufficient without the watering of the sky; while other animals go far in seeking water, so drinking seldom fails them. The context of the noble verses – as it serves to show the greatness of power – likewise serves to enumerate the kinds of blessing. Since cattle are a possession of man, and the general benefits and livelihoods of people depend upon them, their watering is placed before the watering of people, just as the reviving of the land is placed before them, for it is the cause of their life and sustenance; so the precedence is of the type of placing causes before effects. It is also permitted that the mention of what was stated precedes the watering of humans because, when they obtain what waters their land and livestock, they do not lack their own drink. Its sum is that it is of the category of placing what is most important and fundamental in the context of divine favour; and the mention of the watering of humans after this is an addition (irdāf) and completion (tatmīm) for comprehensiveness. The "min" is either partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah) or explanatory (bayāniyyah), and (kathīran) is an adjective for both coordinated items, not in apposition.

ʿAbd Allāh, Abū Ḥaywah, Ibn Abī ʿAblah, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Abū ʿAmr in one narration from them read «wa-nasqiyahu» with a fatḥah on the nūn. It is also narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb – may Allah be pleased with him – that asqā and saqā are two dialects. It was also said: asqāhu means "made the watering available to him and prepared it." (anāsī) is the plural of (insān) according to Sībawayh, and its origin is anāsīn, so its nūn was changed into yā' and assimilated into what precedes it.

Al-Farrāʾ, al-Mubarrad, and al-Zajjāj held that it is the plural of (insī), and said in al-Baḥr: The analogical form would be anāsiyah, as they said for mahlabī, mahālibah.

In al-Durr al-Maṣūn it is stated that fa‘ālī is only a plural for what has a doubled yā' when it is not for relation (nisbah), like kursī and karāsī; and what has the yā' of relation is pluralised on afāʿilah, like azraqī and azāriqah. That the yā' of insī is not for relation is far-fetched, so its proper plural is anāsiyah. In al-Tashīl he said it is the more common form (akthariyy), and according to it what was mentioned is not objected to.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 50:

﴿And We have certainly distributed it﴾. The pronoun refers to the water sent down from the sky, like the two pronouns before it. *Tasrif* (distribution) means changing its states and times and sending it down in different manners. That is, "and with God, Exalted is He, We have certainly distributed the rain ﴿among them﴾", that is, among the people,
[Page 32]
in different lands, at different times, and in varying kinds, such as heavy rain, light drizzle, and others. ﴿That they may take heed﴾, that is, that they may draw a lesson from it. ﴿But most of the people refused except to deny﴾, that is, they did nothing but ingratitude for the blessing and outright denial of it, by attributing it to other than Him, Mighty and Majestic, by saying, "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-station (*nawʾ*)", believing that the stars act to bring it about and have an effect on it by their own essences. This belief, we seek refuge in God Exalted, is disbelief (*kufr*). In al-Kashshaf and elsewhere it is stated that whoever believes that God, Mighty and Majestic, is the Creator of the rains, and has set the star-stations as signs and indicators of them, and by his saying "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-station" means "we were given rain at the time when such-and-such a star sets in the west with the dawn," does not disbelieve, and the apparent meaning is that he does not sin either. The Imam said: whoever holds that the spheres and stars are independently responsible for these things, there is no doubt of his disbelief. As for whoever says that He, glory be to Him, created them with properties and attributes that necessitate these events, his error may well not reach the level of disbelief. I will later, God willing, present a discussion on this question which I hope God Exalted will cause people of understanding to find pleasing, and by which the words of the Imam will be strengthened. The reference of the pronoun in *anzalnahu* ("We sent it down") to the water that was sent down is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and Ikrimah.

A group, from the first (Ibn 'Abbas), recorded, and al-Hakim authenticated, that he said: "There is no year with less rain than another, but God distributes it wherever He wills," then he recited this verse. Al-Kharа'iti recorded in *Makarim al-Akhlaq* the same from the second (Ibn Mas'ud). From this it is understood that *tasrif* is taken to mean division. Some said: it refers to the statement understood from the context, which is the mention of the creation of clouds and the sending down of rain for the great purposes mentioned. Its *tasrif* is its repetition and its mention in various forms and different expressions. The meaning is: "And We have certainly repeated this statement and mentioned it in different manners in the Qur'an and in the other heavenly books, among the people, the earlier and the later, so that they might reflect and know thereby the perfection of His power, Exalted is He, and the vastness of His mercy, Mighty and Majestic, in this. But most of them, of those who came before and after, refused except to be ungrateful for the blessing and to be little concerned with it, or to deny it outright by attributing it to other than Him, exalted is His majesty." Al-Zamakhshari chose this view, and Abu al-Su'ud said: it is the most apparent.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from 'Ata' al-Khurasani that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. Do you not see His saying afterward: ﴿and strive against them with it﴾? It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas by al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*), but the well-known view from him is what preceded. Perhaps what is meant is the evidences mentioned in it for the perfection of His power, Exalted is He, and the vastness of His mercy, Mighty and Majestic, or something similar, so reflect. As for what has been said, that it refers to the wind, it is nothing.

[Page 33]

﴿Had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town﴾: a prophet who would warn its people. Then the burdens of prophethood would have been lightened for you. But We did not will that, and We restricted the matter to you, out of honour and exaltation for you. ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾ in what they want you to do. This is an incitement (tahyij) for him (ﷺ) and for the believers.

﴿And strive against them with it﴾: that is, with the Qur'an, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). This is by reciting what it contains of proofs, admonitions, warnings and reproofs, and by reminding them of the circumstances of the nations that denied. ﴿A great striving﴾: for calling all the worlds to it in the manner mentioned is a great striving whose measure cannot be estimated, either in quantity or in quality. The arrangement of what is mentioned upon what precedes it is in accordance with what the particle fa' (then/so) requires, on the basis that restricting the messengership to him (peace be upon him) is a splendid blessing which ought to be thanked for. What was mentioned is a kind of thanks. It is as if it were said: We sent you as a warner to all the villages, and We favoured you and exalted you, and We did not send a warner to every town. So respond to that with steadfastness and diligence in the call and in manifesting the truth.

In al-Kashf, for explaining the noble nazm (the coherent arrangement of the text), it is said that when there was mentioned what indicates his keenness (ﷺ) to seek their guidance and his being troubled by this, in His saying: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾

[Page 33 continuation marker removed]

and he was reproached with the proofs of power, blessing and mercy, indicating that gathering them together would not benefit them, and that they deny such blessings and are heedless of the greatness of their Originator, glory be to Him. They were made like cattle, "nay, even more astray," and it was concluded that they have no aim but ingratitude for His blessing, exalted is He.

It has been said: ﴿Had We willed﴾ means that We exalted you by this matter so that you would bear its burdens and attain what has been stored up for you of the kind of its recompense. So upon you is striving and steadfastness, and it is no concern of yours that they receive the call with refusal and contention. This was emphasised: his keenness (ﷺ) for the faith of these people, whose hearts are sealed, was made into obedience to them. It has also been said: "So do not obey them." The central theme of the surah, according to what al-Tibi mentioned, is that he (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) was sent to mankind in general, warning them of what is before them and what is behind them. For this reason, the opening of the surah was made its excellence: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾.

The verse, as you have heard, is connected to His saying, exalted is He: "Have you seen…" to the end of the verses. It contains from the exaltation of his station (peace be upon him) what it contains, and it is not directed toward discipline, as has been wrongly supposed.

It has been said: it is connected to what comes before it, in the sense: Had We willed, We would have distributed the warner among them, just as We distributed the rain among them. But We do what is most beneficial for them in their religion and their worldly life, so We sent you to them as a messenger to all of them, so do not obey, etc. In this there is what it contains of indication of the deficiency of that view.

Furthermore, it is permissible that the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ (with it) refers to abandoning their obedience, which is understood from the prohibition. The preposition bā' (bi) in that case may be for accompaniment (mulabasah). The meaning would be: strive against them with what has been mentioned of the rulings of the noble Qur'an, while abandoning their obedience. It is as if it were said: strive against them with severity and harshness, not with leniency and conciliation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾. Otherwise it would be objected that the mere abandonment of obedience is realised without any call at all, and there is no trace of striving in it, let alone a great striving. It is also permissible that it refers to what is indicated by His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town﴾, namely that he (ﷺ) is the warner of all the villages. For if He had sent a warner to every town, it would have been obligatory upon each warner to strive against his own town, and all those strivings would have converged upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Thus his striving became great and mighty on account of that. So it was said to him (peace be upon him): strive against them by reason of your being the warner of all the villages, a great striving comprising every kind of striving. This was objected to on the ground that explaining the cause of the greatness of striving in respect of quantity adds no further benefit, since it is self-evident. What is fitting for the context is explaining the cause of its greatness and magnitude in respect of quality. Abu Hayyan permitted that the pronoun refers to the sword.

You know that the surah is Meccan, and striving with the sword was not legislated in Mecca. Nevertheless, what it entails is not hidden. The verse is cited, in the manner related from the Salaf, as evidence for the great merit of the striving of scholars against the enemies of the religion by means of the proofs they present against them, and the most fortunate of them are those among them who strive with the Qur'an.

[Page 33]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 53:

﴿It is He who let loose the two seas﴾, meaning He sent them forth in their courses, as horses are let loose in a pasture (al-marj). This was related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). It is also said in this sense: amraja, according to what has been reported, but maraja is the dialect of the Hijaz and amraja is the dialect of Najd.

The root of al-marj, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is mixing. It is said: maraja amruhum, meaning their affair became confused. A pasture is called marj because plants are mixed together in it. By "the two seas" is meant abundant sweet water and abundant salt water, without restriction to two specific seas. This returns to what was mentioned earlier of the proofs. As for His saying, ﴿this is sweet, fresh﴾ and so on, it means extremely sweet. Its form is fu'al, derived from farata, which is a metathesis of rafata, meaning he broke it, because it breaks the fierceness of thirst and suppresses it. It was also said that it means cool, as in Majma' al-Bayan (of al-Tabarsi). It is either a new sentence, or a circumstantial clause (hal) with an implied verb of saying, meaning: it is said of them both, "This is sweet, fresh."

﴿And this is salty, bitter﴾. It was also said that this is a circumstantial clause without an implied verb of saying, in the sense: He let loose the two seas differing in extreme sweetness and likewise in saltiness. The demonstrative (ism al-ishara) takes the place of a pronoun. Ujaj means extremely salty, as we have indicated. It was applied to it because drinking it increases the blaze (ajij) of thirst. Al-Raghib said: it is extremely salty and hot, from the crackling (ajij) of fire, end of quote. It was also said that it is bitter, and al-Tabarsi related this from Qatada. It was also said that it is hot, and thus it stands opposite to al-furat (fresh) according to those who explained that as cool.

Talha ibn Musarrif and Qutayba, from al-Kisa'i, read "malih" with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam here and likewise in (Surah) Fatir. Abu Hatim said: this is unusual (munkar) as a reading. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: he meant malih (salty), and it was lightened by dropping the alif, as burd is said for barid in his saying:

My heart has become cold (sarid),
It does not desire to come down (yarid),
Except for a sparse, dry (ârad) cloud,
And a cold (barid) wild shrub,
And a thick, dense bush (multabid).

It was also said that it is a lightened form of malih, since it occurs with the meaning of malih. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in the book Al-Lawami: it is a rare, anomalous dialect, so it is not a lightened form of anything. Yes, it is like milh in the reading of the majority, in the sense of malih. The more eloquent usage, in describing water, is to say "ma' milh" rather than "ma' malih," although the latter is correct, as al-Azhari transmitted from al-Kisa'i. Tha'lab also acknowledged its correctness. Al-Khafaji said: the correct view is that it is heard from the Arabs, as the lexicographers established, and they cited many examples as proof. Accordingly, whoever considered Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) to be wrong in his saying "ma' malih" has erred, being ignorant of the standing of this Imam.

﴿And He placed between them a barrier﴾, meaning a partition (hajiz). It is an Arabic word. It was also said that its origin is barzah, which was then Arabized. The barrier here, as Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan, is the land that lies between them, like the land intervening between the Tigris, which is called a sea because of its vastness. The term "sea" has become widely applied to a great river, so it has also come to be used literally for it, and thus there is no difficulty with the dual. If you refuse to accept that it has become literal, then the consideration of figurative inclusion (taghlib) removes the difficulty between it and the great sea. The meaning is that the land intervenes in their courses; otherwise they both end in the sea, as do all great rivers. The indication of this placing for the perfection of His power, may He be glorified and exalted, is that it is contrary to the requirement of nature. The nature of water requires that its parts be compact, gathered together, covering the earth and surrounding it from all directions, as air surrounds it. The nature of earth also requires that its parts be compact, with no depressions or elevations in it, submerged by water, lying within it like the center of a circle, as the philosophers established. They mentioned, regarding the cause of what was uncovered of the earth and the occurrence of valleys and plains in it, things that are not free from speculation.

"Between them" is an adverbial complement of "placed" (ja'ala). It may also be a circumstantial clause from "barzakh." The apparent meaning is that the tanwin on "barzakh" is for magnification, meaning: He placed between them a great barrier, since despite the passage of ages, the water of neither sea penetrates it to reach the other and change its taste. ﴿And a forbidding ban﴾, meaning extreme repugnance, as if each of them seeks refuge from the other by that expression. The intended meaning is that each one remains with its attribute of sweetness or saltiness, so the sweet sea does not turn salty in its place, nor the salty sea sweet in its place. This is part of the perfection of His power, may He be exalted, and the depth of His wisdom, may He be glorified and exalted. Sweetness and saltiness are not due to the nature of the earth or the nature of water, for otherwise all would be sweet or all salty. It is mentioned regarding the wisdom behind making the great sea salty that it does not become foul through long standing and the passage of ages. It was said: this is also the secret behind making the tears of the eye salty. There are other wisdoms in it, and Allah Most High knows best.

The apparent meaning is that "a forbidding ban" (hijran) is coordinated with "a barrier" (barzakh), meaning: He placed between them this word, and by it is meant what you have just heard. This is among the most eloquent and sweetest of speech. It was also said that it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb of saying, meaning: and they say, "a forbidding ban." It is related from al-Hasan that by al-hijr is meant the land that is set apart between them, and the explanation of barzakh was previously given in a similar way. Perhaps the combining of the two terms in that case is for added emphasis on the matter of the barrier. What we have mentioned earlier is preferable and more profound in meaning. It was also said: by the barzakh is meant a barrier from His power, may He be glorified and exalted, which is not visible. By His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿a forbidding ban﴾ is meant complete distinction and absence of mixing. Its origin is a statement that the one seeking refuge says concerning what he fears, as its details were previously explained. The sum of the meaning of the verse is that He, Most High, is the One who made the two seas mixed in appearance to the eye, yet truly separated, by His power, may He be glorified and exalted, with the most perfect separation, such that the sweet does not mix with the salty nor the salty with the sweet, and the taste of neither changes by the other at all.

This is reported from the majority. But this contradicts what is observed. Great rivers such as the Tigris and what joins it, the Nile, and others, which people witness, when they meet the sea, the taste of a considerable part of them changes in the direction of the meeting point. Likewise, the taste of a considerable part of the sea in the direction of the meeting point also changes. The degree of change varies in strength and weakness according to the variation of the causes that come into play, such as the wind and other things. This is what has been reported by mass transmission.
