No one has reported that he saw on earth two seas, one sweet and the other salty, which joined one another without any change in the taste of either at all. For whoever has even a little discernment, there is no way to interpret the verse as referring to two seas on earth in that manner. But neither has anyone witnessed them, as is well known. I do not see any merit in interpreting the verse in the way mentioned. Adhering to this and similar cold artificialities, when the clear meaning that is free of any turbidity is evident to the fair-minded, only results in giving the disbelievers an opening to criticize the Great Qur'an and in engendering ill opinion of the Muslims.

It was also said that by the barzakh is meant an intermediary. That is, He placed between the intensely sweet sea and the intensely salty sea a water that is intermediate, neither intensely sweet nor intensely salty. It is a portion of fresh sweet water at the point of meeting, mixed with some of the bitter salt water, which broke the fierceness of its sweetness; and a portion of bitter salt water at the same point, mixed with some of the fresh sweet water, which broke the fierceness of its saltiness. The emphatic repugnance between them, understood from His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿and a forbidding ban﴾, applies to what lies beyond that, that is, what is not affected by its neighbor, but remains in its attribute of intense sweetness and intense saltiness. This is, as you see, far-fetched. It was also related regarding the sea that the two seas meant are two specific seas, the Sea of Rome and the Persian Gulf.

Al-Suyuti mentioned this in Al-Durr al-Manthur from al-Hasan through the transmission of Ibn Abi Hatim. This is among the strange wonders, since both of these seas are bitter and salty, so how could it be correct to intend them here alongside His saying, ﴿this is sweet, fresh and this is salty, bitter﴾? Yes, it may be correct in what will come, if Allah Most High wills, in the verse of Surah al-Rahman, namely His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting together, between them is a barrier they do not transgress﴾, because there is no mention there of anything that prevents it. What was reported from al-Hasan, if it is authentic, is perhaps in that verse. Al-Suyuti erred in his transmission of it in discussing this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the two seas are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth. Something similar was mentioned regarding the sea from Ibn Abbas, and that they meet every year. I do not hold this view regarding the verse, nor do I believe the transmission of it from those you have heard of is sound. Although the connection of the verse to this view with what preceded it, His saying, ﴿and We send down from the sky pure water﴾, is more complete, on the view that the rain comes from a sea in the sky, and its indication of the perfection of His power, may He be exalted, is more evident. As for you, the choice is yours. And Allah Most High is the Giver of success.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 54:

﴿And He it is who created from water a human being﴾. This is the water with which Allah mixed the clay of Adam, peace be upon him, making it a part of the substance of humankind, so that it would gather, become pliable, and be ready to receive shapes and forms. Thus "water" (al-ma') refers to the known water, and its definite article is generic (li-l-jins). "Human being" (basharan) refers to Adam, peace be upon him, and its tanwin (indefiniteness) is for glorification. Alternatively, it refers to the human species, which applies to Adam, peace be upon him, and his descendants. The "min" (from) is for origin (ibtida'iyyah). It is also permissible that "water" means the sperm-drop (nutfah), in which case "human being" must be understood as the children of Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿Then He made him [into] lineage and marriage-relations﴾. That is, He divided him into two categories: those of lineage (nasab), namely males to whom lineage is traced, and those of marriage-relations (sihr), namely females through whom marriage ties are formed. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from it He made the two mates, the male and the female﴾. Here the "wa" (and) is for division. The speech contains an implied noun that has been omitted so as to indicate exaggeration clearly. The phrase "and female" was dropped so as to indicate branching explicitly. This making and dividing is entirely clear if "human being" is taken to mean the species. As for taking it to mean Adam, peace be upon him, some have said that it is by way of the species, and that the speech includes what is of the type of istikhdam (a rhetorical device where one word carries two senses), like your saying: "I have a dirham and half of it." Others have said that there is no need to consider this, and that the speech follows the pattern of omission and transitive connection, meaning "He made from him", and it has been used in its original form in the parallel of this verse which you have just heard. Others have said the meaning is: He made Adam a lineage and marriage-relation by creating Hawwa' (Eve) from him, while leaving him in his original maleness.

The sequence of making the species into two categories after the creation of Adam, or of the species by reference to its creation, or of making two categories from Adam after creating him, peace be upon him, as the fa' (then) indicates, is evident. Perhaps it is imagined that the object pronoun in "ja'alahu" (He made him) refers to the water, with the fa' having the same function as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Noah called upon his Lord and said: "My Lord..."﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many a town We have destroyed, and Our punishment came upon it by night or while they were resting at midday﴾. But this is not correct.

It is related from Ali, may Allah honour his face, that lineage (nasab) is that whom it is not lawful to marry, and marriage-relation (sihr) is that whom it is lawful to marry. In another narration from him, may Allah be pleased with him: lineage is that whom it is not lawful to marry, and marriage-relation is kinship through nursing. Interpreting sihr in this way is also reported from al-Dahhak.

﴿And your Lord is ever Competent﴾. Exceedingly powerful, in that He is able to create from one substance a human being with diverse organs and widely differing natures, and to make him into two opposite categories. In a context like this, "kana" (was/is) indicates continuity. If we say that the nominal sentence itself also conveys this, the statement conveys continuity upon continuity. Perhaps this suggests that perfect power is among the requirements of His essence, glorified and exalted is He. It is a matter of wonder what some of those who claim exclusive mastery of verification, from among the scholars of our era whom we have accompanied, may Allah have mercy on him, have asserted: that "kana" in such a context indicates continuity regarding what has never ceased, and the nominal sentence indicates continuity regarding what does not cease, so that combining them conveys the continuous establishment of the predicate for the subject, without beginning or end. From this one may gauge the man's level of knowledge.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 55:

﴿And they worship besides Allah﴾ that which, exalted is His majesty, has not been mentioned, ﴿what neither benefits them﴾ if they worship it, ﴿nor harms them﴾ if they do not worship it. What is meant by this is the idols, or everything that is worshipped besides Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and no created being has independent power to benefit or harm.

﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper (zahir) against his Lord﴾, the One whose signs of lordship have been mentioned, exalted is He and high is He. ﴿Zahir﴾ means one who gives support (muzahir), as said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. The form fa'il in the sense of mufa'il is common, and from it come nadim (companion) and jalis (sitting companion). Al-muzaharah (ẓahāra) means assistance, i.e. he assists Satan against his Lord, glorified is He, through enmity and polytheism. What is meant by "the disbeliever" is the category, so it is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, to censure their disbelief upon them.

It has been said: he is Abu Jahl, and the verse was revealed concerning him. 'Ikrimah said: he is Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him, and what is meant is that he assists the polytheists against his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, by inciting them to disobey Him and to associate others with Him, mighty and majestic is He. It has been said: what is meant is that he assists against the friends of Allah, exalted is He.

It is permitted that this be intended alongside all the other possibilities concerning "the disbeliever." It has also been said: what is meant by (ẓahīran) is "contemptible" (mahīnan), from their saying: "I threw him behind my back (ẓahartu bihi)" when you cast him behind your back, i.e. whoever worships other than Allah, exalted is He, that which neither benefits nor harms him, is contemptible before his Lord,
Page 37
mighty and majestic is He, having no portion with Him, glorified is He. This was said by al-Tabari, so fa'il is in the sense of maf'ul. However, what is well known is that (ẓahīran) means "helper" (mu'in), not "one cast behind the back."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 56:

﴿And We did not send you﴾ in any state whatsoever ﴿except﴾ as one who is ﴿a bringer of good tidings﴾ to the believers ﴿and a warner﴾, i.e., one who warns, exaggerating in warning to the disbelievers. Because the warning is specified to them, the discourse concerns them, and it is intended to indicate the extent of their persistence in the error they are in, the intensive form (ṣīghat al-mubālaghah) was used for it. It has also been said that the intensiveness is with regard to the large number of those warned, for the disbelievers at every time are more numerous than the believers.

Some of them considered their number by including the sinful believers among them, i.e., "and a warner to the disobedient, whether they are believers or disbelievers." The context requires the restriction to the disbelievers, as is not hidden. The meaning is: We did not send you except as a bringer of good tidings to the believers and a warner to the disbelievers, so do not grieve over their not believing.

Say (﴿قُلْ﴾): (this is addressed to the Prophet) to them, warding off from yourself the accusation that you benefit from their faith. ﴿Ma as'alukum 'alayhi﴾ ("I do not ask you for anything in return for it"), that is, for conveying the message, which the word "sending" (al-irsal) indicates; or for what was mentioned of giving good news and warning. It has also been said that it refers to the Qur'an. ﴿Min ajr﴾ ("any reward"), that is, any reward from your side. ﴿Illa man sha'a an yattakhidha ila rabbihi﴾ ("except for whoever wills to take to his Lord"), that is, to His mercy and good pleasure, ﴿sabilan﴾ ("a way"), meaning a path. According to the majority (al-Jumhur), the exception here is disjunctive (munqati', i.e., not of the same kind as what precedes it). The meaning is: "But whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, glory be to Him" by means of spending, which takes the place of a reward, such as charity and expenditure in the way of God, Exalted is He, so that it fits the corrective contrast (al-istidrak). Then let him do so. Some scholars held that the exception is continuous (muttasil, i.e., of the same kind), and that there is an elided noun (mudaf muqaddar) in the sentence. The meaning is: "except the act of whoever wills to take to his Lord a way through faith and obedience, according to what I call them to." This is based on a supposition (al-idda'), and depicting it in the form of a reward is because it is the intended purpose of the act. This is like the exception in the words of the poet:

"There is no fault in them, except that their guest is blamed for forgetting loved ones and homeland."

In this there is a complete uprooting of any trace of greed, and a demonstration of the utmost compassion toward them, since this is attributed to him (ﷺ), even though its benefit returns to them. It has also been said that the meaning is: "I do not ask you for any reward for it except the reward of whoever believes," that is, except the reward that accrues to me from his faith, for the one who guides to good is like its doer. In that case, there is no need for the supposition and depiction mentioned earlier. However, the better view is the one in which the trace of greed is completely uprooted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 58:

﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living, who does not die.﴾ This is for being independent of their wages and for being sufficient against their evils. It is as if the shift from "And rely upon Allah" to what is in this noble composition was meant to convey, by its implication or by the ruling being attached to a fitting attribute, that reliance is not valid upon one who does not possess the mentioned attributes of life and enduring existence. As for reliance being invalid upon one who does not possess life, such as idols, this is evident. As for its being invalid upon one who does not possess enduring existence, being one who dies, it is because he is weak and powerless. So the one relied upon is most like a weak thing that has returned to a bundle of dry straw (qarmalah). It was also said: because when one dies, whoever relied upon him is lost.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in (al-Tawakkul) and al-Bayhaqi in (Shu'ab al-Iman) narrated from Uqbah ibn Abi Thabit, who said: "It is written in the Torah: Do not rely upon the son of Adam, for the son of Adam has no sustenance (qiwam), but rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die." And some of the early generations (salaf) recited this verse and said: "It is not proper for a person of intellect to trust any created being after it."

﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾ i.e., and declare Him free of imperfection, while joined with praising Him, may He be exalted, with attributes of perfection, seeking increase of bounty by thanking Him for His past favors, Mighty and Majestic is He. So the "ba'" is for accompaniment (mulabasah), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Declaring Him free of imperfection was placed first because it is clearing (takhliyah), and clearing is more important than adorning (tahliyah). And in a hadith: "Whoever says: Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him, his sins will be forgiven even if they were like the foam of the sea."

﴿And He is sufficient as one who is Knowing of the sins of His servants﴾ what appears of them and what is hidden, as the plural construct indicates, since it is among the forms of generality, or His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Aware (khabiran)﴾, because khibrah is knowledge of the inner aspects of matters, as al-Raghib mentioned, and whoever knows the inner aspects knows the outer aspects all the more; so this indicates that by correspondence (mutabaqah) and by implication (iltizam).

It is apparent that "bi-dhunubi" is connected to "khabiran," and it is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a specifier (tamyiz). The "ba'" in "bihi" is extra (za'idah) in the agent of "kafa." It is also permitted that "bi-dhunubi" be the complement of "kafa," with the sentence brought to console him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and to warn the disbelievers, meaning: He, Mighty and Majestic, is aware of the sins of His servants such that nothing of them is hidden from Him, so He will recompense them for them, and it is not upon you if they believe or disbelieve.

[p. 39]

﴿Who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne.﴾ Its exegesis has already passed. The relative clause (al-mawsul) is in the genitive case, as another attribute (sifah) of "the Ever-Living" (al-Hayy). He, glorified be He, is described with an active attribute (al-sifah al-fi'liyyah) after being described, exalted is He, with eternity (al-abadiyyah), which is among the essential attributes (al-sifat al-dhatiyyah). The reference to His being characterized by all-encompassing knowledge serves to establish and reinforce the obligation of placing trust in Him, exalted is His majesty. For whoever brought into being these great bodies in this superb pattern and exquisite order, with firm arrangement and sound ordering, at specified times, while He, glorified be He, has complete power to originate them all at once, for sublime wisdoms and beautiful ends whose details the intellects cannot grasp, is most worthy of being relied upon and most deserving that affairs be entrusted to Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ is in the nominative case by way of praise (madh), meaning: He is the Most Merciful. In reality it is another attribute of "the Ever-Living," as in the reading of Zayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman in the genitive. It conveys an increase in the emphasis on the obligation of placing trust in Him, exalted is His rank, even though it does not follow what precedes it in i'rab (grammatical analysis). This is because what is in the accusative or nominative by way of praise, though it departs from following what precedes it in form, since it does not follow it in i'rab, and for this reason it is called "cut off" (qat'), is in reality still a follower of it. Do you not see how they were bound to omit the verb and the subject, to depict each of them in the form of a complement of what precedes it, and to alert to the strength of the connection between them? They cut it off only for the sake of the captivating effect that calls for awakening the listener and stirring him to earnest attention in listening.

It is permitted that the relative clause be in the accusative case by way of specification (ikhtisas), and that it be in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, being an attribute of it, or a subject whose predicate is "the Most Merciful." It is also permitted that "the Most Merciful" be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun concealed in "established" (istawa). And it is permitted, according to the view of al-Akhfash, that "the Most Merciful" be the subject, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so ask about Him one well-informed﴾ be its predicate, according to his interpretation of the verse of the poet:

"And a speaker said, 'Khawlan, marry their maiden,'"

but this is remote.

The apparent view is that this is a sentence disconnected in i'rab from what precedes it, the fa' is fasihah (an eloquent conjunction introducing an implied condition), and the prepositional phrase is attached to "ask" (isal). Asking, just as it is transitive with 'an (about) because it implies the sense of inquiry (tafti sh), is also transitive with bi (about/concerning) because it implies the sense of caring (i'tina'). On this is the saying of 'Alqamah ibn 'Abdah:

"If you ask me about women, indeed I am
well-informed about the ailments of women, a physician."

There is no need to make it in the sense of 'an, as al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj did. The pronoun refers to what was mentioned in summary, namely the creation and the establishment. The meaning is: if you wish to verify what was mentioned or to have detailed what was mentioned, then ask, caring about it, of one well-informed, of great rank, encompassing the outward and inward aspects of affairs, and He is Allah, mighty and majestic, who will inform you of the clear truth of the matter.

What is actually asked about is the details of what was mentioned, not the thing itself, since after its explanation there is no further need for asking. Nor is there in its transitivity by bi, which is founded on implying the sense of caring, which requires that the thing asked about be a serious matter whose concern is important and not already possessed by the questioner, any benefit; for the very creation and establishment, after being mentioned, is not such, as is not hidden.

As for the possibility that the estimated meaning is: if you doubt it, then ask about it one well-informed, with the address being to him (ﷺ) while the intended one is other than him, peace be upon him, this is far from soundness. It was also said: bi (about) is a complement of "well-informed" (khabiran), placed first for the sake of the rhyme-endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayy).

It is also permitted that the speech be of the type of tajrid (abstraction), as in: "I saw in him a lion," meaning: I saw by his sight a lion. So it is as if it were said here: "Ask by his asking one well-informed," and the meaning is: if you ask him, you will find him well-informed. The bi in this case is not a complement, for it is the bi of tajrid, which according to what al-Zamakhshari held is causal (sababiyyah). The well-informed one in this case is also Allah, exalted is He. This view was mentioned by al-Sajawandi and preferred by Sahib al-Kashf, who said: "It is more likely, so that it may serve as a completion (tatmim) to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who created﴾ and so on, for it is for establishing power, with knowledge merged into it." That the pronoun in "about Him" refers to what was mentioned of the creation and the establishment, and that "the well-informed one" (al-khabir) in the verse is Allah, exalted is He, is narrated from al-Kalbi. The interpretation of the well-informed one as Allah, exalted is He, is also narrated from Ibn Jurayj.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, the well-informed one is Jibril, peace be upon him. It was also said: he is the one who found this in the earlier revealed books sent down from Him, exalted is He. That is: ask, by what was mentioned of the creation and the establishment, one who has knowledge of it from the People of the Book, so that he may confirm you. It was also said: if the well-informed one is taken to be those mentioned, then the pronoun in "about Him" refers to "the Most Merciful." The meaning is: if they deny the application of "the Most Merciful" to Him, exalted is He, then ask about Him one who informs you from the People of the Book, so that they may know that what is synonymous with it has come in their books. But this does not fit what precedes it, for it involves the return of the pronoun to the word "the Most Merciful" rather than its meaning, which is contrary to the apparent sense, and because in that case the apparent thing would have been to place it after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What is the Most Merciful?﴾

It was also said: the well-informed one is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the pronoun in "about Him" refers to "the Most Merciful." The meaning is: ask by His attributes, and the address is to someone other than him (ﷺ) among those who do not know that. But this is nothing, as is not hidden. It was also said: the pronoun in "about Him" refers to "the Most Merciful," and the meaning is: ask by His mercy and its details of one knowledgeable who will inform you of them; or the meaning is: ask by His mercy while he is knowing of everything, on the basis that "well-informed" (khabiran) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun, not the object of "ask," as in the previous views.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "well-informed" be a circumstantial clause from "the Most Merciful" if it is made nominative by "established." He said: it is weak for it to be a circumstantial clause from the subject of "ask," because the well-informed one is not asked except by way of emphasis, like: ﴿and it is the truth, confirming﴾. The closest and most preferable view in the verse among the views mentioned is not hidden. It was read: "fa-sal" (so ask).

And when it is said to them, "Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman). The one saying it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or Allah, exalted and majestic is He, speaking through His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. The weight of this noble Name here is not hidden. In it, as al-Khafaji said, there is a meaning: "The servant is nearest to his Lord when he is prostrating." ﴿They said﴾ in mockery and insolence: "And what is the Most Merciful?" This is like Pharaoh's words, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" when Musa, peace be upon him, said to him, ﴿Indeed, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾, while Pharaoh knew Him, exalted and majestic is He, as Musa's words to him indicate: ﴿You certainly know that these have not sent down [such signs] except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence﴾. The question may be about the named entity, and it was asked with "ma" rather than "man" because, in their claim, it was unknown to them. It is like one asks of a visible figure, "What is it?" and once it is known to be a rational being, one asks, "Who is it?" It may also be that the question is about the meaning of the Name, and its being introduced with "ma" is then evident.

It was said: they asked about this because they did not use it of Allah, the Exalted, in the way they used al-Rahim, al-Rahum, and al-Rahim of Him, the Exalted. Or because they thought that by it was meant someone other than Allah, exalted and majestic is He, since among them it had become current to name Musaylima "Rahman al-Yamama" (the Most Merciful of Yamama), so they thought that this was what was meant, taking the definiteness as referring to a known individual. It was also said: because he was Hebrew and the original is "Rakhman" with a dotted kha, which was then Arabized, and they did not hear it [in its original form]. But the more apparent view to me is that this was out of feigned ignorance, and that the question is about the named entity. That is why they said: ﴿Shall we prostrate to that which you command us?﴾, that is, to the one to whom you command us to prostrate without our knowing Him. So "ma" is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted.

The original form of the sentence containing it is what we indicated: then it became "you command us to prostrate to Him," then "you command us His prostration," like "I commanded you the good," then "you command us it" with the omission of the annexed noun, then "you command us." Considering the omission to be gradual is the view of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash), while the view of Sibawayh is that all of that was omitted at once without gradation. It is also possible that "ma" is an indefinite qualified noun, and the returning pronoun is as you have heard. It is also permissible for it to be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), with the lam being causal (ta'lilliyya), and the object of prostration omitted or left unstated, meaning: "Shall we prostrate to Him for the sake of your commanding us?" or "Shall we prostrate for the sake of your commanding us?"

Ibn Mas'ud, al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "yet'muruna" (he commands us) with a ya' at the beginning, taking the pronoun as referring to the Prophet (ﷺ). This statement is the statement of some of them to others. ﴿And it increased them﴾, that is, the command to prostrate to the Most Merciful, and the attribution is figurative (majaz). The clause is coordinated with ("they said"), meaning: they said that and it increased them ﴿in aversion﴾ from faith. In al-Lubab it is mentioned that the subject of "zadahum" (increased them) is the prostration itself, because it is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, prostrated and they distanced themselves from them, mocking. On this view the clause is not coordinated with the response of "idha" (when) but with the whole conditional construction, as is said regarding ("they cannot delay") in His saying: ﴿When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it﴾. But the first view is more preferable and more apparent.

[Page 40]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 61:

﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations (burūj)﴾. The apparent meaning is the well-known twelve constellations (burūj, the zodiacal signs). al-Khatib related this in his *Kitab al-Nujum* from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Originally a burj means a lofty palace, and the word was applied to the constellations by way of metaphor, because they are for the stars like lofty dwellings for their inhabitants. Then the usage spread until it became its literal meaning for them. According to al-Zajjaj, a burj is every elevated thing, so there is no need for metaphor or transfer. Its derivation is from tabarruj, meaning manifestation. What the school of the Ahl al-Hadith (the people of hadith) requires is that they are in the lowest heaven. There is no rational objection to this, especially if we say that their thickness is so great that it contains the stars and what they entail, according to what the astronomers (Ahl al-Hay'a) mention. For them, these are divisions of the greatest sphere, which is called, as it is said, the Throne. I do not know of any report that the word "sky" (sama') is applied to it, although it is linguistically correct. The constellations were named after the images of fixed stars in the eighth sphere that lay opposite them at the time the division was considered. These images move with the slow motion of the other fixed stars. In these times, each image has nearly moved out of what it was initially opposite. Their starting point, according to them, is the point of the vernal equinox, a specific point on the equator of the day which does not move with the motion of the eighth sphere. It meets another point on the zodiac belt which moves with its motion. If the starting point of the burūj does not move with that motion, nothing else moves. Allah the Exalted made three of them vernal: Aries (al-Hamal), Taurus (al-Thawr) and Gemini (al-Jawza', also called al-Tawamayn). Three are summer: Cancer (al-Saratan), Leo (al-Asad) and Virgo (al-Sunbula, also called al-Adhra'). These six are northern. Three are autumnal: Libra (al-Mizan), Scorpio (al-Aqrab) and Sagittarius (al-Qaws, also called al-Rami). Three are wintry: Capricorn (al-Jadi, also called al-Dali and Sakib al-Ma'), and Aquarius (al-Dalw), and Pisces (al-Hut, also called al-Samakatayn). These six are southern. Because the sun is in each of the twelve, the time varies in heat and cold, and night and day vary in length and shortness. Through this, by the customary course in the world of generation and corruption, great effects appear, such as the ripening of fruits, the maturing of crops and similar things that are not hidden. Perhaps this is the reason for the blessing in their creation.

As for what the astrologers (Ahl al-Ahkam) claim of effects when one of them is rising at the time of a birth or the beginning of an action, or at the time the sun enters the point of Aries, which is the starting point of the solar year according to the well-known view, this is pure conjecture and guessing at the unseen. I will discuss this in detail later, if Allah the Exalted wills. They also have a long discussion about dividing them into masculine and feminine, nocturnal and diurnal, hot and cold, auspicious and inauspicious, and other categories. Perhaps we will mention some of it later, if Allah the Exalted wills. Whoever wants it in full should return to their books.

Then, the apparent meaning is that the burūj which were made are not subject to consideration. What is mentioned in the words of the astronomers is that they result from considering the assumption of six known circles cutting the world. So consideration has a role in them, even if it is not in that (i.e., the circles are only assumed), like the fangs of the ghouls, because the point of abstraction exists in them. If the matter is of this kind according to the people of the Shari'ah, namely that the sphere in which they are is considered divided into twelve sections, and each section is called a burj, then the apparent meaning is that the intended sense of Allah the Exalted's making them is the making of that by which this consideration is completed, and by which the matter of difference and variation between those burūj is realized. There is much good in this. It has been said that the verse hints that the consideration of the division was through revelation. It is well known that the first to consider this was Hermes (Hurmus), who, as it is said, was Idris, peace be upon him. So reflect.

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah that the burūj are palaces at the gates of the sky, in which there are guards. It was also said that they are palaces in Paradise. al-A'mash said: The companions of Abd Allah used to recite: "in the sky, palaces" (fi al-sama' qusuran). This has been objected to, on the grounds that the context rejects it, because the verse was brought to alert to what establishes the proof against the disbelievers who do not prostrate to the Most Merciful, and to clarify that He is the one deserving of prostration by showing the signs of His power and perfection, glorified be He. The apparent meaning is that this should be by mentioning matters that are perceptible and known to them, and those palaces are not like that.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid that they are the stars. This was also reported from Qatadah. From Abu Salih it is reported that they are restricted to the large ones. This was applied to them because of their greatness and visibility, especially those from the first of the three ranks of the first of the six magnitudes.

You know that the term burūj has not been known to be applied to stars. So it is better to take them in the first sense reported from Ibn Abbas, which is clearer than the sun. ﴿And placed within it﴾, that is, in the sky, and it was said: in the burūj, ﴿a lamp (sirajan)﴾, which is the sun, as in His saying: ﴿and made the sun a lamp (sirajan)﴾ (71:16). Abd Allah, Alqamah, al-A'mash and al-Akhawan read "surujan" in the plural with a damma on the ra'. al-A'mash also, al-Nakha'i, and Ibn Wathhab read the same, except that they made the ra' sukun. This, as it is said, is of the type of ﴿Indeed Abraham was a nation (ummah)﴾ (16:120), because the sun, due to its greatness and complete illumination, is as if it were many lamps. Or the plural is in consideration of the days and the risings. Both of these are combined in the words of the poet:

The gleaming of lightning or the rays of suns

According to this view, the two readings coincide. Some eminent scholars said: the plural is on its apparent meaning, and what is intended is the sun and the large stars. Some of them explained it as the large stars. The first view has been objected to, on the grounds that it entails singling out the moon for mention in His saying ﴿and a radiant moon (qamaran muniran)﴾ after its inclusion among the lamps, whereas the fitting thing would be to single out the sun for its perfect superiority over the others. It was answered that, after accepting its inclusion among the lamps, it was singled out for mention because their years are lunar, and for this reason they put the night before the day and count the night as belonging to the following day. So they give it more attention. Yet, according to what he mentioned, it entails omitting mention of the sun, which is more deserving of mention than others. The excuse that it is so famous that it is as if it were mentioned, and for this reason it was not joined with others in a single phrase, is of no use.

The moon is well known, and it is applied to it after the third night until the end of the month. It was said: it was named so because it outshines (yaqmuru) the light of the stars. In al-Sihah, it is because of its whiteness. In describing it, there is something that indicates care for it. According to the well-known distinction between daw' (light) and nur (radiance), describing it as "muniran" (radiant) rather than "mudi'an" (shining) indicates that what is observed in it is derived from something else, namely the sun. Indeed, more than one said that the light of all the stars is derived from it, even if the variation of its forms by nearness and distance from it does not appear, as in the light of the moon.

al-Hasan, al-A'mash, al-Nakha'i and Isma from Asim read "wa-qumran" with a damma on the qaf and sukun on the mim. Abu Hayyan judged that it is a dialect form of qamar, like rushd and rashad, and 'urb and 'arab. It was also said that it is the plural of qamra', which is a night illuminated by the moon. The speech then has an elided genitive, that is: "and possessor of qumr nights", meaning possessor of nights of moonlight. The intended "possessor" here is the moon itself, and His saying "muniran" would be an adjective of that elided genitive, because the elided word may be treated as present after its elision, as in the words of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

Barada flows, mixing with the limpid, flowing wine

He means the water of Barada, and so he said "yusaffiqu" with a ya' from below (masculine, agreeing with the water). If he had not observed the genitive, he would have said "tusaffiqu" with a ta'.

[Page 41]

[Page 42]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 62:

﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating﴾. That is, [they are] possessors of alternation (khilfah), each of them succeeding the other, by one taking the place of the other in what ought to be done during it. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was also said: [they succeed each other] in that one follows the other and comes after it. Khilfah is a noun denoting a state, from khalafa (to succeed), like rukbah and jilsah from rakiba and jalasa. Its accusative case is either as a second object of ja'ala (made), or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) if ja'ala means khalaqa (created). Some have construed it to mean "differing" (ikhtilafan). The intended meaning is difference in increase and decrease, as has been said, or in blackness and whiteness, as related from Mujahid, or in what encompasses that and other things, as is possible. In al-Bahr it is said: "So-and-so has khilfah and ikhtilaf" when he frequently goes back and forth to his place of relieving himself. From this meaning is the saying of Zuhayr:

The gazelles and the wild cows walk about in alternation there, and their young ones rise up from every resting place.

And the saying of another, describing a woman who moves from one dwelling to another, in winter and in summer, habitually:

And for her, at al-Matirun, when the ants have eaten what they had gathered, is alternation, until, when she rises up, she settles from Jalaq at the market-place,

In houses in the middle of a village, around which olive trees have sprouted.
End of quote.

It is also permitted that the meaning be: each of them goes and comes back much, and the consideration of the implied annexed noun remains as it is, and likewise in what precedes it.

In al-Qamus: "al-khilf and al-khilfah with a kasra is that which alternates," and according to this there is no need to posit an implied annexed noun; the meaning is: He made them two alternating, and the singular form is because it is originally a verbal noun.

﴿for whoever wishes to take heed﴾. That is, so that they may be two times for the one who wishes to remember: whoever has missed his portion of worship in one of them may make it up in the other. This was related from a group of the early predecessors (salaf). al-Tayalisi and Ibn Abi Hatim related that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) prolonged the Duha prayer, and it was said to him: "You have done something you were not accustomed to doing?" He said: "A portion of my wird remained for me, so I wished to complete it" or he said: "to make it up," and he recited this verse. It seems that tadhakkur (remembrance) is a metaphor for making up what has been missed, which is something upon which the making up depends. In the sentence there is an implied element, as has been pointed out, and it may be an implied element of meaning rather than of grammatical construction.

﴿or who wishes to be grateful﴾: to thank Allah Most High by performing a kind of worship that was not his regular wird. In Majma' al-Bayan: the meaning is: for whoever wishes voluntary prayer after performing the obligatory prayer. It may also be that the meaning is: for whoever wishes to remember and reflect upon the wondrous workmanship of Allah Most High, so that he knows that for what has been mentioned there must be a wise Creator, necessarily existent in His essence, possessing mercy towards the servants; or he wishes to thank Allah, glorified is He, for the blessings that are in them both. This is a good view, almost not to be turned away from were it not transmitted. Apparently the lam according to this is connected to ja'ala. Since the manifest benefit of that is for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to give thanks, it was limited to this. It is also permitted that the lam be causal, and "or" be for enumeration, meaning inclusion of these two meanings, or for choice, meaning independence of each; and there is no prohibition against combining them.

The benefit of this style is to convey independence, for had the conjunction "wa" (and) been mentioned instead, it would have suggested accompaniment. Perhaps in expressing it first with an(na) and the verb rather than the explicit verbal noun, as in the second part, despite its being more concise, is an indication of concern for the matter of remembrance, so reflect.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "an yatadhakkara," which is the origin of yadhdhakkara, the ta' being changed to dhal and assimilated. al-Nakha'i, Ibn Wththab, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Talhah, and Hamzah read "an yadhkura," the imperfect of the triliteral dhakara with the meaning of tadhakkara.

﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾: a resumed statement to explain the attributes and the worldly and otherworldly conditions of the sincere servants of Allah Most High, after explaining the state of those who turn away from His worship and from prostrating to Him, glorified is He, the Mighty and Majestic. Their being attributed to al-Rahman rather than to any other of His names or pronouns, exalted is He, is either to single them out for His mercy or to give them preference over others, since they are those who are shown mercy and blessed, as is understood from the implication of attribution to a derived noun. In this there is also an allusion to those who said: "And what is al-Rahman?"

Most scholars hold that 'ibad here is the plural of 'abd (servant). Ibn Bahr said: it is the plural of 'abid (worshipper), like sahib and sihab, rakil and rijal. This is supported by the reading of al-Yamani, "wa-'Ubbad," with a damma on the 'ayn and a shadda on the ba', for it is the plural of 'abid by consensus. According to this view it derives from 'ibadah, which is to do what the Lord is pleased with; and according to the first view it derives from 'ubudiyyah, which is to be pleased with what the Lord does. al-Raghib said: 'ubudiyyah is the manifestation of humility, and 'ibadah is more emphatic than it, since it is the utmost humility. Some distinguished between them: 'ibadah is doing what is commanded and abstaining from what is forbidden, seeking reward and deliverance from punishment through that; while 'ubudiyyah is doing what is commanded and abstaining from what is forbidden, not for those reasons but purely out of Allah Most High's favour towards him.

It was said: above that is 'ubudah, which is doing and abstaining from the aforementioned purely for His command and prohibition, glorified is He, and for His essential entitlement, glorified is He, to be magnified and obeyed. To this refers the saying of the Most High: ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾. al-Hasan read "wa-'Ubud," with a damma on the 'ayn and the ba', and it is, as al-Akhfash said, the plural of 'abd, like saqf and suqf, and he recited:

Trace the servant to his fathers, black-skinned, from a people of 'ubud.

It is, in every case, the subject (mubtada'), and concerning its predicate there are two views. The first is that it is the sentence in the final part of the noble surah introduced by the demonstrative, and the second, which is the closer, is His saying, exalted is He:

[p. 44]

Allah says: ﴿Those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾. Al-hawn is a verbal noun meaning gentleness and kindness. It is in the accusative either because it is an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "walking humbly," or because it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿yamshuna﴾ (they walk). The meaning is that they walk gently, with deliberation, tranquility, dignity and good bearing. They do not stamp their feet or flap their sandals out of arrogance and insolence. Something similar is related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Fudayl ibn Iyad and others.

From Imam Abu ʿAbd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, it is reported that al-hawn is a man's walk in his natural disposition, with which he was created, without affectation or strutting.

Al-Amidi, in his commentary on the Diwan of al-Aʿsha, reports with his chain of transmission from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he saw a youth strutting in his walk. He said to him: "Strutting is a gait that is disliked, except in the way of Allah, the Exalted. Allah has praised some people by saying, ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾. So moderate your gait."

It has also been said that walking gently is the opposite of walking quickly, and that the latter is blameworthy. Abu Nuʿaym reports in al-Hilya from Abu Hurayrah, and Ibn al-Najjar reports from Ibn Abbas, both saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hastiness in walking takes away the radiance of the believer."

Ibn Abi Hatim reports from Maymun ibn Mihran that ﴿hawnan﴾ means "forbearing" in Syriac, so that it would be a circumstantial qualifier only. The apparent meaning, however, is that it is Arabic, meaning gentleness and kindness. Al-Raghib explained it as a person humbling himself in himself in matters that do not bring him disgrace, and this is the praiseworthy kind. From the same root is the hadith: "The believer is gentle and easygoing (hayyin layyin)."

The apparent meaning is that walking retains its literal sense, and that the purpose is to praise them for tranquility and dignity in walking, without generalization. Yet it follows from their walking in this way that they are, by custom, gentle and easygoing in all their affairs, as has been said.

Ibn ʿAtiyya chose that the purpose is to praise them for avoiding harshness and coarseness in all their affairs and conduct. The meaning is that they live among people gentle in all their matters. The mention of walking is because walking is movement across the earth, which requires dealing and mixing with people, and gentleness is required in this to the utmost degree.

Then he said: As for the view that the purpose is to praise them for walking gently alone, this is false, for many a person walks gently and slowly while being a sly wolf. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to sway in his walk, as if he were walking downhill, and he, peace be upon him, is the foremost of those meant by this verse. There is a discussion here from two angles, so do not overlook it. Al-Yamani and al-Sulami read ﴿yumashshawna﴾ in the passive voice, with doubled shin.

﴿And when the ignorant address them﴾, that is, the foolish and those lacking in good manners, as in the saying:

"Surely let no one act ignorantly towards us, lest we act with more ignorance than the ignorant."

﴿they say: Peace﴾. This statement describes their dealings with others after describing their inner state, or it describes the goodness of their dealings and confirms their gentleness when what calls for the opposite arises, if a person is left to his nature. That is, when they are addressed with evil, they say, as a way of disengaging from them and leaving them alone: there is no good between us and you, nor evil.

So "salaman" is a verbal noun standing in place of the act of greeting, and it is an emphatic verbal noun for its implied verb. The estimate is: "we disengage with a disengagement from you." The sentence is the object of the saying. Sibawayh in al-Kitab took this view. He denied that the common greeting of peace is meant, on the grounds that the verse is Meccan while the greeting is mentioned in al-Nisa', which is Medinan, and the Muslims were not commanded in Mecca to greet the polytheists.

Al-Asamm said: It is a farewell greeting, not a greeting of salutation, like Abraham's saying to his father, ﴿Peace be upon you﴾. It is evident that this returns to disengagement, which is common in Arabic speech. Mujahid said: The meaning is that they say a right word.

This was objected to on the grounds that this explanation is not correct, because what is meant here is that they say this particular phrase, not that they say aword that is sound and right, as shown by His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant﴾. The author of al-Kashf replied that this verse does not contradict this explanation, for their saying "Peace be upon you" is also a sound word. Moreover, the apparent meaning is that the specific wording is not intended, but rather that wording or anything that conveys its sense, any saying that indicates disengagement while free from sin and vain talk. This is good and unobjectionable.

In some histories, as mentioned in al-Bahr, Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi had turned away from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face. He saw ʿAli in a dream as he advanced to cross a bridge, and ʿAli said to him: "You claim this matter through a woman, while we have more right to it than you." This was reported to al-Maʾmun, who then said: "I have never seen him eloquent in reply, as is related of him." Al-Maʾmun asked him: "What did he answer you with?" He said: "He kept saying to me: 'Salaman, salaman.'" Al-Maʾmun said: "O uncle, he answered you with the most eloquent reply," and he alerted him to this verse. Ibrahim was shamed and abashed, and may Allah requite him with what he deserves.

It is evident that the purpose is to praise them for overlooking the foolish and for not answering them in speech. The verse has no reference to their dealings with the disbelievers, so it does not conflict with the verse of fighting, such that abrogation (naskh) could be claimed by it, since this verse is Meccan and that one is Medinan. It is reported from Abu al-ʿAliyah, and chosen by Ibn ʿAtiyya, that it was abrogated with regard to the disbelievers by the verse of fighting.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾ is an explanation of their condition in their dealings with their Lord. Al-Hasan used to say: when he recited what came before this, he would say, "This describes their days," and when he recited this verse, he would say, "This describes their nights." Al-Baytutah (spending the night) means that the night overtakes you, whether you sleep or do not sleep.

The phrase ﴿before their Lord﴾ is connected to what follows it. It was placed first for the sake of the rhyme (fasilah, the closing pattern of the verse) and for specification (takhsis). Al-Qiyam is the plural of qa'im (standing), or a verbal noun (masdar) treated as such. The meaning is: they spend the night prostrating and standing before their Lord, glorified is He, that is, they keep the night awake, wholly or partly, in prayer. It has also been said: whoever recites any part of the Qur'an at night in prayer has spent the night prostrating and standing. It has also been said: what is intended is performing the two rak'ahs after the maghrib prayer and the two rak'ahs after the 'isha' prayer. It has further been said: whoever performs an even number of rak'ahs and then the witr after praying 'isha' has entered into the general scope of the verse.

In sum, the verse exhorts the performance of night prayer. Prostration is placed before standing, and the order is not reversed, even though prostration comes later in the act of prayer, for the sake of the rhyme. Also, it is because prostration is the state in which the servant is nearest to his Lord, glorified is He, and because of the refusal of the arrogant to do so, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said﴾ [to them, prostrate to the Most Merciful, they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"] (the verse).

Abu al-Barahsam read "sujudan" (prostrations) on the pattern of "qu'udan" (sittings), and this is more fitting with "qiyaman" (standing).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 65:

﴿And those who say﴾ (this is said) at the conclusion of their prayers, or at large throughout their times: ﴿"Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever-clinging"﴾, i.e., lasting (lāzim), as al-Tasturi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas. He recited, may Allah be pleased with him, in this regard the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Hatim:

"And the Day of al-Nisar and the Day of al-Jifar were a punishment and were ever-clinging (gharaman)."

Similar to it is the verse of al-A'sha:

"If He punishes, it will be gharaman; and if He gives abundantly, He does not care."

This clinging is either for the disbelievers, or what is meant by it is persistence (imtidad), as in the clinging of the creditor (gharim). In another narration from him, its explanation is "dreadful and severe."

Some have explained it as "destructive" (muhlik). In the reporting of their saying this there is further praise of them, by clarifying that they, along with their good dealings with creatures and their striving in the worship of the Real, fear the punishment and beseech their Lord, Mighty and Majestic, to avert it from them, not being impressed by their deeds, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾. In this is confirmation of their faith in resurrection and recompense. The apparent view is that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed its punishment...﴾ and so on, is part of the speech of those who supplicate, and it is a justification for their aforementioned petition by stating the dreadfulness of its punishment. Likewise His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 66:

﴿Indeed, it is evil as a dwelling-place and a station.﴾ This is a justification for that, based on its bad condition in itself. Leaving out the conjunction (ʿaṭf) indicates that each of the two clauses independently serves as the cause (ʿillah). It has also been said that this is a justification for what was justified by the first clause. Ibn Hisham, in al-Tadhkira, weakened this view, saying that there is no connection between a thing being a debt (gharam) and it being evil as a dwelling-place.

It was answered that the connection is by consideration of necessity (luzum) and the context (maqam), for the context naturally requires necessity. It has also been said that both clauses are from the speech of God Most High from the beginning, and that the statement was justified by both of them in the manner mentioned earlier, or that this was justified by the first, and the first was justified by the second. It has also been permitted that one of them is a quoted statement and the other is an independent beginning, but all of this is as you see.

﴿Sāʾat﴾ is in the sense of (biʾsat) (how evil), and the particular being censured (al-makhsūs bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, its estimated form being "hiya" (it). This is the link (rābiṭ) of this clause to the subject of which it is the predicate, if it is not the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa). ﴿Mustaqarran﴾ is a specification (tamyīz), and in it there is an ambiguous pronoun referring to ﴿mustaqarran﴾ and explained by it. It was made feminine either by interpreting the dwelling-place as Jahannam, or to agree with the particular being censured. Do you not see how Dhu al-Rummah made the boat feminine by interpreting it as a ship, when the particular being censured was feminine in his saying:

*Or a noble she-camel, long-necked, broad-chested, with strong sides, / the supports of the boat-hulls, how excellent is the boat of the land.*

It has been said that ﴿sāʾat﴾ may also be in the sense of (aḥzanat) (she grieved), in which case it is a transitive, inflected verb, its subject being the pronoun of (Jahannam) and its object omitted, meaning: it grieved its people and companions. And ﴿mustaqarran﴾ is a specification or a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It is a verbal noun in the sense of the subject, or a noun of place. But this is not the preferred view.

The apparent view is that ﴿mustaqarran﴾ and ﴿maqāman﴾ are like his saying:

*And he found her saying false and lying.*

What makes this acceptable is that the context (maqām) calls for elaboration, or that it serves as a closing rhyme (fāṣila). It has also been said that the dwelling-place (mustaqarr) is for the disobedient and the station (muqām) is for the disbelievers, and that "inna" in both places is for emphasis regarding the importance of the predicate.

A group recited ﴿wa-maqāman﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm, meaning a place of standing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 67:

﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant﴾, meaning: they do not exceed the limit of generosity. ﴿Nor are they niggardly﴾, meaning: nor do they restrict (spending) with the restriction of the miser. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jabali said: extravagance (israf) is spending on acts of disobedience, and niggardliness (qatr) is withholding from obedience. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba said: extravagance is that you spend the wealth of another.

Al-Hasan, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read *yaqturu* (يَقْتُرُوا) with a fatha on the *ya'* and a damma on the *ta'*. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the *ya'* and a kasra on the *ta'*. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the *ya'* and a kasra on the *ta'*. Al-'Ala' ibn Sabbaba and al-Yazidi read it with a damma on the *ya'*, a fatha on the *qaf* and a kasra on the *ta'*, with the *ta'* shaddah. All of these are dialectal forms meaning "to restrict" (in spending). Abu Hatim denied the quadriliteral form *aqtara* here, saying: "*aqtara* is only used when one becomes poor, and from it comes: ﴿and for the straitened is his measure﴾." He did not know what al-Asma'i and others related of *aqtara* meaning "to restrict."

﴿And was﴾ their spending ﴿between those (two)﴾ mentioned, namely extravagance and niggardliness, ﴿a qiwam﴾, meaning a middle course and a balance. It was named thus because the two extremes are upright and balanced, as though each one counterbalances the other, just as *sawa'* (equal) is named for the equality of the two. Hassan read *qiwaman* (قِوامًا) with a kasra on the *qaf*. It is said that the two are dialects with the same meaning. It is also said that with the kasra it means that by which a thing is sustained. The intended meaning here is what sustains the need, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it.

The word *qiwaman* is a second predicate of *kana* ("was"), confirming the first, which is *bayna dhalika* ("between that"). Alternatively, *bayna dhalika* is the predicate itself. *Bayna dhalika* may be a complement of *kana* according to the view that the incomplete *kana* governs an adverbial of place or time. Or it may be a circumstantial (*hal*) of *qiwaman*, because if it were placed after it, it would be a qualifier. It is also permitted that it be an adverbial complement that is loosely attached to *qiwaman*, or that *bayna dhalika* is the predicate and *qiwaman* is an emphatic circumstantial. Al-Farra' permitted that *bayna dhalika* be the subject of *kana*, and that it be indeclinable because it is attached to an indeclinable word, as in the saying of God: ﴿and from the disgrace of that day﴾ according to the reading of one who opens the *mim*. From this is the saying of the poet:

It did not prevent them from drinking from it, except that a dove sang
in the branches of a tree with *awqal* (fruit clusters).

Al-Zamakhshari criticised this, saying: "Grammatically there is no harm in it, but the meaning is not strong, because what lies between extravagance and restriction is necessarily a middle course, so there is no benefit in the predicate, which is the main point of the sentence." The summary is that the sentence on this view belongs to the type "*kana al-dhahib jariyatuhu sahibaha*" (the goer was his servant-girl's companion), and it is not informative. It is clear that this objection does not apply to the reading *qiwaman* with a kasra according to the second view of it, but it stands on other views.

As for what is said, that it is of the type "*shi'ri shi'ri*" (my poetry, my poetry), and that the meaning is "it was a valued and accepted middle course, not an unaccepted one," this is also not acceptable, because even if such a usage exists, it occurs only where the word is identical, and this case is not like that. Likewise, what is said, that *bayna dhalika* is more general than *qiwam* in the sense of justice, in which the relation of each of the two extremes to it is equal, is also not sound. What lies between restriction and extravagance does not necessarily amount to a middle in that sense, since it may be a little below extravagance and a little above restriction. This is also an unnatural interpretation, because what lies between them includes the adjacent part of the middle and whatever else, as the middle does, without distinction. Such a usage is not employed in ordinary speech, because it is obscure. It is also said: even granting that it is permissible to report the more general by the more specific, it is unlikely that their praise is for keeping to the adjacent part of the middle, with the hardship that this involves, which has been denied of Islam.

In reply: there is no doubt that it is permissible to report the more general by the more specific, as in: "The one who came to me is Zayd." The speaker did not intend strict adjacency but approximate adjacency, as indicated by his saying "a little," and there is no hardship in such a thing. So reflect on this.

Perhaps the reason for describing their spending with what is mentioned after the words of God, ﴿when they spend, are neither extravagant nor niggardly﴾, which implies that their spending is of this kind, is to make explicit that their conduct is among the best of matters. It is well known that "the best of matters is their middle course." The apparent meaning is that spending here includes both their spending on themselves and their spending on others, and the middle course is good in all of that.

Ahmad and al-Tabarani related from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Part of a man's understanding is his gentleness in his livelihood."

Ibn Majah related in his Sunan from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, it is extravagance that you eat everything you desire."

It is related that 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may mercy be upon him, when he married his daughter Fatima to him: "What is your expenditure?" 'Umar said to him: "A good deed between two bad ones," and then he recited the verse.

Poets have praised moderation in affairs and economy in livelihood, both in ancient and modern times. Among that is the saying of one:

Do not go to excess in any matter, but be moderate;
both extremes of the way of right conduct are blameworthy.

And the saying of Hatim:

When you have given your belly its desire,
and your private part has attained the utmost of blame, both together,

And the saying of another:

When a man gives his soul everything it desires,
and does not restrain it, it reaches out to every falsehood,

and drives it to sin and shame by what it calls it to,
out of the sweetness of a fleeting pleasure.

And so on to other than that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 25, verse 68:

﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah﴾: i.e., they do not associate anything with Him other than Him, glorified is He. ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾: i.e., which Allah the Exalted has forbidden, meaning: He has forbidden its killing. This is because prohibition relates to actions, not to essences, so the genitive noun (*al-mudaf*, "killing") was omitted and the noun it governed (*al-mudaf ilayhi*, "the soul") was put in its place, for emphasis on the prohibition. ﴿Except by right﴾: this is related to "they do not kill," and the exception is a *mustathna mufarragh* (an exception in which the excluded element is left unstated, so the sentence is governed by the verb's need for a complement) taken from the most general category of causes. That is: they do not kill it for any cause except a cause of right, which removes its sanctity and inviolability, such as fornication after being married (*al-zina ba'da al-ihsan*) and apostasy after faith (*al-kufr ba'da al-iman*). It is also permitted that *bil-haqq* be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: they do not kill it in any manner of killing except a killing that is connected with right. And it is permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: they do not kill it in any state except the state of being connected with right.

It has been said: it is permitted that it be related to the omitted killing, and the exception is likewise taken from the most general category of causes, meaning: they do not kill the soul which Allah the Exalted has forbidden to be killed for any cause except a cause of right. The exception would then be a *mustathna mufarragh* in an affirmative sentence, to keep the meaning sound by intending generality, or because *harrama* (forbade) carries the sense of negation. The difficulty in this is not hidden. ﴿And do not commit fornication﴾: i.e., do not have intercourse with a private part forbidden to them. The purpose of negating these grave abominations is an allusion to what their enemies among the Quraysh and others used to do. Otherwise there would be no need for it after describing them with the previous attributes of good dealing and of spending the night in prayer, and their great fear of Allah the Exalted, since the mention of these qualities calls for the negation of what was mentioned about them. From this it is known the answer to what has been said: the apparent order is the reverse of this arrangement, and the removal of blemishes (*al-takhliyah*) should precede the adornment with virtues (*al-tahliyah*). So it is as if it were said: those whom Allah the Exalted has purified and cleared, glorified is He, from what you are upon of associating partners with Him, killing a soul that is forbidden, such as burying daughters alive, and fornication.

It has been said: the explicit negation of associating partners, despite the evident faith of these people, is for this reason, or to show the completeness of care and sincerity, and to magnify the matter of killing and fornication by placing them in the same string. It is authentically related through the narration of al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'Which sin is greatest?' He said: 'That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you kill your child, fearing that it will eat with you.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour.'" Then Allah the Exalted revealed, confirming that: ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah﴾, to the end of the verse.

Page 48

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i related, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Some people from among the polytheists had killed much and had committed fornication much. Then they came to Muhammad ﷺ and said: 'What you say and call to is good, if only you would inform us that there is an expiation (*kaffarah*) for what we have done.' Then there was revealed: ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah﴾, to the end of the verse, and there was revealed: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, to the end of the verse."

Imam al-Razi has mentioned that the mention of this after what preceded is because one who is described by those attributes may commit these matters while considering them a form of religious devotion. So Allah, glorified is He, made clear that the one under obligation does not become one of the servants of the Most Merciful by those qualities alone, until his avoidance of these grave sins is added to them. And he said: "As you see, it is so." It is also permitted to say, concerning the reason for placing the adornment before the removal of blemishes: the attributes mentioned in the adornment are more fitting to servanthood, which has been made the title of the subject, because they clearly indicate abandoning self-regard, greater submission, fear, and moderation in conduct with what the Master has permitted one to use. This does not preclude the intent of allusion to what was mentioned in the removal of blemishes. This intent is supported by the continuation with His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾, i.e., whoever does what has been mentioned will meet, in the Hereafter, a punishment whose extent cannot be measured. Interpreting *athām* as punishment is related from Qatadah and Ibn Zayd, and Abu Hayyan transmitted it from the lexicographers, and he recited the verse of the poet:

"May Allah recompense Ibn 'Urwah, since he became disobedient, and disobedience has its recompense."

Ibn al-Anbari transmitted, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he interpreted it for Nafi' ibn al-Azraq as "recompense," and he recited the verse of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

"We made the spearheads drink from his ... and Himyar met from us *athaman*."

The difference is slight.

Abu Muslim said: *al-athām* is *al-ithm* (sin), and the statement is understood with an omitted genitive, meaning: the recompense of a sin; or it is a metaphor, mentioning the cause and intending the effect. Al-Hasan said: it is one of the names of Jahannam. It has been said: it is the name of a well within it. It has been said: it is the name of a mountain.

A group related, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar and Mujahid, that it is a valley in Jahannam, and Mujahid said: in it is pus and blood.

Ibn al-Mubarak related in *al-Zuhd*, from Shafi' al-Asbahi, that in it are snakes and scorpions, in the vertebrae of one of which is the amount of seventy jars of poison, and the scorpion among them is like a saddled mule. And from 'Ikrimah: it is the name of valleys in Jahannam in which are the fornicators.

It was read as *yulaqqa* with a damma on the *ya'* and a fatha on the *lam* and *qaf*, doubled. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Raja' read *yulqa* with an *alif*, as if he intended to omit the damma assumed on the *alif*, so the *alif* was retained. Abu Mas'ud also read *ayyaman*, the plural of *yawm* (day), meaning hardships. The use of *ayyam* in this sense is common, and from it comes "a day full of *ayyam*" (a day of hardships), and the *ayyam* of the Arabs are their battles and fightings.

**Page 49**

﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for «yalqa» (he meets), either a *badal kull min kull* (substitution of the whole from the whole) or a *badal ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion). The substitution from a jussive verb after a conditional particle occurs in the verse of the poet:

*"Whenever you come to us, you will find us in our abodes, you will find coarse firewood and a blazing fire."*

﴿And he will abide therein﴾, that is, in that doubled punishment, ﴿in humiliation﴾, abased and despised. Thus he will suffer both physical and spiritual punishment together. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Ibn Kathir read (yuda'af) with a *ya'* and in the passive voice (*mabni lil-maf'ul*), with the *alif* dropped and with doubling (*tadh'if*).

Shayba, Talha ibn Sulayman and Abu Ja'far also read (nudaʿʿif) with a *nun* that is vowelled with a *damma*, the *'ayn* kasra and doubled, and «al-'adhab» (the punishment) in the accusative. Talha ibn Musarrif read «yudaʿif» in the active voice with «al-'adhab» in the accusative. Talha ibn Sulayman read «wa-takhludu» with the *ta'* of address, as an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person) that indicates the intensity of anger, in the nominative. Abu Haywa read «wa-tukhalladh» in the passive voice, with the *lam* doubled and in the jussive, and it is narrated from Abu 'Amr both in this form and with the *lam* unstressed. Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read «yudaʿifu» and «wa-yakhludu» with *raf'* (nominative) in both, and likewise Ibn ʿAmir. Al-Mufaddal, from ʿAsim, read «yudaʿafu» and «wa-yukhladu» in the passive voice, nominative, unstressed. Al-A'mash read it with a *damma* on the *ya'*, in the passive voice, doubled and nominative.

You have already learned the reason for the jussive. As for the nominative, its basis is *istiʾnaf* (resumption of a new sentence). It is also permissible to make the clause a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) of the subject of «yalqa», meaning: he will meet sin, its punishment doubled for him. The doubling of his punishment, together with the Exalted's words ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ and His words, glorified is He, ﴿And whoever brings an evil deed, he will not be recompensed except with its like﴾, is said to be due to the joining of disobedience to disbelief, and it indicates

God's words, "Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous work" (﴿إلا مَن تابَ وآمَنَ وعَمِلَ عَمَلا صالِحًا﴾): the exception of the believer indicates that disbelief is considered part of what is excepted from (al-mustathnā minhu).

It has been objected that the repetition of the negative particle *lā* (not) conveys the negation of each of those acts individually, meaning: "they do not commit any of them." Thus "whoever does that" (﴿ومَن يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ﴾) would mean "whoever does any of that," so that the object of affirmation and negation is the same, and there is no indication of combination (*al-infiḍām*). The one who is excepted is someone who combined what was mentioned: faith, repentance, and righteous work. Hence the excepted-from clause would not include all of them. The answer may be that the doubling of punishment is relative to a punishment that is less than the things mentioned.

It was rejoined that the given answer is not far-fetched, even if what is less than them is not mentioned. However, the objection is not valid, because the speech is an allusion (*taʿrīḍ*) to the disbelievers. Whoever among them commits any of those acts has added his disobedience to his disbelief. If this is not taken into account, as he [the commentator] has chosen, it would follow that whoever commits a major sin would be eternal in the Fire, and its corruption is evident to us. What was mentioned about the unity of the object of affirmation and negation is not necessary.

Furthermore, the context contains an indication that the excepted-from clause is one who combines their opposites, as you have learned. That is why faith and righteous work are combined, even though work is conditioned by faith. Its mention serves to indicate its absence in the excepted-from clause. For this reason he placed repentance before them. It is possible that repentance was placed first because it is an emptying (*takhliyah*, clearing away of vices). Some have said: the intended meaning of the mentioned doubling is not the combining of two equal measures of punishment, each in proportion to what the disobedience requires. Rather, what is intended is its necessary consequence, which is severity. It is as if it were said: "Whoever does that will be punished with a severe punishment," and that severe punishment is the recompense for each of those acts and equal to it. The indication of the figurative sense is His words: ﴿ومَن جاءَ بِالسَّيِّئَةِ فَلا يُجْزى إلا مِثْلَها﴾ ("Whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like") and similar verses. By "abiding" (*khulūd*) is meant a long stay, which encompasses eternal abiding and other than it. This applies to one who associates partners with God, considering his first instance, and to one who commits one of the last two major sins, considering his last instance. This is as you see it. Similar is what has been said: that the doubling is for preserving what the disobedience requires, for a severe matter, when it lasts, becomes light.

This being said, the apparent view is that the exception is *muttaṣil* (connected), as is the default for it. Abū Ḥayyān said: "In my view, it is preferable that it be *munqaṭiʿ* (disconnected), that is: 'But whoever repents...' etc., because the excepted-from clause, on the assumption of connection, is judged as one for whom the punishment is doubled. So the sense becomes: 'Except whoever repents, believes, and does righteous work, so the punishment will not be doubled for him.' The absence of doubling does not necessitate the remaining of an undoubled punishment." In this there is the following: God's later words ﴿فَأُوْلئِكَ﴾ ("Those") and so on serve as a safeguard (*iḥtirās*) to repel the assumption that the basic punishment remains, by stating that they will not encounter it at all, in the most complete manner. It has also been said, in favor of disconnection, that connection—apart from considering its implication of the continuation of the basic punishment, and even its implication of eternal abiding without humiliation—implies that the doubling of righteous work is a condition for the negation of abiding. This is not so.

Moreover, what necessity compels one to commit what carries an implication, and then cling to the hem of a safeguard? Furthermore, the apparent view is that *man* ("whoever") should be the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and the sentence introduced by *fa* (then) its predicate. It is connected with *fa* because it occurs as a predicate of the relative (*al-mawṣūl*), as in your saying: "The one who comes to me, then for him is a dirham." I incline to what Abū Ḥayyān inclined to, for the totality of what has been mentioned. The mention of the qualified noun in His words, glorified is He: ﴿وعَمِلَ عَمَلا صالِحًا﴾ ("and does righteous work"), along with the usage of *al-ṣāliḥ* and *al-ṣāliḥāt* functioning as a proper name, is for giving it importance and explicitly stating its difference from the previous deeds.

Page 50

﴿فَأُولَئِكَ﴾ ("Those") refers to the relative pronoun. The plural is used in view of its meaning, just as the singular is used in the three verbs in view of its wording. That is: "Those who are characterized by repentance, faith, and righteous work."

﴿يُبَدِّلُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("God will replace") in this world ﴿سَيِّئاتِهِمْ حَسَناتٍ﴾ ("their evil deeds with good deeds"), by erasing the earlier sins through repentance and establishing in their place the later acts of obedience. This is what the words of many of the early scholars (*salaf*) indicate. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "evil deeds" and "good deeds" is the dispositions (*malakāt*) of them themselves.
