That is, God, Mighty and Majestic, replaces the disposition of evil deeds and their motives in the soul with the disposition of good deeds, by removing the former and bringing in the latter. It has also been said: this replacement occurs in the Hereafter, and by "evil deeds" and "good deeds" is meant punishment and reward, figuratively, by the relation of cause to effect. The meaning is that He, Majestic and Exalted, pardons their punishment and bestows upon them, in its place, reward out of His bounty. This is the view of al-Qaffāl and al-Qāḍī.

It is narrated from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, ʿAmr ibn Maymūn, and Makḥūl that this means the evil deeds themselves will be erased on the Day of Resurrection from their record of deeds, and good deeds will be written in their place. They cited the hadith narrated by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Abū Dharr, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'Present to him his minor sins, and set aside from him his major ones.' It will be said: 'You did on such and such a day such and such, and such and such.' He will acknowledge it and not deny it, while being apprehensive of the major sins. It will be said: 'Give him in place of every evil deed he did a good deed.' He will say: 'I have sins that I do not see here.'" He [Abū Dharr] said: "I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) laugh until his molars showed."

Similar to this is what Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "There will come people on the Day of Resurrection who wish that they had multiplied their evil deeds." It was said: "Who are they?" He (ﷺ) said: "Those whose evil deeds God, Exalted, replaces with good deeds." This replacement is called the generosity of pardon. It is perhaps for this reason that Abū Nuwās said:

Your palms bite with regret for what you abandoned out of fear of sin, the joy.

Perhaps the meaning is that his evil deeds are forgiven, and he is given in place of each evil deed what is suitable to be the reward of a good deed, as a bounty and generosity from Him, Mighty and Majestic, not that good deeds are written for him that he did not do and is rewarded for them.

In the words of Abū al-ʿĀliyah there is something clearly denying the wish to multiply evil deeds. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from him that it was said to him: "Some people claim that they wish to multiply sins." He said: "Why is that?" It was said: "They interpret this verse: ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ يُبَدِّلُ اللَّهُ سَيِّئاتِهِمْ حَسَناتٍ﴾." Abū al-ʿĀliyah, whenever he was informed of something he did not know, would say: "I believe in what God has sent down in His Book." He said that, then recited this verse: ﴿يَوْمَ تَجِدُ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما عَمِلَتْ مِن خَيْرٍ مُحْضَرًا وما عَمِلَتْ مِن سُوءٍ تَوَدُّ لَوْ أنَّ بَيْنَها وبَيْنَهُ أمَدًا بَعِيدًا﴾ ("On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it will wish that between it and that were a long distance"). It seems he thought that what he recited contradicts what they claimed of wishing. It is possible to say that what that verse indicates occurs before becoming aware of the replacement. And God knows best.

﴿وكانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا رَحِيمًا﴾ ("And God is ever Forgiving, Merciful") is a concluding parenthetical clause (*iʿtirāḍ tadhyīlī*) that confirms the content of what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 71:

﴿And whoever repents﴾, i.e., from the sins he committed, by abandoning them entirely and feeling remorse for them, ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ by which he makes up for what he neglected. Or: whoever departs from the category of sins altogether (even if he has not committed them) and enters into acts of obedience, ﴿then indeed he turns back to Allah﴾, i.e., he returns to Him, glorified is He, by that, ﴿a turning back﴾, i.e., a return of great standing, pleasing in His sight, exalted, erasing punishment, securing reward. Or: ﴿then indeed he turns back to Allah﴾ the Exalted, Possessor of wide kindness, who loves those who repent and shows favor to them. Or: ﴿then indeed he returns to Allah﴾ the Exalted, or to His reward, glorified is He, a good return. Whichever of these is meant, the condition and the consequent are distinct, and this is to explain the state of one who repents from all sins, whereas what preceded explains the one who repents from their chief sins; so it is a generalization after a specification.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 72:

﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood﴾ That is, they do not give false testimony, as has been related from ʿAlī (may Allah ennoble his face) and al-Bāqir (may Allah be pleased with him). Thus it is from shahādah (testimony). And al-zūr (falsehood) is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or by removal of the preposition, meaning: the testimony of falsehood, or with falsehood. It is understood from the words of Qatādah that shahādah here has a meaning that encompasses what is commonly known by it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from him (Qatādah) that he said: That is, they do not assist the people of falsehood in their falsehood, nor do they give them hope in it.

A group transmitted from Mujāhid that al-zūr means singing (ghinā'). A similar report has come from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah (may Allah be pleased with him). Al-Ḥasan added wailing over the dead (niyāḥah) to it. From Qatādah it is said that it is lying (al-kadhib). From ʿIkrimah it is said that it is a game that was in the pre-Islamic era (jāhiliyyah). From Ibn ʿAbbās it is said that it is an idol around which they used to play for seven days; and in another report from him, that it is the festival of the polytheists. This was also related from al-Ḥasan al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and from this (sense) it is said that it is shirk (polytheism). So they witness these sayings of testimony in the sense of presence (ḥuḍūr), and al-zūr is a direct object with an elided noun, meaning: the places of falsehood. It is also permitted that al-zūr be understood in a sense that encompasses everything false that deviates from the truth: shirk, lying, singing, wailing and the like. It is as if it were said: they do not attend gatherings of falsehood, because attending them implies approval of it. Also: "Whoever hovers around the sanctuary is about to fall into it."

﴿And when they pass﴾ by chance ﴿by vain talk﴾ by what should be discarded and cast aside, of that which contains no good, ﴿they pass by with dignity﴾ that is, they keep themselves honorable, avoiding stopping at it, engaging in it, and turning away from it.

Al-Ḥasan interpreted al-laghw (vain talk), as Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from him, as sins. He and Ibn ʿAsākir transmitted from Ibrāhīm ibn Maysarah who said: It reached me that Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by a place of amusement, turning away without stopping. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ibn Masʿūd has become honorable in the morning and in the evening." Then Ibrāhīm recited: ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of al-laghw is harmful false speech directed at them, or what includes it, and harmful action; and by dignity (karam) is meant pardon and forgiveness toward those who harm them. This is indicated by what a group transmitted from Mujāhid, who said regarding the verse: when they are harmed, they forgive. On this view the sentence has an elided noun, meaning: when they pass by the people of vain talk, they turn away from them, as it has been said:

*"I pass by the base one who reviles me, so I go on, then I say: he does not concern me."*

It is not hidden that this is not necessary.

It has also been said that al-laghw is indecent speech, and their passing by it means coming upon its mention, and their dignity means refraining from it and turning to allusion (kināyah). This is hinted at by what a group transmitted from Mujāhid also, who said regarding it: when they came upon the mention of intercourse, they alluded to it. Some generalized and made what was mentioned an example. It is also permitted that al-laghw be understood as al-zūr in its general sense, namely false matter; it was expressed sometimes by al-zūr because it deviates from the direction of truth, and sometimes by al-laghw because it is its nature to be discarded and cast aside. So in the sentence the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, and the meaning is: those who do not attend falsehood, and when they pass by it by chance, they turn away from it.

﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord﴾ — the Qur'anic verses that contain admonitions and rulings —

Page 52

﴿do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾. That is: they fall upon them while hearing with attentive ears and seeing with watchful eyes. The negation is directed at the qualifier, according to what is most common in the Arabic language. The expression used here, rather than saying "they fall upon them hearing and seeing" or something similar, contains an allusion to the condition of the disbelievers and hypocrites when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord. "Khurur" means falling down without order or arrangement, and the use of this word conveys an exaggeration of the effect of the reminder upon them. It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾ refers to the sins indicated by al-laghw (idle talk), and the meaning is: when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, which include the prohibition of sins and the warning to those who commit them, they do not commit them, and they are not like one who neither hears nor sees. But this is, as you see, far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 74:

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring comfort of the eyes,"﴾ meaning: through their being granted success in obedience, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Mujahid. For when the sincere believer sees his family sharing with him in obedience, his eye is comforted by them and his heart is gladdened, and he anticipates their benefit to him in this world, both while living and after death, and their joining him in the Hereafter. It is also mentioned that at the beginning of Islam, a father or son would be guided while the other was a disbeliever, or a husband or wife while the other was a disbeliever, and the life of that guided person would not be pleasant. So he would supplicate with what has been mentioned. And from Ibn 'Abbas: the comfort of a father's eye through his son is that he sees him writing down jurisprudence (fiqh). The "min" (from) is for the starting point (ibtida'iyya) and is connected to "hab" (grant), meaning: grant us from their direction.

It is also permitted that it be explanatory (bayaniyya), as if it were said: "Grant us comfort of the eyes," and then the comfort is clarified and explained by His words, glorified is He: ﴿from our spouses and our offspring﴾. This is based on "min" coming for explanation, and on the permissibility of the explained (mubayyan) preceding the explainer (mubayyin). The "comfort of the eye" is a metonymy (kinaya) for joy and delight, and it is derived from "qarr", which means coldness, because tears of joy are cold. For this reason, its opposite is expressed as: "God make his eye hot" (asKhana Allahu 'aynahu). On this is the verse of Abu Tammam:

"As for the eyes of the lovers, they were made hot,
and as for the eyes of the gloaters, they were cooled."

It is also said that it is derived from "qarar" (settling), because what delights makes the gaze settle upon it and not look at anything else. It is also said regarding the opposite: "God make his eye hot," in the sense of making him fearful and watchful of what will grieve him, looking right, left, forward and behind, not knowing from where that will come to him, such that his eye becomes hot due to the excessive movement which produces heat. But this involves strain.

It is also said that "a'yun" (eyes) is indefinite, although what is meant by it is the eyes of those who speak, and they are definite; the purpose of indefiniteness of the annexed noun is for glorification, and this does not occur without indefiniteness of the noun annexed to it. And the plural used is the plural of paucity (jam' al-qilla), according to what al-Zamakhshari said, because the eyes of the righteous are few in comparison to the eyes of others.

Abu Hayyan and Ibn al-Munayyir objected to this, saying that although the righteous are few in comparison to others, they are in themselves in great number, and the criterion for the use of the plural of paucity is that the plurality be few in itself, not in comparison to something else. It was answered that what is meant is that the said plural was used in the meaning of paucity, stripped of numerical specificity, by the indication of the great number of those who speak and of their eyes. Ibn al-Munayyir inferred that this is because what is related is the speech of each one of the righteous; so it is as if it were said: each one of them says, "Grant us from our spouses and our offspring comfort of the eyes." So reflect and consider the reason for choosing this plural in other places where what they mentioned here cannot apply.

I myself think that "a'yun" was chosen as the plural of the seeing eye (al-'ayn al-basira), and "'uyun" as the plural of the flowing spring ('ayn al-jariya), throughout the Noble Qur'an. A certain thought occurs to me regarding the reason for this, which I do not consider sound, and perhaps you will attain what will make you independent of mentioning it. And God, exalted is He, is the Giver of success.

Talha, Abu 'Amr, and the people of Kufa other than Hafs recited "wa-dhurriyyatina" in the singular. 'Abd Allah, Abu al-Darda', and Abu Hurayra recited "qurrat" in the plural. ﴿And make us leaders for the righteous﴾, meaning: make us such that they follow us in establishing the rites of religion, through the bestowal of knowledge and the granting of success in action. "Imam" is used both as singular and plural, like "hijan." The meaning intended here is the plural, so that it agrees with the first object of "ja'ala" (make). It was chosen over "a'imma" because it is more fitting with the preceding and following verse endings (fawasil). It is also said that it is singular, and it was used in the singular despite the requirement of agreement, because it is a generic noun (ism jins), so it is permissible to apply it to the meaning of the plural figuratively by stripping it of the restriction of unity; or because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), and that, by being designated for the quiddity, includes the few and the many by its original designation, so when it is transferred to other meanings, its origin is sometimes observed; or because the intended meaning is: "make [each one] of us" leader; or because they are like one soul, due to the unity of their path and the agreement of their word.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, after quoting what has been mentioned, it says: the basis of the explanation is that this supplication issued from all of them together in the manner of companionship, which does not occur; or from each one of them, which is not established. So the apparent meaning is that each one of them issued the words: "And make me a leader for the righteous." Thus they are expressed in the plural form for brevity, and "imaman" is kept in its own form.

It was objected that this contains strain and forced interpretation, along with its contradiction of Arabic usage, and that the explanation does not rest on that; rather, they shared in the narration with one wording because what issued from them was one, and the second option may be chosen, because sharing in the supplication is more likely to bring about its acceptance. So understand this and do not be heedless.

It is related from Mujahid that "imaman" is the plural of "amm," meaning intending, like "siyam" as the plural of "sa'im." The meaning is: make us those who intend the righteous, following them. What was mentioned first is closer, as is not hidden. And there is nothing in that, as al-Nakha'i said, indicating a seeking of leadership; rather, it is merely that they be exemplars in religion and scholars who act upon their knowledge. It was also said: the verse contains an indication that leadership in religion is among the things that should be sought. The repetition of the relative pronoun in the seven positions, although mention of the predicates by way of coordination with the predicate of the first relative pronoun would have sufficed, is to indicate that each of the things mentioned within the scope of the predicates of the aforementioned relative pronouns is a noble attribute in its own right, having a grave station, deserving of being singled out for an independent subject, and that none of it be made a complement of something else. And the placement of the conjunction between the relative pronouns is to treat the difference in designation as if it were a difference in essence, as you have understood in what preceded on more than one occasion.

[p. 53]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 75:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those who possess the qualities described in the relative clauses (al-sila), insofar as they possess them. It indicates that they are distinguished and placed, by means of these qualities, in the row of the visible matters (al-umur al-mushahada). The sense of distance (al-bu'd) contained in it serves to announce the distance of their rank in excellence. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is the clause of His, exalted be He: ﴿they will be rewarded with the lofty chamber (al-ghurfa)﴾. According to the closer view, the clause is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) with no place in i'rab (grammatical case), explaining what they have in the Hereafter of everlasting happiness after explaining what they have in this world of excellent deeds. Al-ghurfa is the high degree among dwellings, and every elevated, lofty building. It has been explained here, according to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, as houses of emerald, pearl, and ruby.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported in (Nawadir al-Usul) from Sahl ibn Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "In it are houses of red ruby, or green emerald, or white pearl, with no break (fasm) or flaw (wasm) in them."

It has been said: it is the highest of the dwellings of Paradise, and the report does not contradict this, since it is possible that the chambers described in it are there. It is reported from al-Dahhak that it is Paradise itself. It has also been said: the seventh heaven. On the explanation of it as a plural — and His saying, exalted be He, ﴿and they will be secure in the chambers (al-ghurufat)﴾ supports it, and it was read in it: (fi al-ghurfa) — the intended meaning is the genus, which is applied to the plural, as you have heard just now. The choice of the plural there — according to what al-Tibi said — is because they are ordered upon faith and righteous deeds, and there is no concealment in the variation of people in these two, and upon that the rewards vary. Here, it is ordered upon the totality of the complete qualities, therefore the singular was used, indicating that the chambers do not vary.

﴿Because they endured﴾, i.e., by means of their patience. The ba' is causal (sababiyya) and ma is verbal-masdariyya (the verbal noun). It has also been said: the ba' is for substitution (badal), as in his saying:

So would that I had among them a people who, when they mount, launch the raid, as horsemen and as riders.

i.e., in place of their patience. The object of the patience is not mentioned, so that it may encompass what preceded of their worship, in action and in abstention, and other kinds of worship; all of it is incorporated in it, for it is either concerning the sins, or concerning the acts of obedience, or concerning God, blessed and exalted be He, and this is higher than both. From this is known the reason for choosing (sabaru) over (fa'alu).

﴿And they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾, i.e., the angels — peace be upon them — will greet them and invoke for them long life and safety from calamities; or some of them will greet others and invoke that for them. The intended purpose of the supplication with it is honor, the casting of joy, and companionship; otherwise, it is already realized for them, and they are given permanence and immortality together with safety from every calamity, so there is no supplication at all there.

Talha, Muhammad al-Yamani, and the people of Kufa other than Hafs read (yalqawna) with a fathah on the ya', sukun on the lam, and a light qaf.

(Verse 25:76) ﴿Abiding therein forever.﴾ They neither die nor leave it. This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back either to the pronoun in (yujzawna, "they will be recompensed") or to the pronoun in (yulaqqawna, "they will be met").

﴿How good it is as a place of settling and dwelling.﴾ It corresponds in meaning to "how evil it is as a place of settling" (in the previous verse), and is similar to it in its grammatical construction (iʿrāb). So reflect upon this and do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 77 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say﴾ is a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to make clear to the people that those who achieve this magnificent blessing, for which competitors compete, have attained it only through the virtues just enumerated, and that without them they would not be regarded at all. That is: say to the people, addressing them directly, concerning what has proceeded from their kind of good and evil: ﴿My Lord would not care for you﴾, meaning: what concern would He have for you, and what regard would He hold for you, ﴿were it not for your calling (du'a')﴾, meaning your worship of Him, Exalted and Majestic, as its detail has passed. For man was created for the knowledge of Allah, Exalted, and obedience to Him, Majestic and Most High; otherwise he is no different from the beasts.

﴿Ma﴾ here includes the meaning of interrogation and is in the accusative position (maḥall al-naṣb). It is a term for the verbal noun. The root of ﴿al-ʿibʾ﴾ (concern, weight) is "weight". The literal sense of the saying "ma ʿabaʾtu bihi" (I did not regard it) is: I did not count for it any of the heavy burdens of my concern, or of what would be a burden upon me, just as you say "ma iktaraṯtu lahu" (I did not care for it), meaning: I did not prepare for it any of my calamities, or of what concerns me.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: what weight would you have with Him, Exalted, were it not for your worship? It is also permissible for ﴿ma﴾ to be negative, meaning: He does not care. In either case, the answer to ﴿lawla﴾ (were it not for) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it: were it not for your calling, He would not have counted you. This is a description of the state of the believers among those addressed.

His saying, glorified be He: ﴿So you have denied﴾ is a description of the state of the disbelievers among them. The meaning is: when I have informed you that My judgment is that I do not count My servants except for their worship, then you have opposed My judgment and have not done the deeds of those mentioned. So the ﴿fa﴾ (so) is like it in the saying of the poet:

"So we have come to Khurasan."

Denial (takdhib) is used figuratively for opposition. It has been said: the meaning is that you fell short in worship, taking it from the saying "kadhaba al-qitalu" (the fighting was not thorough) when it is not pursued with vigour. The first is preferable, though it has been said that the meaning of falling short in worship is abandoning it.

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud), Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn al-Zubayr read: ﴿So the disbelievers have denied﴾. This is according to the meaning: ﴿the disbelievers among you have denied﴾, because the address is general to both groups, as we have indicated. This is what al-Zamakhshari chose and what the author of al-Kashf (Sahib al-Kashf) found pleasing. Other than one, however, chose that it is an address to the disbelievers of Quraysh. According to some, the meaning on this reading is: ﴿My Lord would not care for you were it not for your worship of Him﴾, that is: were it not for His legislative will (al-iradah al-tashriʿiyyah) that you worship Him, He would not have cared for you and would not have created you. This contains a sense of His saying: ﴿I did not create jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾. It has also been said: the meaning is: ﴿My Lord would not care for you were it not for His calling you to monotheism through His Messenger (ﷺ)﴾, that is: were it not for His will for that.

It has also been said: the meaning is: He, glorified be He, would not mind your forgiveness were it not for your calling upon others with Him as gods; or: He would not do anything with your punishment were it not for your polytheism, as He said: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ It has also been said: the meaning is: He would not care for your punishment were it not for your calling upon Him and your humbling yourselves before Him in hardships, as He said: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah﴾, and He said: ﴿So We seized them with adversity and hardship that they might humble themselves﴾. It has been said: the meaning is: He, glorified be He, did not create you while having any need of you, except that you ask Him and He gives you, and you seek His forgiveness and He forgives you. This was related from al-Walid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him.

You know that what al-Zamakhshari preferred does not contradict the address being to Quraysh in meaning, since it was specified for them in His saying: ﴿So you have denied, and it will be an inseparable (lizam) [punishment]﴾, meaning: the consequence of the denial, or its effect, will be an inseparable matter that will befall you until it hurls you face-down into the Fire, as the ﴿fa﴾, which indicates the necessity of what follows for what precedes it, expresses. The pronoun in ﴿yakūnu﴾ (it will be) refers to the verbal noun of the preceding verb, with an implied genitive construction, or it is figurative. It was not explicitly stated for the sake of indicating the extreme clarity of the matter and the awe of its gravity, and to alert that it is something that explanation cannot encompass.

It has been said: the pronoun refers to the punishment. This was stated explicitly by the one who read ﴿the punishment will be inseparable﴾. It is sound from Ibn Masʿud that al-lizam (the inseparable) is the killing of the Day of Badr, and it was related from Ubayy, Mujahid, Qatadah and Abu Malik. Perhaps its application to that is because it was inseparable (lūzima) for the slain among them.

Ibn Jurayj read ﴿takūnu﴾ with the feminine ta', according to the meaning: ﴿the outcome will be﴾. Al-Minhal, Aban ibn Thaʿlab and Abu al-Sammal read ﴿lazāman﴾ with a fatha on the lam, as a verbal noun of "lazima": it is said: "lazima luzūman wa lizāman," like "thabata thubūtan wa thabātan." Ibn Khalawayh reported from Abu al-Sammal that he read ﴿lizām﴾ on the pattern of ḥidhām, making it a verbal noun deviated from al-lizmah, like fijār deviated from al-fijrah. And Allah the Exalted knows best this.

* * *

Among the matters of allusion (bab al-ishārah):

It was said regarding His saying: ﴿And they said: What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ that it is an indication of the deficiency of the state of those who deny the friends of Allah, the Exalted, in that they associate with them in the necessities of humanity, such as eating, drinking and the like. And they said regarding His saying: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾ that the aspect of the trial is looking at oneself and heedlessness in it of one's Lord, glorified be He. This suggests that everything other than Allah, the Exalted, is a trial from this standpoint.

Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said regarding His saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾: We made them aware of their deeds, so they looked upon them with the eye of contentment, and thus they fell from Our eyes, and We made their deeds scattered dust. Although this verse is about the disbelievers, there is a hadith that among the believers there are those whose deeds are made dust, as it includes.

Abu Nuʿaym reported in (al-Hilyah) and al-Khatib in (al-Muttafiq wa al-Muftariq), from Salim, the client of Abu Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There will certainly come on the Day of Resurrection people with good deeds like the mountains of Tihamah, until when they are brought, Allah, the Exalted, will make their deeds scattered dust, then cast them into the Fire." Salim said: "My father and mother be sacrificed for you, O Messenger of Allah, describe these people to us." He said: "They used to fast and pray and take a portion of the night, but whenever something of the unlawful was presented to them, they pounced upon it, so Allah, the Exalted, nullified their deeds."

It was mentioned regarding His saying: ﴿And the Day the wrongdoer bites his hands﴾ up to the verse that its ruling is general to every two loving friends who are in disobedience to Allah, the Exalted.

And from Malik ibn Dinar: carrying stones with the righteous is better than eating sweets with the wicked. And regarding His saying: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, it follows from this, along with their saying "every friend (wali) is upon the footing of a prophet", that every friend has an enemy who openly displays enmity toward him. This contains an indication of the evil state of one who does that toward the friends of Allah, the Exalted. For this reason it was said: their enmity is a sign of a bad end, and we seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted. And regarding His saying: ﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell﴾ there is an indication that they were turned toward the direction of nature, and therefore they were gathered upside down. And regarding His saying: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾

[Page 56]

it is general to everyone who inclines toward the desire of his own soul and follows it in what it inclines to. From here the knowers (al-ʿarifun) scrutinize closely the aims of their souls, to the extent that when they are commanded to do good they do not hasten to it, but examine what you intended by it. It is related of one of them that his soul never ceased urging him to jihad in the way of Allah, the Exalted. He was astonished at this from it, knowing that the soul commands to evil. So he looked closely, and found that it had grown weary of worship and wanted jihad, hoping to be killed so that it would be relieved of the fatigue it was in. It did not intend obedience by this, but intended to flee from itself.

It was said regarding His saying: ﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade?﴾ up to the verse, meaning: Have you not considered how He extended the shadow of the world of bodies? ﴿And had He willed, He would have made it stationary﴾ in the seclusion of nonexistence. Then We made the sun of the world of spirits an indication of the existence of that shadow, by being its mover toward its created purpose for which it exists. Thereby it is known that were it not for the spirits, bodies would not have been created. And regarding His saying: ﴿Then We drew it in to Us with an easy withdrawal﴾ there is an indication that every composite thing will dissolve into its simple elements when it attains its final perfection. In another way: the shadow is everything other than the Light of Lights, by which one is guided to its Creator, who is the sun of the world of existence. This is the condition of those who go from other than Him, glorified be He, to Him, Exalted and Majestic. And regarding His saying: ﴿Then We made﴾ there is an indication of a higher station than that, which is to be guided by Him, Exalted, to other than Him, glorified be He, as in His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for your Lord that He is witness over all things?﴾ This is the station of the truthful (al-siddiqun).

His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Then We drew it in﴾ is like His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾, and: to Allah all matters return. In another way: the shadow is the veil of distraction and heedlessness, and the sun is the sun of the manifestation of knowledge from the horizon of care at the dawn of guidance. Had He, glorified be He, willed, He would have made it permanent, never passing away. Forgetfulness is only known by recognition. And regarding His saying: ﴿Then We drew it in﴾ there is an indication that complete unveiling is achieved gradually at the end of the period of responsibility.

﴿And it is He who made the night a garment for you﴾, by which you conceal yourselves from the sight of strangers and their knowledge of your condition, of ecstasy and the pouring out of tears; ﴿and sleep a rest﴾, a repose for your bodies from the fatigue of striving; ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾, in which you disperse to seek your necessities. ﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾, meaning the winds of longing upon the hearts of the beloved, ﴿as good tidings before His mercy﴾, of manifestations and unveilings; ﴿and We send down﴾ from the sky of generosity the water of the life of knowledge (ʿirfan), ﴿that We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾, meaning dead hearts; ﴿and give drink from what We have created: cattle﴾, and they are those upon whom the attributes of animals have prevailed, whom He, glorified be He, gives drink so as to return them to the performance of acts of worship; ﴿and many people﴾, and they are those who have settled into the gardens of humanity, whom He, glorified be He, gives drink from that so as to wean them from the breasts of humanness to the spiritual drinks. ﴿And We have certainly diversified it﴾, that is, the Qur'an, which is the water of the life of hearts, among them, ﴿that they may remember﴾ by it their original homeland. ﴿But most of the people refuse except disbelief﴾ in the blessing of the Qur'an, and they did not know its value.

﴿And it is He who released the two seas﴾, the sea of the spirit and the sea of the soul. (This) which is the sea of the spirit, ﴿sweet and palatable﴾, from the praiseworthy divine attributes; (and this) which is the sea of the soul, ﴿salty and bitter﴾, from the blameworthy animal attributes. ﴿And He placed between them a barrier and an inviolable partition﴾. Thus it is forbidden for the spirit to be the source of blameworthy attributes, and for the soul to be the source of praiseworthy attributes.

It has been mentioned that the barrier is the heart. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: Two attributes clashed and met in the hearts of creatures. The hearts of the people of knowledge (ahl al-maʿrifah) are illumined with the lights of guidance, shining with the radiance of turning toward Allah. The hearts of the people of denial (ahl al-nakirah) are dark with the darknesses of opposition, turned away from the paths of success. Between them are the hearts of the common people, who have no knowledge of what comes upon them or what issues from them; there is no address with them, nor is there a response from them. It has been said: the sweet sea is an indication of the sea of the Shariʿah (sacred law), and its sweetness is because the Shariʿah is easy, with no hardship in it and no subtlety in its meanings; therefore it became the watering place of the elite and the common people alike. The salty sea is an indication of the sea of the Haqiqah (ultimate reality), and its saltiness is because the Haqiqah is difficult in its paths, such that the intellect of the traveller hardly grasps what is in it. The barrier is an indication of the Tariqah (spiritual path), for it is neither as easy as the Shariʿah nor as difficult as the Haqiqah, but is between the two.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 25, verse 77 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations (burooj)﴾. It has been said: this is an allusion to the fact that He, glorified is He, placed in the sky of the hearts the constellations of stations (manazil) and states (maqamat), and they are twelve: repentance (tawbah), asceticism (zuhd), fear (khawf), hope (raja'), reliance (tawakkul), patience (sabr), gratitude (shukr), certainty (yaqin), sincerity (ikhlas), submission (taslim), entrusting (tafwid), and contentment (ridha). They are the stations of the wandering states: the sun of manifestation (tajalli), the moon of witnessing (mushahadah), the Venus of longing (shawq), the Jupiter of love (mahabbah), the Mercury of unveilings (kushuf), the Mars of annihilation (fana'), and the Saturn of subsistence (baqa'). ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾, without pride or arrogance, because of what they have witnessed of the greatness (kibriya') and majesty (jalal) of God, exalted is His rank.

Some have mentioned that these servants treat the earth as one treats a living being and not an inanimate thing, and therefore they walk upon it gently. ﴿And when the ignorant address them﴾, who are the people of this world, ﴿they say, "Peace (salam)"﴾, meaning: a safety from God, exalted is He, from your evil. Or: when everything other than God, exalted is He, from this world and the Hereafter, and what is in them of pleasure and bliss, addresses them and presents itself to them in order to distract them from what they are in, ﴿they say, "Peace"﴾, the peace of parting and farewell. ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾, because they know that prayer is the ascension (mi'raj) of the believer, and that the night is the time of the lover's meeting with the beloved:

My day is the day of people, until, when the night appears to me, the couches stir me toward you.
I spend my day in speech and in hopes, and the night gathers me and my concern together.

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever a torment (gharam)"﴾. This is an allusion to their great fear of separation and distance from their Beloved, and that is what they meant by the punishment of Hell, not the well-known punishment, for the sincere lover finds it sweet along with union. Do you not hear what has been said:

Would that Sulayma were my bedfellow in sleep, in the Garden of Paradise, or in Hell.

﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾. This is an allusion to the fact that their emanations, according to the receptivity of the one upon whom they are poured, are not extravagant in them, by pouring out beyond need, nor do they hold back, by pouring out less than need. Or it is an allusion to the fact that when they spend their existence in the essence of God, exalted is He, and His attributes, they do not overdo the discipline to the point of destroying the body, nor do they hold back in giving up existence by leaning toward desires. ﴿And those who do not call upon another god along with God﴾, by raising their needs to other than Him. ﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden﴾ to be killed ﴿except by right﴾, meaning: except by the force of the manifestations (tajalliyat) of God, exalted is He. ﴿And do not commit adultery﴾, by dealing with the old woman of this world, and they do not obtain anything from her except by His permission, exalted is He. ﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood﴾, they do not attend gatherings of falsehood, of words and deeds. ﴿And when they pass by idle talk﴾, which is what does not bring them closer to their Beloved, ﴿they pass by with dignity﴾, turning away from it. ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾, but rather they turn to them with hearing and obedience, witnessing with the eyes of their hearts the lights of what they have been reminded of from the speech of their Lord. ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from our spouses﴾, whoever has joined in marriage with us and accompanied us, ﴿and our offspring (dhurriyyat)﴾ who have taken from us, ﴿the coolness of the eyes﴾, by being granted success in righteous deeds, ﴿and make us a leader for the God-conscious (muttaqin)﴾, and they are those who attain the two complete states of annihilation and subsistence. ﴿Those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber (ghurfah)﴾, which is the station of nearness ('indiyyah), ﴿for what they patiently endured﴾: at the beginning, patience upon the obligations of the Sharia; in the middle, patience upon observing the courtesies of the Path (tariqah); and in the end, patience upon what the Reality (haqiqah) requires.

﴿And they will be met therein with greeting (tahiyyah)﴾, which is the intimacy of secrets with the Living, the Self-Subsisting, ﴿and peace (salam)﴾, which is the soundness of hearts from the intrusion of separation. ﴿Abiding therein; excellent is it as a place of settlement and abode﴾, because it is the vision of the Truth (haqq) and the place of the pleasure of the Absolute Beloved.

We ask God, exalted is He, to bestow upon us His good pleasure, and to grant us, with abundant favours and blessings, by the sanctity of the master of His prophets and the most beloved of His beloved ones, (ﷺ), may He honour his station and exalt it.
